News.title: Girl and woman in 40s die at Mersea Island as hero teens race to save family
News.content:
Councillor praises daughter and two other teens for their 'admirable' actions

News Editor Matt Atherton is reporting from the scene.

The dad of one of the teenage heroes who rushed onto the beach to help save three lives has heaped praise on the three teenagers, all three of whom were working at the Seaview Beach Diner at the time of the incident.

Colchester City councillor for Mersea & Pyefleet Ward, Carl Powling, 55, told the Mirror: "Mersea's a tidal island, so the tide comes in once, or twice a day. If the spits were covered by water and the tide was turning to go out, [the victims] could go into deep water very, very quickly if they were to walk off the sand thinking it would go straight.

"So, if you're not particularly good swimmers, then you can get stuck. And then you get the rip tides. And there's been a lot of media coverage lately, isn't there, about the reservoirs, rivers, etc.?

"With the riptides, they can quickly pull you out, and when the tide is turning and definitely going out, you get a very, very strong undercurrent that will take you away very fast."

Mr Powling also said the teenage heroes were forced to stop people from recording the horrific incident on their phones.

He added: "The actions of the girls is actually really admirable. From the onset of the incident, where the members of public called the ambulance, emergency services, the people that went in to help try and pull people out. The fact that the three girls went out to assist.

"One of them was on the phone directing the police exactly where to come, you know, directions down to Mersea. Then the way they tried to move people back, the crowds back, the level-headedness and calmness of them, is, is actually for their age group, is, is phenomenal. They saw everything that was going on.

"They were stopping people trying to film it, keep people away. Then the RNLI, the coastguard, everyone arrived, emergency services and them. But what they did it, it's admirable for the local teenagers here to be fair."

News.title: Executed football journalist 'may have been burned alive' as mafia probe continues
News.content:
Executed football journalist 'may have been burned alive' as mafia probe continues

The charred remains of Luigi 'Luca' Esposito, a well-known sports journalist from the Salerno region of Italy, were found following a fire in a remote field

View 2 Images The charred remains of Luigi 'Luca' Esposito have been found (Image: Jam Press)

An Italian football journalist may have been burned alive, it has emerged, as an investigation continues into his brutal death.

‌



Luigi 'Luca' Esposito was reported missing on Saturday night after not returning calls from friends. Detectives now believe the attack took place before 12pm. The charred remains of his body were discovered when firefighters were called to the scene of a blaze at a remote field in Salerno, Italy on Sunday.

‌



The 53-year-old would normally have been in contact with work colleagues to discuss article headlines - but this did not happen, with his last WhatsApp login recorded at 10.47pm. Keys to the car he had been driving were found next to his body and his mobile phone was missing.

‌



It was initially reported that he had been shot dead before being set on fire. An autopsy has now been carried out but has not been able to determine whether Esposito was still alive when he was burned, giving it a 50% probability, reports Il Fatto Quotidiano.

View 2 Images Esposito was a well-known journalist (Image: Jam Press)

British Airways flight makes emergency landing after fault discovered mid-air READ MORE :

Investigators are awaiting the return of histological and toxicological tests with samples having been taken. This normally takes up to two months.

‌



The autopsy was performed by coroner Giovanni Casaburi, in the presence of Esposito's family consultant, Giuseppe Raimo.

Local media reports the corpse was so badly burned that identification was initially impossible, with investigators only able to ID the body after the set of car keys matched those belonging to Esposito.

The investigation so far has found that Esposito got to the rural location of Contrada Cioffi in the Salerno province at around 11pm in his white Lancia car, based on nearby CCTV.

‌



He then left his car and continued on foot, with the theory that he was on his way to meet somebody. The autopsy showed he suffered injuries typical of a beating including blows to his head and fractures to his pelvis, face and ribs.

Also revealed was that there were no traces of bullets in his body, contrary to initial reports suggesting he suffered gunshot wounds. It has not been ruled out that the fractures were caused by extreme heat from when he was burnt.

Prosecutors in Salerno are treating the case as a murder, with top anti-mafia chief Raffaele Cantone leading the investigation.

‌



The Salerno region, where Esposito was based and found dead, is well-known locally as a stronghold of the notorious Camorra syndicate - one of the oldest and most powerful mafia organisations in Italy.

Operating since the 19th century, the Camorra's are infamous for infiltrating almost every aspect of Campanian society, from business to football to local politics, terrorising the population through a cycle of violence, corruption and intimidation. Esposito's sister said he was a calm man with no known enemies.

While investigators continue to probe Esposito's private life for any possible motives, his professional dealings have also come under scrutiny.

‌



The victim, originally from Nocera Inferiore, was a passionate fan of Serie B side Salernitana 1919, running one of the club's most popular fan sites, working as a sports columnist for local news outlet La Città di Salerno, and appearing as a pundit on Italian broadcaster OttoChannel TV, covering Serie B sides including Avellino and Juve Stabia.

Colleagues said he was outspoken, fearless and full of contacts in the football world.

But the mystery deepened after it was revealed that Esposito told friends and family for years that he also worked a day job at the Campania Regional Environmental Protection Agency (ARPAC) - claims the agency has strenuously denied.

‌



According to Italian outlet Rai, Esposito told colleagues and friends on the day of his disappearance that he had spent the morning conducting inspections on behalf of the agency.

Following his death, ARPAC put out a statement categorically denying the journalist had ever worked for them, writing: "The person indicated does not appear to have an employment relationship with Arpac, either as an employee or as a manager."

The agency also clarified that: "There is no evidence of any professional relationship between the agency and Esposito, who appears to be completely unrelated to the Agency's activities."

Article continues below

Esposito had also claimed for years to be a member of The Order of Biologists of Campania and Molise (OBCM). But in a fresh statement following his death, OBCM President Arnolfo Petruzziello announced the journalist is not registered with the Order and has never had a professional relationship with them.

Police have not yet made any arrests and an investigation into Esposito's death is ongoing.

News.title: One of the world's most unusual beaches that tourists say 'looks like the Moon'
News.content:
One of the world's most unusual beaches that tourists say 'looks like the Moon'

This 'spectacular' beach on a beautiful European island has often been labelled as the most unusual in the world, with its otherworldly scenes compared to those found on the moon

View 4 Images This stunning beach in Europe is one of the most unusual in the world (Image: Getty Images)

One of the world's most unusual beaches is often compared to the Moon.

There are some spectacular beaches all around the world, from the sugar-white sands along Florida's Emerald Coast to the glistening turquoise waters in the Maldives encircling their signature overwater villas. Yet, there's one shore that is frequently labelled the most unusual in the world, and it's just hours from the UK.

Resembling the otherworldly scenes of the Moon rather than at a typical sandy or pebbly shore on the Med, Sarakiniko Beach is truly remarkable. Found on the beautiful Greek island of Milos, the beach is strikingly formed of bone-white volcanic rock that has been naturally carved by the Aegean Sea and northern winds.

View 4 Images Sarakiniko Beach in Greece consists of smooth, bone-white volcanic rock (Image: Getty Images)

The unique rock formations are smooth and curved, with many serving as diving boards for visitors to jump or dive into the crystal-clear turquoise waters that engulf the volcanic terrain. Cliff diving and jumping are major activities at Sarakiniko Beach, with many also swimming through its natural caves and snorkelling in its azure waters.

Visitors can also lounge on its smooth, white surface, and have often cited its outer-space characteristics. One holidaymaker shared on TripAdvisor: "You have to visit to take a swim, jump from a higher or lower rock into the sea or just take a sun-bath. Great place that looks like the moon."

A second commented: "Spectacular, a totally different place, I had never seen anything similar. Lovely. A shame that time did not accompany us because we would have loved to have had a snack and take a bath in this romantic place. It is like reaching a moonscape but with white stones."

View 4 Images There are carved out passageways and coves (Image: Getty Images)

"This place looked like we were on another planet. So beautiful and unique a beach," a third noted. While a fourth added: "Very nice beach with very clear waters. It stands out from all the beaches due to the white rocks... worth a visit."

Despite its striking scenes, visitors have been warned about the sea anemones that lurk on the rocks in the water, which can cause painful skin reactions. However, it hasn't deterred people from jumping in its pristine waters or marvelling at the moon-like scenes of this incredible shoreline in Greece.

Sarakiniko Beach is conveniently located about a 10-minute drive from the main port town of Adamas on Milos island, in the Cyclades group of the Aegean Sea. It's also easily accessible from the island's capital, Plaka, within a 10-minute drive, and just a 15-minute drive from the charming fishing village of Pollonia.

View 4 Images It's become a hotspot for cliff diving and jumping (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

The best way to reach Milos is to catch a direct flight from London to Athens, which takes less than four hours, then a quick 45-minute flight from the Greek capital to Milos. Ferries are also available from Athens to Milos, with the quickest journey around two and a half hours, although this can significantly increase depending on the weather, so a flight might be the best option.

News.title: Madeleine McCann's brother Sean reveals 'excitement' before competing in Commonwealth Games
News.content:
Madeleine McCann's brother Sean reveals 'excitement' before competing in Commonwealth Games

Sean McCann, 21, who will make his first appearance at the Commonwealth Games, was just two years old when his sister Madeleine, three, disappeared from the family's holiday apartment in Portugal in 2007

Sean McCann is ready for home Commonwealth Games 2026

Madeleine McCann's younger brother has spoken of his excitement as he prepares to represent Scotland at the Commonwealth Games. Sean McCann, 21, is due to make his first appearance at Glasgow 2026 in the pool this weekend. Madeleine disappeared from her family's holiday apartment in Praia da Luz, Portugal, at the age of three, back in 2007, and has been missing ever since. Sean was just two years old at the time.

‌



McCann is a distance freestyler and is expected to compete in the freestyle relay events at the slimmed-down Games. Madeleine vanished on May 3, 2007 and has been missing since, presumed dead. Her disappearance prompted a worldwide manhunt.

‌



View 3 Images Sean McCann is swimming for Scotland (Image: Getty Images for Commonwealth Sport)

‌



Retirement warning for millions of people relying on money from family inheritance READ MORE :

Sean has enjoyed a meteoric rise in sport in recent years and is now looking ahead to the summer. He said: “I’m very excited, it’s my first senior games so I’m just looking forward to representing Scotland and doing my absolute best,” he said in a message released by Loughborough University, where he is a student. “It’s the pinnacle really of representing Scotland at the Commonwealth Games, especially at a home Games. I’ve got lots of family up in Glasgow so that makes it even more special.

"I was there in 2014 Commonwealth Games, watching as a kid, so to make it now, twelve years later, is really a full circle moment.” He said his studies and life at Loughborough helped him flourish. “At my home club I didn’t really have anyone doing the same events as me, which meant in training you were always working by yourself," he added.

View 3 Images Kate and Gerry McCann attend a press conference for the launch of the book 'Madeleine' in 2011 (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



“But here, there’s always been people who are better than me, similar to me, so we push each other all the time. We’re all striving towards the same sort of things. You can never really slack off with the quality of athletes around you.

“You’ve got to have a strong mentality in distance swimming; I always tend to build my way into a race – that’s how I like to pace it. I’m going in as more of an underdog; I don’t feel like there’s any pressure on me. I should be able to go in and perform at my best.” McCann also spoke about what drew him to Loughborough as he balances sporting and educational priorities. “I study Chemical Engineering; I spoke to coaches in Britain, and they said ‘if you want to pursue distance swimming, this is where to go’," he added.

View 3 Images Sean McCann competing at a previous Youth Games event (Image: Facebook)

Article continues below

“Alongside that, it was number one for the degree as well, which made it the obvious choice in the end. There’s so much talent just around the campus. Wherever you go, you always see athletes around. The pool’s amazing, the gym’s amazing – it’s the place to be, and I really love training here.”

King Charles is expected to tell the audience about the importance of togetherness in his speech to open the Games tonight. KT Tunstall is headlining the show which takes place from 8pm to 10pm at Glasgow’s OVO Hydro. The 14,300-seater venue is more accustomed to hosting the world’s biggest music stars than international sporting events. Organisers describe the show as “a creative kaleidoscope and Clyde-built journey packed full of music, humour and Scottish surprise”. The King will formally declare the Games open by reading aloud the message he placed inside the King’s Baton at Buckingham Palace on Commonwealth Day, March 10 last year. It has spent the past 500 days travelling to all 74 competing nations and territories, each of which decorated its own version, before being reunited on stage during the Parade of Nations at the opening ceremony.

Web link: www.lboro.ac.uk/sport/commonwealth-games-2026/

News.title: 'Horrendous pain saw my skin change colour and go up five dress sizes'
News.content:
'Horrendous pain saw my skin change colour and go up five dress sizes'

Amandeep Kaur says she often passes out and is left drenched in sweat - but doctos have no idea why

View 4 Images Amandeep Kaur is still battling with her condition (Image: Cover Images)

A mum has battled with pain for almost a decade which is so bad, it causes her to pass out, gain weight, and her skin changes colour - and doctors still do not know what is causing it. Amandeep Kaur started experiencing the pain out of the blue in 2017 after going out for a meal with her mum and sister.

‌



The 43-year-old, from Stoke-on-Trent, continued to suffer from issues but, despite tests, doctors could not find a diagnosis, although they suspected colitis. She described it as twisting, relentless pain that leaves her overwhelmed and unable to function.

‌



As she continues to wait for answers, Amandeep said the uncertainty has affected every part of her life — from her mental health to her career and social life — and has put strain on her relationship.

‌



Amandeep, who works in safeguarding and is a mum of two, met her partner in December 2019, but said she hid the true extent of her symptoms for the first year because she felt embarrassed discussing bowel problems early on. In the days before seeing him, she would barely eat in an attempt to avoid triggering a flare-up. On dates, she would pick at her food and make excuses, telling him she was eating “clean” or had no appetite.

She said she avoided eating in front of him and often turned down invitations to go out because she was anxious about being far from a toilet. The misunderstandings led to arguments, she said, with her partner questioning whether she was depressed. At times they slept in separate rooms, which she felt made it easier to conceal what she was dealing with.

View 4 Images Amandeep is often left in agony (Image: Cover Images)

‌



"I kept it from him because it is embarrassing. You're in a new relationship and you really don't want to disclose gut issues." She avoided eating in front of her partner, worried it would trigger her symptoms, and often declined invitations to leave the house so she could stay close to a toilet.

"We ended up in arguments. He was asking me if I was depressed. Why I wouldn't leave the house. We used to end up sleeping in separate rooms, but that was good because it made it easier for me to hide the symptoms," she says.

"We weren't living together, so it was easier to hide my symptoms. But when I moved in with him, it was hard because I was constantly in the loo. It wasn't until I had an accident and he noticed that I had to tell him.”

‌



Longevity expert's five health tips for people in their 30s to do now READ MORE :

New research by Holland & Barrett suggests Amandeep is far from alone. The health retailer found that 90% of people said they would hide digestive issues from a new partner rather than speak openly about them. The same research said around a third (31%) would avoid eating on a first date to reduce the risk of digestive trouble, while 30% said they would choose date activities that don’t involve potential “tummy triggers”.

Holland & Barrett’s report on preventative health also found that more than one in five people in Britain (22%) say they struggle with gut health or digestion.

The episode that caused it in 2017 saw her skin colour change and she began to feel faint and dizzy, prompting her to head to the bathroom. She left the restaurant soon after and spent the night in agony. The next day, Amandeep collapsed at home. She said she only realised what had happened when she regained consciousness slumped over her laptop. Her sister, seeing how much pain she was in, called 999.

‌



She says she now lives with constant pain and rectal bleeding, alongside flare-ups so severe they have caused her to collapse. During the worst attacks, she says she can be drenched in sweat. Last year, she said, her sons came home to find her collapsed in the living room and her eldest had to call an ambulance.

View 4 Images Amandeep being treated by a paramedic (Image: Cover Images)

Her most recent hospital admission was in May, after 10 days of diarrhoea and vomiting. Scans showed inflammation in her intestines and lymph nodes, but she said doctors still could not tell her what was driving the illness.

‌



Amandeep said her partner’s attitude changed when he saw how serious her condition could be during a hospital admission. While he initially joked about it being “old age”, she said he has since become her biggest support, helping her through flare-ups and repeated trips to hospital.

Despite multiple scans, tests and medications, Amandeep said she remains without a diagnosis. Her next step is a colonoscopy, with an appointment scheduled for July — although she said it needs to take place while she is experiencing a flare-up so doctors can see what is happening.

She said the impact has been enormous. Struggling emotionally, she turned to food for comfort and by 2020 said she had gone from a size 10 to a size 20. She described bingeing on crisps, cakes, chocolate and toast, and ordering large takeaways — but said she still wouldn’t eat in front of her partner, instead waiting until he was asleep or at work.

‌



View 4 Images Amandeep Kaur is hoping that a change of diet will help her (Image: Cover Images)

The weight gain dented her confidence, she said, leaving her avoiding photos and feeling uncomfortable in her own body. Although she has since begun losing weight, she believes the condition has also affected her friendships.

Amandeep said she has sometimes lied about why she couldn’t attend events, and over time stopped being invited out as much. She said it was upsetting, but she could understand how it happened: "In the past I have lied to people about why I can't make events. I've definitely lost friends because of it. I don't always get invited to things anymore, which is a bit sad. But I understand why."

‌



Day-to-day life now involves constant preparation. Amandeep said she often sleeps on the sofa so she can make repeated trips to the bathroom without waking her partner. Whenever she leaves the house, she packs spare clothes, towels and wipes in case of accidents — something she said she used to do for her children when they were little, but now has to do for herself.

She also described humiliating moments that most people never see, including accidents in her car while travelling home or going to work. There have been times, she said, when she has been parked outside work, had an accident and had to call in sick.

Now she says she is determined not to let embarrassment dictate her life. She has changed her diet, including kefir and Greek yoghurt, and started using Holland & Barrett multi-seed toppings in the hope it will help ease symptoms.

‌



She has also begun rebuilding her confidence by attending Pilates classes and going to events on her own — something she says she would never have done before.

Amandeep said she is speaking out so others living with unexplained bowel problems feel less isolated. She believes there should be no stigma around digestive illness, describing it as a “hidden disability” that can be draining and life-altering. And she wants anyone going through similar experiences to know they are not alone and that support is available.

What is colitis?

Ulcerative colitis is a long-term condition where the colon and rectum become inflamed, according to the NHS. The colon is the large intestine (bowel) and the rectum is the end of the bowel where poo is stored.

‌



Small ulcers can develop on the colon's lining, and can bleed and produce pus.

Symptoms of ulcerative colitis

The main symptoms of ulcerative colitis are:

recurring diarrhoea, which may contain blood, mucus or pus

tummy pain

needing to poo frequently

Article continues below

You may also experience extreme tiredness (fatigue), loss of appetite and weight loss.

The severity of the symptoms varies, depending on how much of the rectum and colon is inflamed and how severe the inflammation is. For some people, the condition has a significant impact on their everyday lives.

News.title: 'I left neighbour polite note on car - now they're just being petty'
News.content:
'I left neighbour polite note on car - now they're just being petty'

A couple who moved to a rented property in London and made friends with their neighbours realised they weren't as cordial as they first after an issue

View Image The couple moved to London before making friends with their neighbours (stock) (Image: Sergio Amiti via Getty Images)

When you move into a new home, it can be a complete lottery as to who you end up living next to. For one couple who relocated to a rented home in London, their neighbours initially seemed friendly enough – but their true colours quickly emerged following a significant row over the driveway.

‌



The pair had settled into the area and enjoyed nothing but amicable exchanges with the husband and wife residing next door. However, one day the couple discovered their neighbour was utilising their driveway for their own car, despite not seeking permission beforehand.

‌



The frustrated neighbour turned to the R/LegalAdviceUK Reddit forum to vent about the circumstances and seek advice.

‌



They said: "I approached him and made introductions and asked that they just ask us in the future so we know who is parking in the driveway, and I let him know it was our plan to get a car and we didn't want to have a problem parking with them trying to also park in the driveway.

"He was not particularly receptive to my polite request, but I'm sure he was clear on what I was asking of him. About 45 days later, a car parks in the driveway. I didn't recognize it as the one that the neighbour had used last time, and another neighbour across the street had been having parties around the time of the World Cup, so I thought maybe the car was from their visitors.

"I put what I feel is a polite note on the car saying 'It is not very neighbourly to park in someone's driveway without permission. Please do not park in my driveway again'.

‌



"The car is gone the next day (Saturday) and then on Sunday it shows up again and the note gets put back through my mail slot on my front door - no apology or explanation - and the neighbours enter their home and don't say anything.

"Now I know the car was my neighbour's car, and I now I know that they have no intent to ask permission or to abstain from using our driveway."

‌



Upon discovering their neighbours' true intentions, the couple turned to their landlord for help in erecting signs at the property. The landlord, however, showed little interest in resolving the matter.

The man said: "My wife speaks to the wife and she said that her husband asked her to ask us if they could park there but she forgot. And then she saw our note and thought that it was a rude way for us to handle the situation.

"Now they have parked that car, which I believe is borrowed, in our driveway everyday since then which has been 11 days.

‌



"Our landlord has not committed to the signage and thinks that it should be up to us to sort out with the neighbour. The council's advice department suggested that if the landlord was not receptive to resolving the problem that we should contact a solicitor, which seems extreme."

What are my legal rights if somebody parks on my driveway?

According to The RAC, while there is no criminal law against the indecent act of someone parking on your driveway without your consent, your driveway forms part of your property, meaning that by driving onto it the person is committing an act of trespassing. Trespassing, however, is classed as a civil offence not a criminal offence, meaning the police don't have the power to make an arrest.

If the offence is committed on a public highway or the car is blocking the driveway while parked on a public road, the council has the power to act.

‌



However, when a car is situated on a driveway, it is technically on private property – and the council has no authority to remove it. The only remaining avenue is to pursue a civil trespassing case, as the courts do hold the authority to order the vehicle's removal from the driveway.

A solicitor could obtain the civil court's permission to establish the legal owner of the vehicle in question, and a judge would need to issue a formal court order for its removal.

An alternative option is to bring a legal claim for nuisance on the basis that the driver is disrupting your use and enjoyment of your property. Be warned, though – going through the courts can be a lengthy and potentially expensive process if you don't have legal expenses insurance.

Article continues below

Another solution, which is not recommended by police, is to engage a private tow truck to remove the vehicle. Should the car sustain any damage, you could be held liable for the repair costs.

The Ask The Police website says: "Don't damage/clamp the vehicle or have it removed by a third party for destruction or storage without first seeking legal advice. If you do any of these things, you may commit a criminal offence or the owner may pursue a civil action against you.

"Under no circumstances would we advocate you merely pushing the vehicle on to a road and leaving it there as you may commit a number of offences."

News.title: West Mersea beach tragedy as woman and girl die despite heroic actions of local teens
News.content:
West Mersea beach tragedy as woman and girl die despite heroic actions of local teens

Essex Police confirmed that a woman in her 40s and a teenage girl died after a group of people got into difficulty in the water at West Mersea Beach with three others taken to hospital

View 7 Images Emergency services were called to West Mersea Beach after a group of people got into difficulty in the water (Image: Daniel Rees/Newsquest/SWNS)

A woman in her 40s and a teenage girl have died after getting into difficulty at a beach in Essex despite the heroic efforts of three young café workers.

‌



Emergency services were called to West Mesea Beach, Mesea Island, just before 5.30pm last night with reports that several people had got into difficulty in the water. Ambulance crews, police, an air ambulance and the coast guard were all called to the scene, but despite their best efforts, the woman and teen girl were pronounced dead.

‌



A third person was taken to hospital in a serious condition, where they remain according to Essex Police, and two others are in hospital with non life-threatening injuries. An investigation has been launched with police believing that those involved knew each other.

‌



Three young workers at a nearby café, described as heroes, rushed out to help the group after they got into difficulty in a "riptide", the Mirror learned. The teens, who work at the Seaview Beach Café, were among the first on the scene after hearing a commotion outside.

View 7 Images Workers at the Seaview Beach Café raced out to try and help those in trouble (Image: Matt Atterton)

Leonie Powling, 19, was one of those workers who dropped everything to help. She told the Mirror: " We had someone run to the café saying they needed help, so we all stopped what we were doing and ran to the beach. We saw some people on the beach, and there were still some casualties in the water.

‌



"We started running around, trying to find anyone with a kayak or a paddleboard. We couldn't just run into the water because there was a riptide, and everyone would've just been sucked in. We were sat with a casualty making sure she was okay. There was another casualty we got out of the water, who was struggling to breathe at that point.

"One of the workers went up to her, patted her on the back and said: 'You need to make yourself throw up.' After that, the RNLI got into the water and got the other casualties out. The ambulance and the police turned up and we were all leading them to where the casualties were.

"I'm feeling fine now, to be fair, but it's not good to know people have died. But it's good to know that some of them survived. That's the best thing about it. We got some people out, safe and okay. One is in serious condition, but will hopefully get better. With the other two, we're just thinking about the family. It's heartbreaking."

‌



View 7 Images The tragedy unfolded on West Mersea Beach in Essex (Image: Matt Atterton)

Melanie Shuker, 64, is the owner of the Seaview Beach Diner, her great niece Leonie was among those who rushed to help. She said: "It was my day off and I heard all the emergency services coming down to the beach area. I had a phone call from Melissa - my colleague - and one of her daughters was working here, as was my great niece.

‌



"I drove straight away down here. The girls had heard shouting on the beach, people shouting 'help me, help me', because it was very close to the beach. Then two girls ran into the café quite hysterical and asked for help, if anybody could help them. All of the girls - who were aged from 16 to 19 - all of them went to the water's edge where a man had pulled, I believe five people from the water.

"One of the girls that worked here called emergency services and pinpointed the exact location to emergency services. Between the girls they took one of them over, banged them on the back till they brought up seaweed and stuff like that, so it was quite traumatising for them. I'm proud of them all to just cope with it - it's the first time they've had to deal with something like that."

Detective Chief Inspector Al Pitcher of Essex Police said: "Today, our thoughts remain with the family members who are coming to terms with their loss. We are grateful to the people who have already spoken to us and helped with our enquiries. We would ask anyone who was at the beach at the time, and who has not yet spoken with officers, to please get in touch, to help us understand what happened."

‌



Anyone who was in the area at the time and has information or footage which may help police is asked to contact the force on 101, quoting in cident 1090.

View 7 Images Those involved in the tragedy are believed to be known to each other, according to police (Image: Matt Atterton)

Kiera French, 18, was working at the Seaview Beach Diner when the tragedy unfolded. She said someone ran in shouting for help, telling the Mirror: "Some people got into trouble in the water - quite a few of them. There was obviously quite a lot of panic on the beach.

‌



"Someone was screaming for help, I guess because he couldn't swim. Two young girls came over to the café asking for a life buoy. I pointed them in the direction of one, then got straight on the phone to 999. I stayed on the phone to 999, and then when they arrived they took over. I just think they didn't know about the tides and got caught out. It's just unfortunate they didn't know how strong the tide was."

It’s not the first time a tragic incident has unfolded on this stretch of the beach, which has a perilous hidden drop between sandbanks that can become “deadly” at high tide to those unfamiliar with the area. In June 2023, 30-year-old David Cole died after bravely rescuing his three-year-old son from a riptide off West Mersea Beach. Locals have long campaigned for better signage, life rings and life guards along the shore on West Mersea beach.

View 7 Images The teens working at the café have been praised for their actions and calm demeanour during the incident (Image: Matt Atterton)

‌



Melissa French, who works at the café, told the Mirror: "It was a tragedy waiting to happen. With one lifebuoy, one life ring, that's not really adequate; there should be them all the way along the beach." She added: “The sea was a little bit choppy last night, but on the previous occasion three years ago when the man died, it was like a millpond, it was like glass, the water. So it's not a strong current, it's not that they shouldn't have gone in... It's just if you don't know the water. If you step down, all of a sudden you're from standing on a sandbank you're up to your waist in water."

The dad of one of the teenage heroes who rushed onto the beach to help save three lives heaped praise on his daughter. Colchester City councillor for Mersea & Pyefleet Ward, Carl Powling, 55, said he's proud of all three staff at the Seaview Beach Diner who were called into action. He also said the victims were likely caught unawares about how the sand spits suddenly change direction under water.

He told the Mirror: "Mersea's a tidal island, so the tide comes in once, or twice a day. If the spits were covered by water and the tide was turning to go out, [the victims] could go into deep water very, very quickly if they were to walk off the sand thinking it would go straight. So, if you're not particularly good swimmers, then you can get stuck. And then you get the rip tides. And there's been a lot of media coverage lately, isn't there, about the reservoirs, rivers, etc.? With the rip tides, they can quickly pull you out, and when the tide is turning and definitely going out, you get a very, very strong undercurrent that will take you away very fast."

‌



Mr Powling also said the teenage heroes were forced to stop people from recording the horrific incident on their phones. He added: "The actions of the girls is actually really admirable. From the onset of the incident, where the members of public called the ambulance, emergency services, the people that went in to help try and pull people out. The fact that the three girls went out to assist.

View 7 Images East Anglian Air Ambulance said it had sent a helicopter to West Mersea (Image: Daniel Rees/Newsquest/SWNS)

"One of them was on the phone directing the police exactly where to come, you know, directions down to Mersea. Then the way they tried to move people back, the crowds back, the level-headedness and calmness of them, is, is actually for their age group, is, is phenomenal. They saw everything that was going on. They were stopping people trying to film it, keep people away. Then the RNLI, the coastguard, everyone arrived, emergency services and them. But what they did it, it's admirable for, for the, for the local teenagers here to be fair."

‌



A spokesperson for the East Anglian Air Ambulance service confirmed it sent a helicopter to West Mersea yesterday evening as part of the emergency response. A spokesperson for the East of England Ambulance Service confirmed that two people died at the scene, one person was taken to hospital by air ambulance and three were taken by road ambulance.

The spokesperson said: "Following reports of multiple people in distress in the water at Sea View Holiday Park, West Mersea, we dispatched multiple resources including our Hazardous Area Response Team, critical care paramedics and two air ambulances. Sadly, despite best efforts, two patients could not be resuscitated. One patient was transported by air to hospital, and a further three patients were transported by road to hospital."

Local residents and witnesses described the tragedy as a "nightmare". Rita Coombs, who lives in West Mersea, said she saw emergency services helping a group of people on the beach. She told the BBC: " It was absolutely horrific. I can't praise the emergency services [enough]. It was beyond all belief - they worked so hard. She said she tried to support emergency services during the "nightmare that was unfolding."

‌



"The feeling was we just wanted to go out and help. Our hearts were going out to those people fighting for their lives," she added. "It's a very sad island at the moment. We're just sending our thoughts to the people that have passed and the people left behind. It's tragic, absolutely tragic."

Beach hut owner Beverly Smit, 60, from West Mersea, said she heard the emergency response and went to see what was going on. She said: "By the time they were re-sussing the person on the beach, the helicopters were still in the fields."

She said she spoke to a day tripper who had rented a neighbouring beach hut and tried to help. Ms Smit, who works for a local dentist, said: "He saw and they were calling for help and the children and adults were out there. He swam out I think three times. Two of the children he brought back were not in good condition. It's not an easy swim when the tide's coming in, you're swimming against the tide, the water yesterday was particularly cold."

‌



Ms Smit said she and members of her local rowing club have helped save people in the sea previously. She described the incident as a "massive scale of rescue and tragedy really." One woman, who did not give her name, said the incident happened at high tide. She said: "The tide was a lot further in than it is now, and that sandbank, they were on there and the tide came in. It comes in very quickly and you have to be careful."

Speaking as she sat at a beach hut, the woman said there was "quite a commotion" and "just total panic". Discussing the aftermath of the incident, she said there was a "helicopter coming in, the helicopter circling and sirens going everywhere."

The eyewitness added: "That was quite alarming, for a small place like this, I think that's why so many people are shocked. I mean the beach was packed with people, they were coming down to see what was going on."

‌



She said the emergency services" worked diligently" and described the incident as "absolutely tragic."

View 7 Images The Mirror is calling for urgent action to tackle water safety

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organsations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

‌



The campaign is calling for:

* The Government to launch an urgent public awareness campaign ahead of the summer holidays which targets parents and children on TikTok and other social media platforms. This should include lifesaving techniques and advice such as avoid diving into the water and information on cold water shock.

* Water companies and those in control of high risk large water bodies, to ‘do the right thing’ by bringing in the correct safety equipment.

‌



* Compulsory lessons in schools (ahead of the holidays) on how to survive if you get into difficulty in the water, which should include the Water Safety Code, the RNLI ‘Float to Live’ campaign, and Phone-Float-Throw bystander advice.

* Put in place ‘Sam’s Law’. We urge the Government to make it law that safety equipment should be installed around high risk large bodies of water and make damaging this safety equipment an aggravated criminal offence to damage or steal this safety equipment. Currently it is already a criminal offence under theft or criminal damage but the penalties are low for these very minor offences.

* And finally the appointment of a Minister for Water Safety, as they have in Wales and Scotland, as drowning must be accepted as a preventable public health issue.

News.title: Should Andy Burnham introduce a wealth tax? Take our poll and have your say
News.content:
Should Andy Burnham introduce a wealth tax? Take our poll and have your say

The new PM Andy Burnham has previously suggested he backed a wealth tax, and recently claimed his government may have 'to ask for a little more' from the richest

View Image Andy Burnham has previously suggested he backed a wealth tax (Image: PA)

More than 100 UK-based millionaires - including former Match of the Day presenter Gary Lineker - have signed a letter urging new Prime Minister Andy Burnham to tax their wealth.

‌



Organised by the group Patriotic Millionaires UK, the letter called for higher taxes not on everyday workers, but on the very richest in the UK.

‌



Mr Burnham has previously suggested he backed a wealth tax, and recently claimed his government may have “to ask for a little more” from the richest.

‌



Patriotic Millionaires, along with the group Tax Justice UK are proposing an annual 2% tax on wealth above £10million. Tax Justice UK says it would affect around 20,000 people in the UK – fewer than 0.04% of the population.

‌



Gary Lineker among 120 millionaires urging new PM to make them pay more tax READ MORE :

Former Match of the Day presenter Lineker, who added his name to the letter of 120 millionaires, said: “Our fantastic country deserves all of us to get behind it. I’m proud to stand with people across the UK who want to live in a more equal society.”

He added: “Paying your fair share is a basic British value, but so many ordinary people are already paying more than they can afford. Our richest people can do more and most want to. To live up to our national values our new government must raise taxes on extreme levels of wealth for a fairer, better, more hopeful Britain.”

Before entering No10 earlier this week, Mr Burnham did not rule out a wealth tax in an interview with the former Spurs star. The new Labour leader said: “I’m not going rule things out right now. I do believe we need a greater sense of fairness and people feeling that things are being done in the right way and a fair way.

Article continues below

“But at the same time, you know, I don’t want to sort of be perceived as somebody who’s coming in with grudges and agendas and, you know, going to just immediately find or demonise one group or create a new way of dividing people.”

Wes Streeting, who was appointed Defence Secretary earlier this week, called for this measure when he quit Keir Starmer’s Cabinet in May, saying it was a “wealth tax that works”.

News.title: Police missed chance to examine Manchester synagogue attacker's phone before attack
News.content:
A police chief has apologised after admitting phones were seized from the Manchester synagogue attacker months before the car and knife assault but they were not examined.

Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, was on bail for an alleged rape when he carried out the attack on Heaton Park Synagogue in Crumpsall on 2 October 2025, in which two Jewish men were killed.

His devices, which contained evidence of his extreme views, were seized after he was arrested in February and September but not analysed.

Greater Manchester Police Chief Constable Sir Stephen Watson said he was "deeply sorry", conceding that "the information contained within these devices would have inspired further investigative action".

Sir Stephen said: "In conducting an internal review, it became apparent that GMP had seized Al-Shamie's mobile devices, at the point of each arrest.

"The significance of the data contents of these devices was substantial in respect of evidencing an extremist mindset.

"I am disappointed at the prospect of adding to the distress of all of those affected by the terrible events last October.

"For this, I am deeply sorry."

The apology came after the sentencing of Mohammad Bashir, who plotted a separate attack on the UK's Defence Academy in Shrivenham with Al-Shamie.

Details emerged in the case at Manchester Crown Court that the pair had been discussing their extremist views in WhatsApp chats, including preparing for a "war".

Meanwhile, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) confirmed it was investigating "all previous contact between Greater Manchester Police and Jihad Al-Shamie prior to the terror attack on 2 October 2025".

A spokesperson for the police watchdog said this included the actions taken by police in response to reports of crimes committed by him.

One officer is under investigation by the IOPC for potential misconduct in relation to their handling of allegations of rape and other sexual offences against Al-Shamie.

"This does not necessarily mean that disciplinary proceedings will follow. This decision will be made on conclusion of the investigation," the spokesperson said.

News.title: Police officer was violent rapist who attacked women over 14 years, BBC reveals
News.content:
A police officer who took his own life in May was a violent rapist who carried out a spate of sexual attacks and attempted murders of women over at least 14 years, the BBC can reveal.

PC Alan Greer's first known victim was a woman he raped in her home in Glasgow in 2012 after she had called the police to report being the victim of a crime.

The woman reported the sex attack by Greer late last year, sparking one of Police Scotland's biggest ever anti-corruption inquiries.

Detectives have so far uncovered a further eight victims, five of whom were sex workers, attacked while Greer was off duty.

It has emerged that Greer used hundreds of prostitutes throughout his police career, and it is anticipated more victims of his violence will be identified.

Assistant Chief Constable Lynn Ratcliff, gold commander for the investigation, said what the inquiry had found was "truly shocking".

She said: "This officer has clearly abused his power and has revisited someone that he's encountered in the course of his duties.

"But this victim was brave enough to come and speak to us, and that really was the trigger point for us starting our investigation.

"That's allowed us to proactively identify eight further victims."

News.title: 'What was their crime?': BBC visits Iran school where strike killed 120 children
News.content:
The school day had begun as usual, Amaineh says.

Because it was the Islamic holy month of Ramadan, the children gathered inside the prayer hall to recite the Quran, she recalls, before she began teaching her pupils a new letter of the Persian alphabet.

But, as the first attacks of the war unfolded across Iran, she says the headteacher announced the school would be closing, and teachers began contacting parents, urging them to collect their children.

Only five of Amaineh's 15 first-grade pupils were left in her classroom on the upper floor, she says, when she first heard an explosion not far from the school. She says she was in the corridor and rushed back for the children.

"Just as I went to leave, a missile struck the school," says Amaineh. "Something hit my head and my students' heads - we were all sent flying."

Then, she says, thick black smoke filled the classroom: "I couldn't even see the pupils I was holding in my arms. We couldn't breathe."

She says she remembers hearing another explosion, as well as the sounds of screaming, children crying and then the school itself collapsing â "destroyed all at once".

"Blood was pouring from me and the students," she adds.

News.title: Gary Lineker among millionaires asking Andy Burnham to tax them more
News.content:
Millionaires including former footballer Gary Lineker and music producer Brian Eno have written to new prime minister Andy Burnham asking to be taxed more.

In an open letter, 120 well-off Britons told Burnham: "We can afford it. We're not talking about higher taxes on those who get up and go to work for their income every day, but on the very richest whose income is derived from the wealth they hold."

Organised by Patriotic Millionaires, the letter said it would lead to a more equal society, and urged a "devolution of wealth and power from the very richest".

People can already give money or stocks voluntarily to the Treasury using a donation facility.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Lineker is "very welcome to pay more tax he can write a cheque to the Treasury, no one is stopping him."

Patriotic Millionaires support a 2% tax on wealth over Â£10m.

"Millionaires are a patriotic bunch," the letter states. "We love this country and we want it to succeed.

"But success requires investment and a primary source of untouched capital investment is sitting with us, in untaxed potential."

Other signatories include Richard Curtis, director of Notting Hill and Ian Gregg, the former managing director of Greggs and son of the bakery chain's founder. Scottish crime writer Val McDermid and former financial trader turned equality campaigner Gary Stevenson also signed the letter.

Chief Secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said she would welcome UK millionaires increasing the amount of tax they pay but said any major changes would be announced during a Budget.

"I welcome the fact that people of good means are saying that they want to pay more. They can pay more," she said and pointed to the Treasury's donation link.

The renewed call for higher tax on the wealthy follows a similar campaign in previous years.

Burnham did not rule out a wealth tax when asked about it by Lineker - formerly the BBC's highest paid presenter - a few days before he became prime minister.

He suggested he may have "to ask for a little more" tax at some point.

Lineker was paid around Â£1.3m a year before he left the BBC. He is worth a reported Â£30m.

The latest call from Patriotic Millionaires said there is a "need to embrace a new kind of devolution of wealth and power, from the very richest in order to reinvest back into our greatest asset in every region".

It added that in its own poll, the majority of millionaires wanted a higher tax on themselves.

"There are a few people left with outdated economic thinking and few others desperate to hold onto every penny they can... Those that can't see past the end of their own self interest have no place in designing a Britain for the future," the letter said.

News.title: Airport drop-off fees up by a third - here are the priciest
News.content:
Drop-off fees at the UK's major airports have risen by a third on average since last summer, new analysis has found.

The RAC motoring group looked at the cost of pulling up to the closest point to terminals at the 20 busiest airports, 16 of which had put up their prices since last year.

London airport Gatwick topped the list by charging a "farewell fee" of Â£10 for 10 minutes, after lifting it by Â£3 from last year. Stansted also charges Â£10 but drivers are allowed 15 minutes at its "express set down" outside departures.

Airports UK, the trade body, said that free drop-offs were available and fees were part of airports' business models and climate change objectives.

The RAC said that the price of dropping people off in "kiss-and-fly" areas rose by an average of Â£1.70 to Â£7 compared to this time last year.

London City Airport, which only started making people pay this year, is the most expensive on a per-minute basis. Its Â£8 charge for five minutes works out at Â£1.60 per minute.

Birmingham is the cheapest, charging Â£7 for 15 minutes which equates to 47p per minute.

There have been increases in Northern Ireland too. At Belfast International Airport, it is now Â£5 for 10 minutes in the drop-off zone, up Â£2 on last year.

In contrast, none of the top 10 airports in the EU charge for drop-offs, according to RAC research.

News.title: 'Every victim will feel the same,' says mother of PC Harper over early prison release
News.content:
But, two prison staffers told the BBC that governors were told to stop work on the implementation of the Sentencing Act two weeks ago. The government maintains there has been no decision to delay its introduction.

PC Harper's mother, Debbie Adlam, said the release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers - two of the passengers in the getaway car which killed Harper - was "sprung" on her family.

Cole and Bowers - who were 17 at the time - were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter but could be released after six years under the act.

The driver of the car, Henry Long - who was 18 - was jailed for 16 years for manslaughter but would not be eligible for early release.

"It just feels like another let down for Andrew really, when you look at the horrific way he was killed, we have to live with that," she told BBC Radio 4's Today Programme.

"The feeling that Andrew hasn't been given proper justice, it is very personal obviously... every victim will be feeling the same."

The Sentencing Act is the government's attempt to find a permanent, more sustainable solution to a prison overcrowding crisis after an emergency scheme was introduced by the Labour government in 2024.

Tens of thousands of inmates have already been let out of prison early under those measures.

Unlike the 2024 plan, the new act includes no exemptions for prisoners convicted of serious crimes, domestic abuse or terrorism.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday he could not commit to changing the policy completely but would "look at it in detail before we go further forward".

He also acknowledged there was "pressure on prison places" and a failure to invest in the system created "an unacceptable situation".

Adlam said her message to Burnham was to "look at the big picture for the country".

"As a country you cannot have a justice system that works that way, just because it's full doesn't mean it's good enough to let people go, you need to find ways and I'd like to know what's being considered".

"I think the justice system has been lacking for quite some time and it needs a proper overhaul really."

Asked if the scheme will go ahead, Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds told the BBC: "That is something that he [Burnham] and the Justice Secretary will set out in the coming weeks."

News.title: Glasgow set to welcome the world for scaled back Commonwealth Games
News.content:
When the fastest man on the planet won Commonwealth relay gold for Jamaica in 2014, more than 50,000 fans cheered him home at Hampden.

But the athletes seeking to emulate Usain Bolt when the Games return to Glasgow - including mile world record holder Josh Kerr - will be competing at Scotstoun Stadium in front of 11,000 spectators.

This time round almost everything is on a smaller scale but organisers are confident fans will create a Tartan Army-style atmosphere for the 3,000 competitors who will be chasing glory.

From Friday until 2 August, 215 gold medals will be up for grabs - compared to 261 when Scotland last staged the Games - but Glasgow 2026 will see a record 47 para-sports events.

News.title: Rain to return this weekend as parts of UK on brink of drought
News.content:
If you cannot remember the last time it rained, you are probably not alone.

June was actually wetter than average in the UK, which might come as a surprise given our recent run of weather, but for England and Wales the majority of that rain came down in the first two weeks of the month.

Since 15 June, most of England has recorded less than 10mm of rain with large areas of central southern England seeing 3mm or less. Meanwhile, Wisley in Surrey has had no rain at all for 36 consecutive days.

Most of Wales has seen less than 25mm (1in) of rain since the middle of June, but it has been particularly dry in the north-east with Rhyl in Denbighshire recording only 3mm.

A Thames Water hosepipe ban came into force on Thursday, adding to other bans already in place for customers of other water companies across the south of the UK, as parts of southern, central and eastern England were declared to be close to drought.

Northern Ireland had a very wet June, recording 67% more rain than average, and it was also very wet in western Scotland. However, July has been much drier than average in Northern Ireland and most of Scotland, though the rain has continued in the Highlands, with Aultbea already reaching the July average rainfall, and with more on the way.

News.title: Friend of Manchester synagogue attacker jailed for plot on military base
News.content:
A man who planned an attack on a military base with the Manchester synagogue attacker has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 17 years.

Mohammad Bashir, 31, drove his friend Jihad Al-Shamie on a 10-hour round trip to conduct hostile reconnaissance at the UK's Defence Academy in Shrivenham, Oxfordshire, on 14 August 2025.

Weeks after that journey, Al-Shamie, 35, was shot dead by police after carrying out the Heaton Park Synagogue attack, in which two Jewish men were killed.

Bashir, from Cheetham Hill, was sentenced at Manchester Crown Court after pleading guilty to one count of preparing an act of terrorism.

Sentencing Bashir, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told him that by August last year he had become a "firmly committed jihadist".

He and Al-Shamie were "equally engaged" in planning an attack on a British military target "in which you and he expected to kill and be killed", she said.

She rejected his claim to a probation officer that he no longer held extremist views and regretted his actions.

The judge said: "I consider you remain dangerous. You have given no grounds that your attitude has really changed at all."

Following sentencing, Manchester-born Bashir, who also holds a Pakistani passport, smiled to family members in the upper public gallery of the courtroom as he walked from the dock.

News.title: 'Life-changing' MS drug to help people walk now on NHS in England
News.content:
The first drug to help people with multiple sclerosis walk is being made available on the NHS in England.

Fampridine boosts nerve signals to make it easier for some people to move and live independently.

Aysen Slack, who used to pay for fampridine privately until it became too costly, said the decision would make a "huge difference".

Up to 5,000 people in England could benefit each year. The drug is already available elsewhere in the UK.

Multiple sclerosis is caused by the immune system attacking the protective covering around nerve cells - known as myelin.

This damage impairs the ability of nerves to carry electrical messages from the brain to the rest of the body - including those needed for the precise control of muscles needed to walk.

Fampridine is known as a "signal booster" as it helps those electrical messages still get through.

Clinical trials showed around four in 10 people taking the drug had improvements in their walking speed and in how long they could walk for.

This could be the difference between getting around the house or needing help at home or enabling people to go out and see friends and family.

Current NHS support includes physiotherapy and walking aids.

The drug has previously been rejected for use by the NHS in England as it was not considered value for money, although it did become available in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

News.title: Former River City actor Iain Robertson jailed for nine years for rape
News.content:
The trial heard how Robertson, of Carbeth in Stirlingshire, raped a woman on one occasion between 2018 and 2019 as well as a separate sex assault.

The pair came to know each other from working together on River City.

The woman said she did not want anything sexual to happen, but believed Robertson did.

The relationship became intimate, but the woman later told Robertson she wanted their relationship to go back to being platonic.

She said one evening she was at his home in Glasgow's Tradeston and planned to sleep on the sofa, but Robertson allegedly told her she could join him in bed as "nothing would happen".

However, the witness said that the actor instead "had sex" with her.

She did not say anything to Robertson at the time, but said she did not participate in what happened and she did not want it to happen.

She also described an earlier incident when Robertson carried out a sex act on her and she "just waited for it to be over".

He was also found guilty of engaging in a course of abusive behaviour against her.

News.title: Animal lover run over by own car while saving cat on hill
News.content:
An animal lover was run over and killed by her own car after she got out to save a cat as the handbrake failed on a slope, an inquest has heard.

Jacqueline Davies, 75, climbed out of the driving seat of her red Ford Fiesta to move the cat to safety on 6 July while on a hill, but her car rolled forward and fatally struck her.

Gwent Coroner's Court heard Davies, from Hollybush in Cwmbran, Torfaen, was able to dial 999 after the incident, but died in hospital.

In a statement, Davies' family said she had a "strength that inspired those around her" and added they were "desperate for answers".

The inquest heard Davies was taken to University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff with serious injuries, and died the following day.

Coroner Rose Farmer said her provisional cause of death was given as a major haemorrhage, injury to the inferior vena cava - the largest vein in the body - and trauma.

Her family said: "We are heartbroken beyond words at the sudden loss of our beloved mum.

"She was a strong, independent, spirited mum who was never scared to speak her mind, and that was one of the many things we loved about her.

"She was honest, determined and full of character, with a strength that inspired those around her.

"Our family is devastated and life will never be the same without her.

"We are trying to come to terms with what has happened but we are also desperate for answers."

Gwent Police wants anyone travelling in the area of Bryn Millwr, Hollybush, on 6 July between 10:00 BST and 10:30 who may have witnessed the crash to contact officers.

The inquest into Davies' death will resume on 13 April 2027.

News.title: Woman charged with man's retirement home murder
News.content:
A woman has been charged with murdering a 77-year-old man at a supported living retirement home.

Harry Heslop died after an incident at Cedar House in Foxwood Drive, Stockton, at about 02:45 BST on Tuesday, Cleveland Police said.

Rebecca Hackett, 41 and from Stockton, has been charged with murder and possession of a bladed article and is due to appear at Teesside Magistrates' Court later.

A second woman, aged 54, remains on bail while inquiries continue, the force said.

Det Ch Insp John Bonner said the force's thoughts were "firmly with Harry's family and loved ones at what is an extremely difficult and distressing time for them".

He thanked the local community for "their patience and support" and said police would be in the area to offer reassurance.

"As a criminal investigation is ongoing, we would ask people not to speculate as this may prejudice legal proceedings," Bonner said.

Housing association Thirteen Group, which runs Cedar House, previously said it was "deeply saddened" by the incident.

News.title: Secret court documents reveal potential scale of illegal sewage spilling
News.content:
Most of the sewage spills into England's waterways in the last two years may have been illegal but gone unpunished, according to new analysis.

UK law states that raw sewage should not be released during "normal" weather conditions, yet until now the regulator has not clarified exactly what that means.

But campaigner Prof Peter Hammond obtained a definition in secret court papers, and said it shows that for more than 80% of the time sewage was being spilled, the weather was "normal", making the spills possibly illegal.

The water companies and the regulator, the Environment Agency (EA), rejected the analysis and said they were working to reduce spill numbers.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe public memorial to be held later this year, family says
News.content:
A public memorial for Ann Widdecombe will be held later this year, her family has said in a statement.

Former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman Widdecombe, 78, was found dead in her Dartmoor home with serious head injuries earlier this month.

Her family thanked the public for "the wide expression of condolences" but asked that her private service, to be held in the coming weeks and for which invitations have already been sent, is "limited to those closest to Ann".

"We understand that there is significant public interest in the funeral of Ann Widdecombe," the statement said.

"A private service for family and close friends will be held in the coming weeks, and invitations for this ceremony have been distributed.

"A more public memorial will follow later in the year, the details of which will be released in due course.

"While we are very grateful for the wide expression of condolences, the family would ask that this initial service is limited to those closest to Ann."

Tributes poured in to Widdecombe from TV stars and across the political spectrum following her death.

Anton Du Beke, who was her partner on Strictly Come Dancing in 2010, said he was devastated , which he called the "saddest of news".

"I had the most brilliant time with Ann on Strictly Come Dancing, she became a real friend, she was fun, she was upbeat, she was positive, she was supportive, she was game, wanted to enter into the spirit of the whole thing," he said in a video on X.

Kemi Badenoch, leader of the Conservative Party for which Widdecombe served as shadow home secretary from 1999 to 2001, said the party was "reeling".

She described Widdecombe as "a very fun and feisty woman who spoke her mind", while the then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer said Widdecombe was a "distinguished politician".

In a video posted on social media, Farage said Widdecombe was "an extraordinary woman" and "someone who gave her life to public service, to fighting for the things she believed in".

He described her as "a devout Christian and somebody with strong socially conservative views. Perhaps not popular in modern Britain but that is what Ann believed in".

News.title: Main ferry out of service for longer than planned
News.content:
The Isle of Man's main ferry will be out of action for longer than anticipated while "essential works" are carried out.

The island's ferry operator said "further necessary repairs" were needed after the Manxman entered drydock last week for scheduled maintenance.

The vessel has been replaced on the Douglas-Heysham route by former flagship ferry Ben-my-Chree, the Isle of Man Steam Packet Company said.

Back-up freight vessel MV Arrow is also set to return to the island while the Manxman is out of action. The operator said it was "reviewing its operational plans to minimise disruption" to passengers wherever possible.

The Ben-my-Chree had been due to take over as sole operator on the firm's Larne route from Friday.

That sailing will now be carried out by the fast craft Manannan.

News.title: Supporters across India send food via delivery apps to sustain the 'Cockroach' protest

The food arrives almost as steadily as the protesters.

Every few minutes, delivery riders on motorbikes pull up outside the protest site with bags of burgers, snacks and bottled water. Volunteers collect the food, stack it along other donated supplies and distribute it to demonstrators.

Supporters across India are helping sustain the country's “Cockroach” movement by ordering meals through online food delivery apps for protesters camped in the capital. The steady stream of food has become a visible sign of the growing support for a youth movement that has emerged as one of the biggest challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government in years.

Many contributors have never set foot at the protest site in New Delhi and don't know each other. Instead, they send meals directly to the demonstrators, often instructing delivery riders to hand them to any protester they see.

Shakti Vashisth, 24, sees every food delivery as a reminder that the protest extends far beyond those camped on the streets. Each meal, she said, is a sign of support from someone who cannot be there in person.

“There are a lot of people that I can understand might not be able to come here, but they are sending their love,” she said.

The “Cockroach” movement, which started over repeated leaks of high-stakes medical college and government job entrance examinations, and led to some committing suicide, has expanded into a broader call for government accountability, drawing thousands to demonstrations at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in New Delhi that has become the movement’s base.

Demonstrators at the protest site have stood their ground despite a major crackdown on Monday when police used tear gas and batons to stop them from marching toward Parliament. The violence fueled public anger and the crowds now extend beyond students, with young professionals, parents and others joining the sit-in.

Now, the growing crowd needs sustenance and the steady flow of donations helps sustain the protest camp. From home-style Indian meals to pizza, burgers and other fast food, volunteers hand out meals and bottles of water to protesters.

The support has been staggering, with protest organizers asking people to stop sending food orders as they have begun to exceed the number of protesters on site.

“The amount of food coming in is overwhelming. It’s difficult to even keep count,” said Bhoomi Kapoor, a volunteer.

Motorbike courier Neg Singh said he had already made 19 trips to the protest site. On one run, he picked up 70 pizzas, an order so large it took three delivery riders to carry it through the crowds. The order was placed from someone in Noida city, some 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) from the protest site.

For Singh, the protest has brought more than extra work. It has also drawn him into the movement itself.

“We also feel deeply connected to this protest. We support it wholeheartedly,” he said.

——

Associated Press reporter Verda Subzwari contributed to this report.

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Arsenal identify new targets after Saliba blow, Liverpool hijack PSG’s bid for winger
News.content:
Arsenal are set to sign a centre-back this summer after it was confirmed that Premier League title winner William Saliba has been ruled out for an “extended period” with a back injury. The Gunners could turn to Aston Villa’s Ezri Konsa or former Manchester City centre-back John Stones, who is available as a free agent.

Arsenal are also set to step up their pursuit of Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes but the Magpies are said to be frustrated by the lack of contact from the Premier League champions in what could turn into a protracted transfer saga. Newcastle are holding out for a fee similar to Sandro Tonali’s potential £100m move to Tottenham Hotspur.

Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola has set out his targets for the transfer window and has confirmed the Reds “definitely need to sign a winger”. Liverpool have now reportedly turned their attention towards Monaco’s Maghnes Akliouche, who is also wanted by Paris Saint-Germain, while PSG’s Bradley Barcola is also still a target.

Manchester United are still interested in adding another midfielder after signing Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans and are said to be in talks with Roma for France international Manu Kone, while Chelsea have agreed to loan Alejandro Garnacho to Aston Villa after their record signing of Morgan Rogers.
