World.title: Schools under scrutiny
World.content:
Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown addressing the region’s One Back-to-School Conference held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover, on Tuesday.Anthony Lewis

POINT, Hanover — The Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown has sounded the alarm over what he alleges are numerous accounting breaches in primary schools within Kingston and St Andrew.

“The breaches are too many. Here is what is happening now, colleagues. We are getting documents from the Integrity Commission (IC) for principals to be investigated… Accountability is stepping up,” he said.

Brown made the revelation, Tuesday, during the second of a three-day back-to-school conference for Region One that was held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover.

“Stakeholders in the communities are writing to the ministry. They talk about what they observe in schools. They go to a school and they get no receipt for the money they pay. They call you and ask if they should get a receipt and what it should look like,” he told an audience of educators.

The regional director said primary schools are the main offenders.

“Do you know where we tend to find the bulk of the breaches now? The primary schools. It’s a serious problem,” said Brown.

While he conceded that there may be administrative issues such as inadequate staff that impact how money is handled, he said there can be no excuse for some of the behaviour seen.

“Some simple things. Why would you keep money in excess of a million dollars locked up in a room for two, three weeks, months, and so forth? The bursar not being there caused that? So what I’m saying: I know you need those people, and we are working on that, but don’t do things to set up yourselves in the process,” added the senior officer.

Brown used the opportunity to explain proper administrative procedures when handling school funds.

“I beg you, lodge the money in a reasonable time frame. Money must be lodged intact. Can somebody please explain what the FAA (Financial Administration and Audit) Act means when it says ‘money must be lodged intact’? ‘[It means as soon] as collected,” he emphasised.

He explained that if five $100-notes are collected, that exact configuration must be deposited into the account.

“Don’t use it to make any change for anybody who wants to pay somebody something. That is what they mean [by] to lodge the money intact. If you are guilty, don’t say anything. Just sit like nothing is wrong but pray a prayer in your heart. I’m giving you 30 seconds to ask God to forgive you,” stated Brown to an outburst of laughter.

“You saved the money, but the law says treat it a particular way,” added the senior officer.

During his address Brown also expressed gratitude to the Ministry of Education for providing the region with additional professionals to conduct audits of schools within the region.

“We want to publicly say thanks to the members of the central ministry team, our CEO, [and] the permanent secretary. We spoke and they have given us a large number of people to build out the finance unit in the region. I have about five or six additional staff members now so we can do more audits. Clap the central team for that,” he said magnanimously.

World.title: Danger in John’s Hall
World.content:
A bedhead and concrete block are among items used to alert commuters to danger on the John’s Hall road in St James..

MONTEGO BAY, St James — An old bedhead and the top of a broken table used to cobble together a crude guard rail serve as warning that there is danger on the road between John’s Hall and Spring Mount in southern St James. One section appears on the verge of collapse, much like a nearby house whose foundation was eroded by Hurricane Melissa, last October, and commuters are worried.

“I’m afraid but mi just have to drive on it, can’t do better,” a shopkeeper who identified herself as Sancia told the

Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

“If little rain fall it gone, because underneath it, it’s deteriorating,” she explained.

The gaping cavern in a section of the Spring Mount Road is just a few kilometres up the hill, impassable as residents eagerly await word from the Government on when it will be repaired. Now, they have added the danger at John’s Hall to their list of urgent issues.

When contacted, community relations officer for the National Works Agency (NWA), Western Region, Janel Ricketts said they are aware of this latest development at John’s Hall. Though none were seen by the Observer, she said signs are in place to help guide motorists.

“This too, like Spring Mount, is on the radar of the NWA but in terms of an update, I don’t have that right now,” she told the Observer.

For shopkeeper Sancia and others who use the road, help cannot come soon enough as the alternative route is longer and more costly. What was once a straight route from John’s Hall to Montego Bay has now become a meandering journey to Sunderland, around Blackshop, and through Patosi.

“And the hottest part is we dropping out right at the square down there and we don’t reach Montego Bay as yet. It’s going to be more money, more gas, more everything,” Sancia lamented.

She also highlighted challenges being faced by students in that area of the community.

“Children that live here now that have to go Maldon are paying double or triple fare because they have to take taxi from here go to Montego Bay and a next taxi go and vice versa,” Sancia explained.

“It bad for everybody: Parents, children, business owners,” she added.

A roadside vendor in John’s Hall who chose not to provide his name spoke of the downturn in business he has seen as commuters from southern St James have had to find new routes.

“It rough because the road block up that side so people can’t come down. They would stop and buy drinks, food stuff, shop stuff; that’s not happening again,” he said.

He also pointed to the impact it has had on other areas of life that used to generate income, such as sporting competitions.

“Football was a thing where the different communities partake in and now them can’t come,” he said.

“Spring Mount people a bawl now because nobody can’t come down. We just want to see the road fix, the two place; because without it we don’t have any real livelihood, nobody can’t come, nobody can’t go,” he said.

A motorist who gave his name as Richard said travelling to the area has been a financial challenge and, like area residents, he is also worried about the increasing deterioration at John’s Hall.

“With this breakaway now, we would have to find a next way to go in town, it’s really pressuring. I hope they do something fast, whether it’s construction to start the new road or they find something better that we can travel on. But do something better,” Richard appealed.

World.title: Russia chokes Ukraine’s lifeline Black Sea export corridor
World.content:
The attacks forced shipping giant Maersk to stop operations at the Chornomorsk Fishing Port in the Odesa region this week, redirecting cargo to Romania’s Constanta Port. Ukraine says it would still provide security, but the vessel owners decided to halt traffic due to heightened security threats.

“Previously, there had also been many hits on ships, but most of them concerned ships already docked in ports,” Andrii Klymenko, head of the Black Sea and Baltic Strategic Research Monitoring Group, told POLITICO. Vessel owners have halted operations, wanting to see how the situation unfolds and what new solution Ukraine can find, Klymenko added.

Russia's actions prompted Ukraine to request an urgent U.N. Security Council meeting for July 27, urging all states to immediately demand that Moscow stop its attacks on freedom of navigation in the Black Sea.

The attacks intensified after Ukraine conducted a series of successful strikes against Russian shadow fleet oil tankers in the Azov and Black Seas, forcing Russia to halt exports earlier this month.

But it would be wrong to say that’s a response, because Russia never paused the attacks on Ukraine’s ports and cargo, Klymenko said. “This narrative would only help Russia to force a maritime ceasefire on us, which would benefit only the Kremlin, as it has to sell oil,” the expert added.

Ukraine’s Navy spokesman Dmytro Pletenchuk said there is a big difference, as while Russia shells vessels operating in a completely legal way, Ukraine targets cargo vessels breaking maritime law by illegally transporting sanctioned oil or entering ports of Ukraine’s occupied territories.

“The war in the sea never stopped. We have already been in a similar situation. Yes, pressure increased, and yes, shipping companies see risks and reduce operations. But we will keep working to restore maximum capacity of our maritime corridor," Pletenchuk added.

Russia’s blockade of Ukrainian ports in 2022 strangled vital agricultural exports and helped drive global food prices more than 60 percent higher by March. But after Ukraine’s navy established a protected maritime corridor in the Black Sea, the country exported more than 168.9 million tons of cargo through it, including over 100 million tons of grain, much of it bound for countries in the Global South, despite repeated Russian attacks on Odesa’s ports.

World.title: Donald Trump’s envoy threatens tariffs if Burnham hits Big Tech with new taxes
World.content:
Warren Stephens, U.S. Ambassador to the United Kingdom attends bilateral talks with U.S. President Donald Trump and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer at Trump Turnberry golf club on July 28, 2025 in Turnberry. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Warren Stephens also warns UK social media ban is “a little draconian from a freedom of speech point of view.”

LONDON — Donald Trump’s ambassador to the U.K., Warren Stephens, has warned Britain could face further tariffs, if new Prime Minister Andy Burnham raises taxes on American tech giants.

“If we go down further taxation on primarily American companies, that could certainly [elicit a tariff response],” Stephens told Sky News on Thursday morning.

The warning comes as Burnham announces his plans to slash business rates bills for pubs, clubs and live music venues by shifting the tax burden elsewhere.

World.title: EU fines Google €890M for breaching Big Tech rulebook
World.content:
The larger fine covers Google’s self-preferencing in search, where the Commission found Google gives its own shopping, hotel, transport and sports results better placement than it gives competitors. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images

Brussels orders U.S. search giant to overhaul how it ranks rivals in search results and how it polices its app store — or face further penalties.

BRUSSELS — The EU fined Google €890 million on Thursday and ordered the U.S. internet giant to overhaul how it ranks rivals in search results and how it polices its app store, as it concluded two investigations into whether the company had breached the bloc’s flagship Big Tech law.

Google becomes the third company to face significant fines under the EU’s three-year-old Digital Markets Act, a rulebook meant to fast-track investigations into dominant tech platforms that has been denounced by Washington as discriminatory because most of the companies covered by it are American.

“Google has fallen short of effective compliance with the Digital Markets Act, and today we have taken decisive yet balanced enforcement action sanctioning these breaches,” said Teresa Ribera, the European Commission’s executive vice-president for competition policy. “The best products should succeed because they’re better, not because they’re owned by the company running the search engine.”

World.title: US ambassador shrugs off Ed Miliband’s jibes at ‘idiot’ Trump
World.content:
Pushed on whether Miliband could work effectively with his White House counterparts, Stephens said only: “People were people. People’s view of President Trump in 2016 is probably a lot different than it is … now.”

While Miliband was “wrong then,” Stephens acknowledged he had also made remarks “where you come back a few years later and say, Yeah, why did I say that? I don’t think that’s really right.”

Miliband was previously quizzed about his combative comments following the U.S. president’s second election victory in 2024. He has described his prior statements as “irrelevant,” adding: “I genuinely don’t think that Donald Trump is reading my tweets. I don’t have such a high opinion of myself.”

The foreign secretary’s predecessor-but-one, David Lammy, also had a history of posting critical tweets about Trump before taking on the top diplomacy job. But he was able to point to a friendship with U.S. Vice President JD Vance.

World.title: Le parquet de Paris ouvre une enquête sur le site “libertin” Wyylde
World.content:
La plateforme Wyylde est au cœur d’une vaste enquête de justice sur l’affaire dite des viols “libertins”, relatée par Le Monde dans une série d’articles. Dix-neuf hommes ont été mis en examen pour viols avec tortures et acte de barbarie dans cette procédure, qui a pour figure-clef “Christophe B.”. Pendant plusieurs années, ce dernier a utilisé Wyylde pour trouver des hommes prêts à avoir des relations sexuelles avec ses compagnes.

Christophe B. a également utilisé Wyylde pour diffuser en direct des vidéos de ces actes sexuels, visionnables par les inscrits sur le site.

“Libertinage” grand public

Actif dans plusieurs pays européens, dont la France, l’Allemagne, l’Italie, le Portugal ou l’Espagne, le site Wyylde revendique sept millions d’inscrits et quelque 700 000 visites par jour. Il dépend de la société Koala Interactive, immatriculée à Levallois-Perret en région parisienne, et qui compte plusieurs dizaines d’employés en France.

Cette entreprise opère depuis plusieurs années sur le marché des sites de rencontre “pour adultes”. Après avoir lancé dans les années 2000 le site Netechangisme, Koala Interactive et son fondateur, le développeur Kais Ahmed, ont lancé Wyylde.

Si une partie de la plateforme est gratuite, son modèle repose sur un abonnement payant qui donne accès à une messagerie, des tchats, des partages de photos et de vidéos ou encore des diffusions en direct. Wyylde revendique une communauté “respectueuse, ouverte et libre”.

Sur le site, consulté par POLITICO, on trouve cependant plusieurs dizaines de lives simultanés de vidéos d'exhibitionnisme ou de relations sexuelles en direct.

Wyylde s’était fait remarquer à l’automne 2024 avec une campagne de communication dans le métro parisien et dans les réseaux de transports de plusieurs métropoles françaises. Sur ses affiches, Wyylde promettait alors aux potentiels utilisateurs de venir “vivre ce que l’on ne peut pas montrer ici”.



Cette campagne a été lancée en parallèle du procès dit “de Mazan”, qui a vu comparaître plus de cinquante hommes accusés du viol de Gisèle Pélicot. Son époux, Dominique Pélicot, orchestrateur des abus, avait recruté ces hommes en passant par un autre forum en ligne, coco.gg.

Le site Coco constitue lui-même un précédent dans la manière dont la justice appréhende ces plateformes qui hébergent des contenus potentiellement illicites. Après l’ouverture d’une information judiciaire pour “fourniture d’une plateforme en ligne pour permettre une transaction illicite en bande organisée”, le site a été fermé par la justice en 2024. Son fondateur, Isaac Steidl, a été ensuite inculpé en janvier 2025 à Paris, notamment pour complicité de détention et diffusion d’images pédopornographiques.

World.title: Does Burnham need to watch what he says?
World.content:
The latest policy announcement from Burnham’s new government is a 20% tax break for pubs, clubs and live music venues. That means pubs could save an estimated £1,100 a year.

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy delve into the details and again ask, how will this be funded?

The two also discuss Burnham’s communication style and if it might need more discipline now that he’s in No.10. This is in light of the new PM’s comments on a potential review of early prison release in England and Wales.

The Foreign Office has withdrawn its remaining UK staff from Iran as Donald Trump ramps up pressure on Tehran. Sam and Anne talk about what this could mean for the new Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.

World.title: Greek gas concession unlocks EU’s Russia sanctions package
World.content:
Greece had initially resisted the proposed ban on shipping Russian gas to customers outside the bloc, arguing that it went beyond what EU leaders had previously agreed and would be ineffective because vessels could simply re-register abroad.

Greece secures gas carve-out

Athens ultimately got what it wanted: Its Dynagas shipping company will be allowed to ship Russian liquefied natural gas from the Arctic Ocean to customers that aren’t in the EU.

The rules will cap Russian gas exports based on historical shipment levels and prohibit new contracts, preventing EU-flagged shipments from increasing Moscow’s revenues.

A third diplomat said the LNG export exemption will remain in place for one year and renew automatically unless EU capitals agree to end it during a review. Because sanctions decisions require unanimity, withdrawing the exemption could prove difficult.

In return, Greece agreed to a 12-month oil price cap freeze. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen celebrated the news on Bluesky, writing that it would prevent “the Russian war machine” from benefiting “from market shocks.”

The package will make it harder for people who served in the Russian armed forces to enter the EU. Although several capitals pushed for a blanket ban, implementation concerns led governments to agree on narrower restrictions.

World.title: Canada pushes new UK government to join defense bank
World.content:
Earlier this month at the NATO summit in Ankara, both the U.K. and Canada unveiled the initial membership of their separate funding mechanisms for partners' defense industries. Rachel Reeves, removed as chancellor by Burnham this week, had resisted Britain's membership of Canada’s scheme.

The DSRB aims to raise £100 billion by providing loans to governments and defense firms and was backed by nine countries. Britain has partnered with the Netherlands, Finland and Poland on its own Multilateral Defence Mechanism — which is more geared towards joint procurement than to lending AAA-rated capital.

McGuinty said he doesn’t see “any reason why creative negotiation and smart thinking” cannot pull the work of the two schemes together.

He added: “Personally, I don't think it's as productive having two separate mechanisms, and I think this is a wonderful opportunity for the U.K. and Canada to align on this front. So, I'm hopeful.”

“Using Canadian language: I think it’s smart hockey," he said, "using public finance and triple-A ratings and government-backed capital in order to be able to fund your SMEs who are having a hard time dislodging capital from commercial banks and other sources, and creating an international one in order to be able to foment greater investments in defense.”

Streeting to reopen the case for joining

On Wednesday, the new U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting set out a positive case for Britain joining the DSRB as he spoke to journalists at the Farnborough International Airshow.

World.title: Lavrov tells Rubio 'unacceptable' for US to continue arms sales to Kyiv
World.content:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned Washington against continuing arms sales to Kyiv during a meeting with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the Philippines on Thursday, the Kremlin said.

 

During the meeting, which took place on the sidelines of the ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) foreign ministers' summit, Lavrov told Rubio that it would be "unacceptable" for the US to continue arming Ukraine, according to a statement released by Russia's foreign ministry.

"Lavrov briefed his American counterpart on the actual situation along the front line and emphasised that it would be unacceptable to further arm the Kyiv regime," the statement reads.

Lavrov also reaffirmed Moscow's "readiness for a political and diplomatic settlement of the conflict," it said, adding that the two parties had also discussed the situation in the Persian Gulf, where the US remains locked in conflict with Iran.

US President Donald Trump has signalled his support for Ukraine's long-range strikes against Russia, which have sought to target Russian energy infrastructure.

"It's an escalation, but it's also an escalation that can help lead to an end," Trump said of Ukraine's strategy during the NATO summit in Ankara earlier this month.

Ukrainian strikes on Russia and annexed Crimea

Russian authorities have said that Ukrainian strikes killed four people overnight into across Russia and Russian-occupied territories.

In a post on Telegram, Sergey Aksyonov, the head of Russian-occupied Crimea, reported that two people were killed and five were injured following strikes on the region, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014.

In the western Russian region of Voronezh, Alexander Gusev, the local governor, said a three-year-old boy also died after a drone crashed into a house and caused a fire.

Alexander Shuvaev, the acting governor of Belgorod, which is also in western Russia, said one person was killed following an attack on the Shebekinsky district.

Ukraine's air force said Russian forces had launched a ballistic missile, five cruise missiles, and 168 attack drones at Ukraine overnight.

It said local air defences had "shot down or neutralised" two Kh-59/69 cruise missiles and 154 drones.

World.title: EU online child safety push holds platforms firm and lets parents off easy
World.content:
Teenagers’ use of social media and digital services is a popular subject among politicians worldwide, including those in the European Union (EU).

 

While some countries are currently considering bans up to age 16, others are considering more modest approaches with lower thresholds.

Meanwhile, a digitally advanced Estonia openly rejects the idea of an EU-wide minimum age for social media use, emphasizing the importance of digital literacy among minors, teachers and parents, as well as stronger enforcement of existing legal frameworks, such as the Digital Services Act (DSA).

(c) Child Safety Online: Protecting and Empowering Minors in a Digital World, July 2026. Euronews courtesy of EU Tech Loop

A few weeks ago, a special expert panel, led by Prof. Dr. Jörg M. Fegert and Dr. Maria Melchior, presented a report on child safety online, offering actionable recommendations.

While the report is overall balanced and recognizes that not all minors under 18 should be treated the same, it leaves significant room for interpretation for EU policymakers, also echoing the Commission's focus on new platform obligations while relying largely on soft measures for parental involvement.

Current legal frameworks in action

The conversation on the matter is quite simplistic at the Member State level, focusing primarily on the minimum age of use for social media and other digital services.

Additionally, countries like France have recently banned smartphones in schools.

While the topic is easy to communicate and yields significant political dividends, the technical details and institutional capacity needed to enforce such requirements are rarely part of the discussion.

The conversation on protecting minors online at the EU level is neither new nor ignored.

Previously, the EU outlined numerous provisions across various laws meant to protect children online.

The Digital Services Act (DSA), for example, is used to assess platforms’ design features that might be harmful, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) outlines protections to safeguard children’s personal data and consent online, and the Audiovisual Media Services Directive (AVMSD) was recently expanded to cover new forms of audiovisual content and video-sharing platforms.

The list continues with the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act), the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD), the Consumer Rights Directive (CRD), the Unfair Contract Terms Directive (UCTD), the General Product Safety Regulation (GPSR), the Product Liability Directive (PLD), the Political Advertising Regulation (PAR), the widely criticised Chat Control 1.0 and proposals for Chat Control 2.0, along many more guidelines, cooperation mechanisms, strategies, political statements and digital literacy programs.

Much like other discussions surrounding online consumer protection, the current debate on protecting minors focuses on introducing new regulatory layers and mechanisms rather than better enforcing existing rules.

To this end, the EU has launched its age-verification app, will likely soon propose an EU-wide minimum age for social media, along with additional platform obligations, and is advocating for ex-ante design requirements, such as banning infinite scrolling.

Complications: bypassing, data security and fragmentation

The UK’s and Australia's negative experiences of teenagers bypassing local restrictions through various means, including VPN use or migration to fringe and less regulated platforms, have significantly complicated the political conversations.

EU policymakers now have to consider real-world examples from abroad and outline precautionary measures to prevent a similar scenario from happening in Europe.

So far, the effort has not been successful: earlier this year, the EU Commission unveiled an age-verification app, however, it drew criticism for being unreliable, as AI agents could bypass it "within minutes".

Additionally, the EU must respect the European data protection and data minimization principles, especially given the increasing number of data leaks across both private digital platforms and public services.

Lastly, the fragmented approach to the minimum age of use among EU Member States may complicate efforts to reach an EU-wide agreement on the matter.

Countries that have rushed to introduce their own versions of such laws will likely resist the expert panels’ recommendation to focus on restricting access for minors under 13 years old, citing the very same report stating that "countries may prefer to adopt a higher threshold than 13 years".

Building resilience: involving parents and caregivers

The report says that minors' safety online is primarily a responsibility of social media and digital services providers, putting parents and caregivers into a secondary role:

"Social media and other digital services providers retain primary responsibility for keeping minors safe on their services. In addition, parents and caregivers have important roles in supervising children’s and adolescents’ time online, and in guiding minors in addressing the risks they face in social media+ environments together."

It is true that the role of parental supervision decreases as the child develops, becomes more autonomous, and is increasingly influenced by peers.

It is also true that sometimes parents do not have the means, time or digital literacy to make use of existing parental control tools.

However, the cultural change that the EU Commission and many local politicians envision will only be possible if regulatory and literacy measures are combined and accompanied by better parental involvement.

Especially given that parents themselves are sometimes enablers of rule-bypassing and of giving their own children unrestricted access to the digital world.

There is very little data on European parents using existing parental control options, however, the survey from 2020 conducted by the EU Kids Online Network states that, on average, only 22% of European parents used existing parental control tools.

Only the French and Maltese parents were somewhat more involved, while only 12% of Lithuanian parents and 14% of Czech parents used parental control mechanisms back in 2020.

The special expert panel takes a relatively soft approach to parental involvement, focusing on digital literacy, guidelines, and supportive tools.

However, meaningful cultural change usually requires combining soft measures with hard obligations — not just for digital platforms, but for parents as well.

While the EU maintains a comprehensive child protection framework enforced by local agencies, the current political conversations on minors online lack direct incentives or accountability mechanisms for parents.

Without clearly defined parental responsibility to curb excessive screen time, cyberbullying and online abuse towards other children, many parents may remain passive, relying entirely on local or EU-wide regulations rather than taking proactive ownership of their children’s digital well-being.

This story was originally published on EU Tech Loop and has been shared on Euronews as part of a syndication agreement.

World.title: 'Armour of God: Ultimatum': Jackie Chan starts shooting in Kazakhstan
World.content:
Famous Hong Kong actor, filmmaker and stunt performer Jackie Chan arrived in Kazakhstan to start filming the fourth Armour of God movie.

 

He will return as Asian Hawk, a treasure hunter, who springs back into action in the quest to find an ancient artifact known as Tumar worth more than €20 million.

On Saturday, the crew officially started filming by breaking a ceremonial dish.

"Many years of preparation, finally, we start the movie. We have a long way to go. Only the first shot, we have a thousand shots," Jackie Chan said.

Filming will take place in Almaty city, Almaty and Mangystau regions and Baku from July to October 2026, while some scenes will be shot in Hong Kong. The Bozzhyra Grand Canyon located in Mangystau region will be the primary filming location.

Why Kazakhstan?

The film is a Kazakhstan-China collaboration, produced by the Kazakh company Sәlem Entertainment and the Hong Kong company Billion Target.

Salem Entertainment Executive Producer Igor Tsay told Euronews that Central Asia is a completely new filming location for Jackie Chan, which is why he chose it as the ground for his next film.

"Kazakhstan has great potential for filming large-scale, A+ class movies with world-famous stars, and Jackie Chan was the first to pay attention to our region," Tsay said.

He explained that Chan was interested in unique natural landscapes, diversity of locations and special atmosphere of the country.

"All we had to do was seamlessly weave Kazakhstani locations into the script so that they became not just a beautiful backdrop, but an important part of the film's on-screen world," the producer added.

Tsay also noted that Chinese and Kazakh teams are working together well, with each side eager and keen to swop share experiences.

"As a veteran of the film industry, Jackie exemplifies the key qualities of professionalism, discipline, determination and passion, both on screen and on set," he said.

Jackie Chan is not directing

Armour of God: Ultimatum will be the first in the franchise to be directed not by Chan, but by Kazakh director Robert Kun.

Kun, whose career also started with stunt performances, has worked for various projects for Disney, Paramount, Universal, and 20th Century Fox.

"Robert is the perfect bridge between ideas and their implementation. He has the most extensive directing experience in our region working on action projects of this scale, which is probably why he was chosen," Tsay explained.

He noted that Chan oversees all creative processes and remains the primary bearer of the franchise's spirit and values. Every decision in the production process undergoes a rigorous approval process.

Stunts in the movie will be handled both by JC Stunt Team and Kazakhstani action studio Kun-Do. Robert Kun earlier said that Chan had the idea to combine several styles in staging the larger-scale fight scenes.

"Jackie always wants to do something he's never done before in his life, and, as you understand, over more than half a century of his career, he's performed so many stunts that there's not much room for imagination, but our team is capable of surprising not only the franchise's main star, but also future audience," said Igor Tsay.

Armour of God: Ultimatum is scheduled to premiere in February 2027.

World.title: 9 things European entrepreneurs should know before becoming digital nomads
World.content:
The digital nomad lifestyle has seen a massive boom in popularity in the last few years.

 

According to Expatnetwork, Google searches for “digital nomad visas” surged 1,135% worldwide in 2024.

Given the freedom, flexibility and increasing global opportunities, it may not come as much of a surprise that both everyday European remote workers and business owners alike want to escape as quickly as possible to the next laptop-friendly beach.

However, for entrepreneurs, this move is far from a casual one and requires considerable planning and strategy. This includes everything from choosing the right visa and understanding tax implications, to planning finances and finding the right insurance.

Euronews Business looks at the nine most important things European entrepreneurs, especially small business owners, need to keep in mind before going full digital nomad.

Finding the right visa category

The very first step before planning to go abroad as a digital nomad should be researching and finding the best country that suits the stage your business is at right now, as well as your lifestyle and long-term goals.

This also means finding the right visa category for you. While several countries like Brazil, Costa Rica, Thailand and Indonesia have dedicated digital nomad visas, others like Australia and Japan, still prohibit working on a standard tourist visa.

"Before booking your flight, research whether your chosen destination offers a visa tailored to business owners, as well as what the eligibility criteria are, the minimum income requirements, how long you can stay and whether you can renew your visa if you decide to extend your time abroad," Alex Miles, chief operating officer at business credit card company Capital on Tap, advised.

Understanding tax and legal implications

Your tax and legal obligations are some of the most crucial factors to keep in mind while moving abroad as a business owner. If disregarded, you may find yourself paying taxes in two jurisdictions, which could significantly hurt profit margins, or facing huge legal costs, penalties or compliance issues down the line.

"Relocating abroad can affect both your personal tax residency and your business’ legal obligations. Depending on where you move and how long you stay, you could become liable for tax in more than one country," Miles pointed out.

"Before making the move, it's worth speaking to a tax or legal professional who can explain how double taxation agreements work, whether your tax residency will change and what reporting requirements you'll need to meet," he added.

Setting up finances for international spending

Another important factor is managing your finances properly for international spending.

This includes setting up new bank accounts, applying for loans abroad and testing various payment solutions to find the one that best meets your business’ needs.

"Consider using business banking and payment solutions that offer competitive exchange rates, low foreign transaction fees and support for multiple currencies. Keeping your business and personal finances separate will also make bookkeeping, budgeting and tax reporting much simpler," Miles explained.

Choosing the right workspace and internet options

While choosing the right internet connection and workspace for your business may seem obvious, it is still often one of the most underestimated factors for how smooth, efficient and reliable your business operations may be.

Similarly, the wrong workspace and patchy internet can cause a lot of unnecessary stress and friction, especially during the early days of working in a new country, when entrepreneurs may already have to deal with a medley of new adjustments.

"Before choosing a destination, research internet speeds, mobile data coverage and the availability of coworking spaces if you don't plan to work from home," Miles noted.

Reviewing your insurance cover

Insurance is another often overlooked factor, with several business owners filing it away as something to look at later on when they have time, rather than of utmost urgency.

However, having the wrong insurance cover, or none at all, can cost you much more than expected in unforeseen circumstances.

Many entrepreneurs may also assume that standard travel insurance policies will cover them for long-term remote working, expensive business equipment or business related activities, which may not be the case.

"When comparing insurance providers, ensure that you have the right travel, health and business insurance in place to suit your needs. Ensuring you're properly covered can protect you against unexpected costs such as medical emergencies, lost or stolen equipment and business interruptions that could otherwise be costly," Miles explained.

Keeping time zone differences in mind

Several digital entrepreneurs don’t adequately account for the toll of different time zones while moving abroad. However, this is one of the things that could potentially make or break your business, with far-reaching consequences on everything from operational issues to mental and physical health.

"It’s important to consider how you'll manage meetings, deadlines and day-to-day communication. For example, if you're relocating to Australia, the 8-11 hour time difference (depending on the time of year) could mean early morning or late-night calls become part of your routine," Miles warned.

"Before committing to a destination, ask yourself whether your business can realistically operate across those hours," he added.

Protect your devices and data

Given the sharp rise of cybersecurity attacks and other data breaches seen worldwide in recent months, it is vital to protect your devices and data as much as possible. This is especially if you don’t have a dedicated office building or home set-up and will be changing working locations frequently.

"Remote working often means connecting to public Wi-Fi, which can increase cybersecurity risks. Protect your business by using a VPN, enabling multi-factor authentication on all business accounts, regularly updating your devices and avoiding accessing sensitive information over unsecured networks," Miles noted.

Don’t forget emergency funds

Moving abroad, whether as a digital entrepreneur or otherwise, can be extremely chaotic and unpredictable, even in the best of circumstances.

As such, having a financial safety net should be non-negotiable, especially if you don’t want to be taking money out of your business to cover unplanned expenses.

"Unexpected costs such as visa delays, medical emergencies, or sudden changes in accommodation can quickly add up. Having a financial buffer ensures your cash flow remains steady and your business operations aren't disrupted by personal travel hiccups," Miles said.

Plan for long-term revenue stability and business continuity

Finally, while all of the above factors are vital to making sure your business stays healthy and profitable while being a digital nomad abroad, it is even more important to not lose sight of the long-term vision and goals set for the business.

"While working abroad can offer flexibility and inspiration, it’s important not to overlook business continuity. Consider how your revenue streams will be affected if client demand fluctuates, payment cycles change, or you’re operating outside your usual market hours," Miles cautioned.

World.title: Brussels slaps €890 million fine on Google despite looming new US tariffs
World.content:
The European Commission announced a €890 million fine against Google on Thursday over alleged self-preferencing practices and unfair treatment of app developers, just as the Trump administration prepares a fresh round of trade duties.

 

The fine caps an investigation the Commission launched in March 2024 under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), a law setting out a list of dos and don'ts for large tech companies that dominate key digital markets.

The flagship element of the case, leading to a fine worth €460 million, concerns Google's search engine allegedly giving systematic preferential treatment to its own services — Google Shopping, Google Hotels, Google Flights — while downgrading competitors in search results.

Self-preferencing first took centre stage as a legal theory in the landmark Google Shopping antitrust case, confirmed by the EU Court of Justice in 2024, more than a decade after the investigation was formally opened in 2010.

The DMA later codified the concept, with the explicit aim of speeding up enforcement and stripping out many of the evidential hurdles required under traditional antitrust law.

The second strand of the case, amounting to the remaining €430 million, concerns accusations from app developers that Google prevents them from telling consumers how to leave its ecosystem, for instance by promoting cheaper offers available outside its app store or flagging alternative payment systems.

Decision's implications

Beyond the monetary sanction — and arguably more consequential for Google — the Commission has ordered the company to end its non-compliance: treating third-party services without discrimination and letting app developers communicate freely with users.

Google must comply with the Commission's decision within 60 days or face periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of its worldwide turnover.

Google, for its part, argues its services are designed to optimise the user experience, and that changing its search results or app store policies would harm the European digital ecosystem.

"This isn't fair competition; it's product degradation driven by a small group of self-serving complainants, with European businesses and consumers taking the hit. Regulation should improve products, not make them worse," said Google President of Global Affairs Kent Walker.

Google has already begun testing changes to its search service and app store. The Commission says it will continue to monitor their implementation, and considers some of them significant progress towards compliance.

Google did not confirm whether it intends to appeal the decision.

The conclusion of the probe is, on paper, the product of a largely bureaucratic assessment of whether the tech giant breached the bloc's prescriptive rules for fairer, more contestable digital markets. But it risks becoming another point of contention in transatlantic tensions.

US trade tensions

A major fine against an American corporation is set to become another flashpoint with Washington. The Trump administration has repeatedly made clear it views EU digital rules as a trade "irritant," at times equating such fines with commercial tariffs.

A year ago, Brussels and Washington struck a trade deal known as the Turnberry agreement to resolve their trade dispute, under which the EU agreed to remove duties on most US industrial products and accept a 15% US tariff on its own exports.

The Trump administration was forced to adopt new tariffs on a different legal basis after the US Supreme Court ruled the duties it had imposed in 2025 illegal.

That new regime is set to expire this week, and the White House is weighing additional duties expected to target forced labour and overcapacity, following a Section 301 investigation touching on German drug pricing.

EU-US trade tensions have already shaped how Brussels decided to sanction American tech giants in the past. Last September, a fine against Google over its digital advertising business was shelved amid pressure from within the Commission and from the US government.

Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič emerged as the main internal opponent of issuing sensitive sanctions before a deal with Washington was finalised. After that internal rift became public, the Commission went ahead with the fine — but the episode showed how susceptible the EU's investigations were to outside political pressure.

World.title: UK airports hiked drop-off fees by a third since last summer, while continental Europe stays free
World.content:
Sixteen of the UK’s 20 busiest airports have increased their charges for dropping off passengers, with the average cost increasing by a third since last summer, according to a new analysis by British motoring service RAC.

 

Using the UK's ‘kiss-and-fly’ zones rose by an average of £1.70 (€2) to £7 (€8.20) compared to this time last year.

The latest to hike the charge is Stansted, London's third-busiest airport. Drivers now have to pay £10 (€12) instead of the previous £7 (€8.20) for express drop-offs of up to 15 minutes, making it the second-most expensive fee in the UK.

Earlier in the year, London Gatwick raised its 'kiss and fly' fee to become the most expensive in the UK.

In comparison, many airports on the continent still allow free or low-cost drop-offs.

UK airports hike passenger drop-off fees

Stansted's hiked fee also impacts longer stays of up to 30 minutes, for which drivers are now charged £28 (€32.50).

AGS Airports, which operates both Glasgow and Aberdeen in Scotland, increased drop-off levies to £7 (€8.20) for 15-minute access at their terminals in February, citing rising costs.

At Glasgow Airport, drivers who overstay their 15 minutes will also have to pay a 'premium charge' on exit.

At the beginning of the year, Bristol airport started charging £8.50 (€10.20) to park for 10 minutes at the Drop Off & Pick Up car park next to the terminal, as well as the Short Stay car park a short walk away.

This was followed by London Gatwick, which hiked drop-off fees at both its North and South terminals to £10 (€12) for 10 minutes’ parking.

Other London airports are also pricey. Luton charges £7 (€8.20) for 10 minutes, while London City charges £8 (€9.60). Heathrow also charges £7 (€8.20), but drivers must drop off and depart immediately without waiting.

Elsewhere in the UK, Manchester costs £5.50 (€6.45) but only allows a five-minute stay, while Leeds is £8 (€9.60) for 10 minutes.

Two of the few airports to have a free drop-off option are Birmingham, which only charges after 10 minutes (there is also a premium set down costing £7 for 15 minutes), and Inverness, which is up to 15 minutes.

Airports on the continent offer free passenger drop-off

The price hikes have frustrated travellers, particularly as public transport is often not an option for many passengers, particularly at airports outside of London.

Clive Wratten from the Business Travel Association told the BBC that airports were "pulling the easiest revenue lever" by increasing their parking fees.

"Pricing people out at the kerbside does not suddenly make public transport viable - it just pushes more cost onto workers, businesses and the taxi community," he said.

"The consumer drop-off gouging at UK's airports continues to escalate unabated and is, in my opinion, a national disgrace that should be declared illegal," one comment on Business Traveller said.

It comes in stark comparison to airports on the continent, where 'kiss and fly' zones are often free.

Venice Marco Polo airport allows cars to park for up to 20 minutes directly outside the terminal at no cost.

At Milan Malpensa, there's a free waiting area between terminals one and two for up to 60 minutes.

Ljubljana's 'kiss and fly' zone is free for 10 minutes, as are the drop-off zones at Paris Charles de Gaulle and Paris Orly.

How to avoid the UK's airport drop-off fees

Many of the UK's costly drop-off fees can be avoided if you are happy to walk a short way to take a free shuttle.

Consumer website MoneySavingExpert has detailed how to find free parking at major airports.

At Bristol, for example, there's a free one-hour waiting zone by the 'Silver Zone' car park to the south of the terminal, with frequent buses to the terminal.

For Glasgow, drivers should head to the long-stay car park, where it is free to wait for up to an hour. It's a 10-minute walk to the terminal, or there's a free shuttle bus that takes seven minutes, the website says.

Drop-offs of up to 29 minutes are free in London Heathrow's various park and ride car parks for the different terminals, and passengers can take a free bus transfer to the terminal.

However, while these options save money, they also require more forward planning from travellers who have to budget in extra time.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: Lenacapavir will slow HIV infections if there's enough of it and it reaches at-risk groups
World.content:
Lenacapavir is one injection, twice a year. It's a big improvement for people in high-risk groups, currently taking a pill a day against HIV infection. But its long-term impact depends on its reaching those very people.

For a healthy young woman in South Africa, the greatest risk of HIV may come from someone she wants to trust, but can't.

She may not know her partner's HIV status, may not always be able to insist they use a condom, and may have little control over whether he has other partners.

There is an option: Daily Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) pills keep antiretroviral drugs in the body at high enough levels to stop HIV before it can establish any infection.

But PrEP only works if she keeps taking the medication.

Miss too many doses and drug levels can fall too low to provide sufficient protection.

She may forget, resent having to take a daily pill, or fear that a partner or relative will find the medication, causing stigma. She may also experience side effects from PrEP or struggle to obtain new supplies.

Zimbabwe takes a big shot toward an HIV-free future To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How can lenacapavir help?

Taking medication consistently — known as adherence — is a challenge for people with conditions like hypertension and diabetes. With PrEP, however, the difficulty is even greater.

"You're asking people who are healthy, who don't have any illness, to take a tablet every day," said Salim Abdool Karim, director and co-founder of the Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa. "That's a high bar."

"Repeated studies, including our own, show that patients who start taking PrEP, by month three, about half of them have given it up. By the end of the year, you're left with only a handful that are still taking PrEP," Abdool Karim told DW.

Lenacapavir sharply reduces that daily burden: It requires just one injection every six months.

"That's infinitely easier to do than to remember to take a tablet every day," he said. "For those who receive the injection every six months without fail, it works superbly because adherence is effectively complete."

But lenacapavir is still too expensive in some regions and access is low.

How does lenacapavir last so long in the body?

Most established PrEP drugs block enzymes that allow the virus to reproduce and spread —it uses the enzymes to copy its own genetic material and insert it into a human cell's DNA.

Lenacapavir works completely differently. It is the first PrEP drug to target the capsid, a cone-shaped shell that surrounds the viral genetic material. But the capsid is also essential to the virus' replication process — and therefore a promising target.

Lenacapavir attacks the capsid of HIV, shown in green because they are vital for the virus' ability to replicate and spread in the body Image: Cavallini James/BSIP/picture alliance

"[Lenacapavir] is the most potent molecule we know of against HIV," Wesley Sundquist, a University of Utah biochemist and leading expert on the HIV capsid, told DW.

Sundquist said lenacapavir remains effective over long periods and that it is potent even at low concentrations.

"It sets up a little depot that slowly dissolves," said Sundquist.

Which groups would benefit from lenacapavir (if they can get it)?

Abdool Karim pointed to three groups where HIV incidence remains stubbornly high and greater PrEP uptake is urgently needed:

Adolescent girls and young women in parts of Africa

Younger gay men in the West

Vulnerable gay communities in Eastern Europe and Central Asia

In South Africa, a rollout for people at risk began in June 2026, backed by a July 2025 agreement between the drug's developer, Gilead, and a public-private financing organization called the Global Fund.

Gilead agreed to supply lenacapavir at no profit to up to 2 million people over three years.

Earlier, in October 2024, Gilead also agreed to allow the production of cheaper, generic versions of the drug in 120 resource-limited countries, where HIV infection rates are high.

But some countries still lack access to the drug.

Latin American countries excluded from lenacapavir deals

Melissa Scharwey of Doctors Without Borders said some Latin American countries, including Brazil, Mexico, Peru and Argentina, have been excluded from recent rollouts of lenacapavir, despite their having participated in its clinical trials.

Even within eligible countries, vulnerable groups may still be missed, Scharwey told DW.

"There's by far not enough of it," said Scharwey, calling on Gilead to increase supply and sell directly to MSF at an affordable price of around $40 per shot.

The decisive question in driving down HIV, according to University of Washington epidemiologist Monisha Sharma, is whether the drug reaches the people and places where HIV is spreading most rapidly.

"In our modeling of South Africa, Zimbabwe, and western Kenya, providing lenacapavir to approximately 2–4% of the adult population, with targeted uptake among people at greatest risk, averted approximately 12–18% of new infections over ten years," Sharma told DW.

Is injectable HIV medication really a 'silver bullet'? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Lenacapavir 'unlikely to eliminate HIV on its own'

"Lenacapavir could substantially accelerate progress toward lowering incidence, but it is unlikely to eliminate HIV transmission on its own," said Sharma.

"This impact is highly dependent on affordable lenacapavir drug prices, efficient distribution channels, and targeted uptake among people with the highest HIV risk," she added.

That final condition is what gives Abdool Karim his greatest concern. Lenacapavir can largely solve the adherence problem for people who receive it. It cannot solve the harder problem confronting HIV specialists: identifying and reaching those in greatest danger.

"The problem is that those at highest risk need to come forward to take the medication. And often those at the highest risk don't see themselves at risk. That's why they're at risk," said Abdool Karim. "If we cannot reach those at highest risk, then we're not going to make a dent in this epidemic in the manner in which we were hoping."

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

World.title: US citizens are ramping up pressure on data centers
World.content:
Rapid data center construction across the US fueled by AI comes with serious threats to the environment, public health and energy supply. Local opposition has blocked or delayed dozens of projects.

When construction on a major Amazon data center in the small rural county of Frederick, in Maryland, got underway, community activist Elizabeth Bauer found her peace with it.



But when it expanded by about 1,000 acres beyond its original plans to dig into green space and farmland without addressing the community's concerns, she took a stand.

Together with other locals she is protesting the proximity of the construction site to residential areas, which she says is causing dust and pollution that is exacerbating asthma among the population.

Protesters in Frederick demand that farmland is used for farming, not to host data centers Image: Elizabeth Bauer

"I'm okay with data centers in the right place. I'm not okay with them taking prime farmland," Bauer said.

Protest against data centers is getting louder

Bipartisan backlash against data centers has gotten louder in the US, with nationwide demonstrations calling on politicians to take action.

The US District of Columbia, Maryland, and Virginia region has been a flashpoint over data centers. Virgina alone has currently around 640 data centers listed.

These conflicts are not only related to the construction phase, but longer-term impacts. Data centers require vast amounts of energy to operate — as much electricity as 100,000 households according to the EPA.

But those under construction could consume 20 times as much, largely due to the increased demand for data storage and processing capabilities needed to support AI development and use.





Overall, data centers account for 4.4% of US power, but a study by investment banking firm Goldman Sachs projects an increase of up to 8.5% by the end of 2027.

Data centers devour power and water

The battle in Frederick reflects the tensions across the US, which is already home to 4,600 data centers — around 1,000 more than the next ten countries combined.

Almost 40% of citizens live within a five-mile radius of at least one, and that number is likely to rise given that more than 1,500 more sites are under construction. Nowhere in the world is the concentration higher than in North Virginia, where they account for 70% of the world's internet traffic.





This is all happening against a backdrop of discontent, with a recent Gallup poll suggesting that 71% of the population opposes data center development in their communities.

Data centers can use up to five million gallons of water each day (as much as a city of 50,000). Yet, it is not uncommon for them to be built in areas under water duress. According to the US drought monitor, Frederick County is experiencing a severe drought.



Francesca Dominici, a professor of biostatistics at Harvard's School of Public health, says tech companies also regularly disregard the concern.

"They're not looking at the water issues at all," she said. "They prioritize where they can get the land cheaper, where they can get the local politician to give the approval faster."

Higher fuel bills and air pollution

States with high concentrations of data centers have seen a 267% increase in electricity prices over the last five years.

Residents at a town hall meeting, here in Kenmore, New York, protesting against data center plans Image: Craig Ruttle/Sipa USA/picture alliance

"Electric utilities are building massive amounts of new transmission lines to serve data centers," said Hannah Wiseman, a professor in environmental law at Penn State University. "But the costs of those transmission lines are being socialized among the rate payers."

There are also concerns that data centers could overburden the grid meaning they have to resort to backup diesel generators. In the case of the Frederick community, the planned center would have 99 diesel generators, which comes with health risks.

"Exposure to fine particulate matter, even at a low level, [means] increased risk of birth defect, respiratory, cardiovascular, neurocognitive and early deaths," said Harvard's Dominici, adding that they also threaten local wildlife and minimize plant growth and yield.

How are data centers regulated?

Despite negative effects on communities, Wiseman says locations of data centers are mostly regulated at the municipality level, and that many states offer data center developers a regulatory environment that allows rapid development. Regardless of proximity to people or nature.

"Lots of local governments have chosen not to issue land use regulation, in which case a data center developer can pretty much do whatever they want."

At a federal level, US President Donald Trump cut red tape for developing data centers as part of his 2025 executive order "Removing Barriers to American Leadership in AI."

Many tech companies have insisted that localities sign non-disclosure agreements to limit communities' understanding of the scale of the projects and consequences of widespread resource consumption.

So instead of inviting resident input, they are working directly with municipality officials to draw up their plans.

Data centers and the global water crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Wiseman also notes that tech and development companies are increasingly collaborating with state governments in establishing zoning and power consumption standards.

"They've been involved in all the state regulatory proceedings to create special electricity rates for data centers," she said. "It appears that tech companies are getting more involved now in the many state legislative proposals to preempt local control."

How tech companies respond to the pushback

Though tech companies argue that data centers invigorate local economies, a University of Michigan study found that they generate temporary construction jobs to local communities, but not long-term tech positions.

There are some suggestions that these companies are looking to build trust with local communities. In March, Microsoft stopped using NDAs with local governments for data center development, saying they wanted to build more trust with their neighbors. And Meta says it is piloting and deploying low-carbon concrete in data center construction.

Why people are throwing AI data centers into the ocean To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dominici says she sees "a win-win future path" that combines technological advancement with community benefit. "I would love to see nonpartisan scientific evaluation of all the impact, and the data center can act based on minimizing this impact as much as possible."

Putting the brakes on, at least temporarily

And protests in local communities seem to have paid off. Just last week, New York became the first US state to halt construction of new large-scale data centers for up to a year. Moratoriums have also been proposed in other states, and some counties and municipalities have issued their own temporary bans.

In Frederick, Bauer and fellow activists continue to push back against the data center going up in their back yard. They've collected enough signatures to propose the ordinance be subject to a referendum in the county elections, though any idea of that happening was quashed by Maryland's supreme court.

The county has responded to this blowback by issuing a temporary pause on new data center construction, yet Bauer feels the democratic process failed Frederick residents.

"The average citizen has no chance," she said. "This whole effort was not to fight data centers, it was to give people a voice."

Despite challenges, Bauer still sees hope. She said there are county council candidates in the upcoming Frederick election that oppose expansion.

"If the new council comes in, they can overturn this map completely," she said. "We're disappointed, but we are not giving up."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker, Sarah Steffen

World.title: Thailand: 5 soldiers killed in attack on security checkpoint
World.content:
The attackers stole three AK-47 rifles, three bullet proof vests and three mobile phones from the soldiers. A low-level conflict has been simmering in Thailand's southern provinces for two decades.

Five Thai soldiers were killed in an attack on a military checkpoint in Narathiwat province in the country's restive south.

At least six civilians were also injured in the attack, including a 10-year-boy, local officials said.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul on Thursday called the attack a "brazen act of terrorism" that posed "a serious threat to national security."

What do we know about the attack?

The incident took place on Wednesday when around 10 people opened fire at the security checkpoint and threw pipe bombs at soldiers from the Thai Rangers auxiliary force, before fleeing the scene.

Thailand's Internal Security Operations Command said the attackers stole three AK-47 rifles, three bullet proof vests and three mobile phones from the soldiers.

Their vehicle was later found abandoned and set on fire 21 kilometers (13 miles) away from the scene.

A low-level conflict has simmered since 2004 in Thailand's southernmost provinces, with rebels in the Muslim-majority area fighting for greater autonomy in Buddhist-majority Thailand.

More than 7,000 people have been killed in the conflict. Government spokesperson Ratchada Thanadirek said the past few months in particular had seen a series of violent incidents carried out by a "terrorist network seeking to instill fear among the public and target state officials."

World.title: EU fines Google €890 million over competition rules
World.content:
The European Commission said it found that Google had preferenced its search engine and app store in ways that unfairly harmed competition.

The European Union has imposed fines of €890 million ($1.015 billion) on US tech giant Google for violating EU digital regulations.

The European Commission said it found that Google had preferenced its ubiquitious search engine and its Play app store in ways that unfairly harmed competition.

What did the EU say about the fine?

"We found that Google harms businesses offering similar services, such as shopping or sports, by not granting them the same level of prominence on Google Search," Digital Commissioner Henna Virkkunen said.

"We also found that Google has restricted app developers from offering cheaper offers to customers in the Google Play app store," she said.

The commission stressed that Google could face further fines if it does not take steps to comply with regulations.

"The best products should succeed because they’re better, not because they’re owned by the company running the search engine," Competition Commissioner Teresa Ribera said. "European consumers have a right to be told by app developers where to sign up to the best offers, even when the app store owner does not get a cut."

The EU has described Google and its parent company Alphabet as a "gatekeeper" alongside other major US firms — namely Amazon, Apple, Meta and Microsft — and China's ByteDance, saying that the companies control access for consumers.

Top Google executive Kent Walker criticized the fine, describing it as "product degradation driven by a small group of self-serving complainants."

He said that the penalty would "strip away real-time search features Europeans love — like instant pricing and direct availability for hotels, flights, and restaurants — and dismantle safety protections on Google Play."

Brussels aims to curb Big Tech under anti-trust and safety regulations Image: Virginia Mayo/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

What is the EU's policy on Big Tech and competition?

The European Union has been working to rein in Big Tech companies in the face of larget market shares held by major US and Chinese firms.

The European Commission already imposed a €4.3 billion penalty on Google in 2018, accusing the company of abusing Android system's market dominance by requiring phone makers to pre-install Google Search and the Google Chrome web browser. The firm lost its appeal against the fine in February.

The EU has also fined tech firms under safety regulations, with Chinese retailer Ali Express being hit with a €550 million fine earlier this month after the bloc had found shortcomings in the firm's efforts to curb illegal, unsafe and counterfeit goods.

On July 10, the EU threatened social media giant Meta with a heavy fine unless it changes "addictive design" used on the platforms Facebook and Instagram.
