While Poland already hosts various allied forces, the presence of German troops is particularly symbolic given the two countries’ difficult history. “United, we will prevail,” wrote the General Staff of the Polish Armed Forces (SGWP), announcing the deployment. “This is what allied cooperation looks like in practice, which translates into greater military readiness and strengthens NATO’s defensive potential.” Polscy i niemieccy żołnierze razem wzmacniają granicę z Rosją. Takie rzeczy możliwe tylko za Tuska ☺️ pic.twitter.com/oNBME2gBsv — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 22, 2026 Last December, the Polish and German defence ministries revealed that a “mid-double-digit number” of German troops would be deployed from mid-2026 until the end of 2027 to support implementation of Poland’s East Shield operation, which seeks to bolster defences along the borders with Belarus and Russia. They said that the German personnel would mainly engage in engineering work, such as digging trenches, laying barbed wire and constructing anti-tank barriers. Today, Poland’s SGWP confirmed that “several dozen” German troops, including “highly specialised engineering forces” along with their equipment, had since June been temporarily deployed to “support the Polish armed forces in expanding defence infrastructure on NATO’s northeastern flank”. It emphasised that the East Shield project is “purely defensive in nature” and comes in “response to threats stemming from, among others, Russian aggression against Ukraine”. While the armed forces did not reveal the location of the deployment, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated in a social media post that it was on the Russian border. Poland has a 210-km frontier with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. German public broadcaster Deutsche Welle reports that the activities of the German sappers are focused in particular on improving defences around the so-called Suwałki Gap, a strategically important stretch of land around the Polish-Lithuanian border between Belarus and Kaliningrad. “Together, we are ensuring Europe’s security,” said Lieutenant General Alexander Sollfrank, the Bundeswehr’s operational commander, announcing the deployment today. “Through our engagement in Poland, we are strengthening NATO’s defence capabilities and underscoring the alliance’s unwavering commitment to ensuring peace through unity and credible deterrence.” Poland and Germany have signed a bilateral security agreement that will see the two neighbours and NATO allies increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity https://t.co/6BPX2WxvxH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 SGWP, which shared footage of Polish and German forces installing anti-tank barriers, said the work aims to “hinder and delay an aggressor’s actions in the event of a threat”, thereby “increasing the time for a response from the Polish armed forces and the entire [NATO] alliance”. It also seeks to “create conditions for the efficient reception, deployment and use of NATO forces on Polish territory”. SGWP welcomed “the involvement of the German contingent as a practical expression of allied solidarity and the result of consistently developing military cooperation between Poland and Germany”. It also noted that the cooperation would help the two sides improve their ability to operate jointly, including “developing the competencies necessary for conducting a joint defence operation”. However, it emphasised that the current deployment is focused on training and engineering, with no combat component, and that the German troops are unarmed. SGWP also emphasised that the East Shield operation remains entirely a Polish national programme. The leaders of eight countries on the EU's eastern flank have met in the first summit of its kind to discuss closer security cooperation. The agreement is a sign that the two countries now stand “shoulder to shoulder, as equals”, declared German defence minister Boris Pistorius. Poland is also currently seeking a new permanent US military base on its territory, after President Donald Trump recently pledged to boost American troop numbers. Poland’s climate and environment ministry has inaugurated the first of 11 planned “community forests” around large cities, with the aim of giving residents a place for recreation and contact with nature while also helping to fulfil the government’s pledge to reduce logging. Plans for the forests were announced in 2024, and the first has now been established around Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city. Ten other major urban centres, including Warsaw, Kraków, Poznań and Łódź, are set to follow. Dotrzymujemy słowa. Powołaliśmy pierwsze lasy społeczne w Polsce, to lasy ochronne wokół Wrocławia. Kolejne miasta przed nami. @MKiS_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/RxhsMZShj9 — Paulina Hennig-Kloska (@hennigkloska) July 21, 2026 “This is a historic moment and the beginning of a new approach to forest protection – with residents in mind first and foremost,” said climate and environment minister Paulina Hennig-Kloska at an inauguration ceremony outside Wrocław on Sunday. “Community forests are places where residents can relax, play sports and simply spend time close to nature,” she added. “At the same time, they are crucial to our security and quality of life: they retain water, regulate the climate, purify the air and protect the soil.” An area covering 13,000 hectares (32,124 acres) has been designated as a community forest around Wrocław. Forest management there will now be aimed at “maximising the forest’s social functions”, says the ministry, while timber harvesting is also restricted. The area will be divided into three zones, including “natural forests”, where nature will be left to take its course, and “near-natural forests” with minimal intervention. However, the largest zone, amounting to over 8,000 hectares, will be “social forests”, which the state forestry agency says “will be managed in a way that ensures the comfort of those who use the forest and its benefits related to wellbeing, physical exercise and recreation”. Hennig-Kloska noted that, in the latter area, educational trails as well as hiking and cycling paths would be established. However, given that such facilities already exist in many forests, it remains unclear how the new community forests will differ. The ministry is now conducting consultations and analysis on establishing community forests around ten other designated urban centres: Bielsko-Biała, Tricity (Gdańsk-Gdynia-Sopot), Katowice, Kielce, Kraków, Łódź, Poznań, Szczecin, Toruń-Bydgoszcz and Warsaw. On Sunday, Hennig-Kloska said that the “next in line” to have their community forests established are Kielce and Bielsko-Biała, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Shortly after coming to power in December 2023, the current government announced that it would halt planned logging in some forests. The former Law and Justice (PiS) administration had faced criticism for overseeing an increase in logging, especially in Białowieża Forest. The current government also launched plans to create Poland’s first new national parks in over two decades. However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last year vetoed that move, arguing that it would “block the economic development of the region” and threaten Poland’s security. Poland has joined a European Union project developing a secure satellite internet service that would provide an alternative to networks such as Elon Musk’s Starlink. Warsaw has committed €656 million (2.8 billion zloty) to the IRIS² programme, with the money coming from Poland’s EU post-pandemic recovery funds. In return for joining the project, Poland will gain access to the secure satellite communications network for government institutions, the armed forces and emergency services, while the growing Polish space industry will be eligible to compete for contracts linked to the development of the constellation Today Poland🇵🇱joins the EU🇪🇺space programme #IRIS² w/additional €656 mln. 🇵🇱 is on a remarkable space journey to build a strong space economy & secure connectivity for the defence of Poland, the Eastern Flank & 🇪🇺. IRIS² brings greater unity & strength for the entire Europe. pic.twitter.com/TwS59vpXtm — Andrius Kubilius (@KubiliusA) July 21, 2026 “This is a big day for Poland, the eastern flank and the entire European Union,” declared the EU’s defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, at a signing ceremony in Warsaw on Tuesday. “By investing in space, Poland is investing in its security, its economy and its future.” Speaking alongside him, Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said that IRIS² would help “ensure our security and strategic independence” while “demonstrating that Poland aims to be a leader in the European space industry and remain at the centre of EU security efforts”. “No single country is able to build such a [satellite] constellation so efficiently, which is why we are joining this major project – to be part of it and one of its managers,” he added. The IRIS² programme aims to deploy a constellation of nearly 300 satellites in low and medium Earth orbit, providing encrypted, interference-resistant communications for governments, defence agencies, emergency services and selected commercial users across the EU. First announced in 2022, the project is part of the EU’s efforts to reduce dependence on non-European satellite operators amid growing concerns over cybersecurity, hybrid threats and the resilience of critical infrastructure following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “It is super important for Europe to have a sovereign capacity, and Starlink will never do that,” said Eva Berneke, CEO of Eutelsat, one of the companies involved in the project, quoted by Politico Europe. The project is expected to cost €10.6 billion, including €6.5 billion in public funding and around €4 billion from private investors. IRIS² is expected to become operational in 2030. 🇪🇺 The IRIS program is Europe's replacement for Starlink. The constellation will consist of over 300 satellites to serve Europe alone. Security and sovereignty! Like Galileo, it could surpass its US counterpart. Fewer satellites, smarter coverage. Eventually more could be added pic.twitter.com/Uswmuotw7F — Mariska den Eelden 🇪🇺🇳🇱 (@eeldenden) February 22, 2025 As part of its contribution to IRIS², Poland will finance six large satellites in medium Earth orbit (MEO) and six smaller satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO). It will also build a ground gateway station in Warsaw to connect the satellites with GovNet, the country’s secure government fibre-optic communications network. Earlier this year, the Polish government approved the use of money from its share of the EU’s post-pandemic reconstruction fund to cover its contribution to IRIS². Sięgamy gwiazd!! Polska przystępuje do europejskiego programu budowy bezpiecznej łączności satelitarnej 🛰️📡! W ten sposób zaspokoimy wszystkie potrzeby łączności służb i administracji państwowej. IRIS² zapewni nam bezpieczeństwo i niezależność. Dziękuję @KubiliusA za współpracę pic.twitter.com/c8u2QH0Wyn — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) July 21, 2026 Once the system is up and running, Poland’s police, border guards and other emergency services would be able to use the network during natural disasters, power outages and other emergencies when terrestrial communications infrastructure is unavailable. The system would also make it possible to provide temporary connectivity for civilians through emergency hotspots, says Poland’s interior ministry. Polish companies will now also be able to compete for contracts covering satellite manufacturing, telecommunications equipment, software and ground infrastructure, expanding the country’s role in Europe’s space industry. “It is estimated that each zloty invested in the project will generate a five-zloty return through new jobs, innovation and the development of domestic technologies,” the ministry said in a statement. World.title: Archaeologists uncover synagogue in Warsaw Jewish cemetery destroyed by Germans in WWII

Archaeological work at a Jewish cemetery in Warsaw has uncovered the foundations of and many objects from a former synagogue and funeral home that was destroyed by the Nazi-German occupiers in 1943. The finds were made at the cemetery on Okopowa Street, which, at around 33.5 hectares in size and with some 250,000 people buried there, is the second largest in Poland, after the Łódź Jewish cemetery, and one of the biggest anywhere in the world. Following the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Germans liquidated the ghetto, sending most of its remaining inhabitants to the gas chambers and destroying the buildings that remained there, including the synagogue and burial houses. In June this year, archaeological work began at the site of the former synagogue, commissioned by Warsaw’s Jewish community, which owns and manages the cemetery. The two-storey building, designed by architect Adolf Schimmelpfennig, a Pole of Dutch Lutheran descent, was constructed in 1877 and existed until 15 May 1943, when it was destroyed with explosives. The archaeological work aims to “uncover, document and preserve the remains of this historic complex, maintaining the memory of this place and passing it on to future generations”, says the office of the conservator of monuments for Masovia, the province in which Warsaw is located and which is supervising the work. Archaeologists have so far discovered numerous items that offer “silent testament to the daily life of the community that was connected to this site for decades”, says the conservator. They include ceramic floor and wall tiles, glass bottles and tiles from stoves used at the funeral home. “Every discovered brick, fragment of flooring or piece of furniture helps reconstruct the history of one of the most important buildings in historic Warsaw,” adds the conservator. Among the finds is an item that relates to a well-known and tragic story from the war, a door plaque from the office of the then-director of the cemetery, Abram Pozner. Pozner brought members of his extended family to the funeral home at the start of the war, where they were initially able to remain in relative safety, away from the horrors of the ghetto that the occupiers forced Jews to live in. As life became ever more brutal and dangerous for Jews, Pozner created an underground hideout within the cemetery. The Germans eventually found the bunker and killed most of those hiding there. However, two of them managed to survive imprisonment in German labour camps, one of whom, Avraham Carmi, remains alive today and lives in Israel. The current archaeological work is expected to be completed by the end of July, after which the foundations will be re-covered with earth. Warsaw’s Jewish community then hopes to restore the previous building, adapted to current conditions and needs, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “The goal is to determine whether the funeral home could be rebuilt on these remains, or whether it would make more sense to display them as a monument within a newly constructed building, and also whether erecting a building on this site is even realistic,” cemetery director Witold Wrzosiński told the newspaper. Archaeologist Szymon Lenarczyk, who has led the work at the site, says he has proposed that the structure of a future building should feature an underground room where discovered artefacts can be displayed. Before World War Two, Warsaw was home to around 350,000 Jews, a third of its population and more than any city in the world other than New York. However, the vast majority were killed in the Holocaust, meaning that only a small Jewish community remains today. World.title: Kraków launches €43m “pre-design” tender for planned metro system
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A planned metro system in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has moved a step closer after the authorities launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. City authorities say the plans – which will include a feasibility study, environmental report, geological research, and assessment of the project’s impact on existing buildings – are a major milestone in the development of what would be only Poland’s second underground railway network. #Krakow #metro #projektowanie #przetargi 🚇Kraków ogłasza przetarg na opracowanie dokumentacji przedprojektowej dla budowy metra. W ramach uruchomionego postępowania powstaną m. in. dokumenty, analizy i decyzje, które pozwolą przygotować dokumentację niezbędną do finalnego… pic.twitter.com/0jcYL4HGRq — Kraków (@krakow_pl) July 13, 2026 The idea of building a metro in Kraków has been discussed for decades and, in 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the project. However, only in 2024 did the city’s then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, announce plans to build a system. In September last year, the city unveiled the metro’s planned route, with two lines travelling through the city’s historic centre from its southwestern and southeastern suburbs to its eastern outskirts. In May this year, Miszalski, who had made developing the metro part of his election campaign in 2023, was removed as mayor in a recall referendum. But the project has nevertheless continued, with the municipal authorities last week announcing a tender for pre-design of the metro. The work will include confirmation of the planned structure of the system as well as the location of stations, tunnels and other infrastructure. The city has allocated 188 million zloty for the pre-design in its budget for 2026 to 2031. Studies of feasibility and impact are particularly important given that the planned route of the metro envisages it skirting around Kraków’s Old Town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site that contains many historical structures. The tender follows months of preparatory work, initial market consultations, analyses and discussions with experts, said Maria Wojtacha, director of Kraków’s public works department. “Although this process doesn’t yet mean that construction has begun, it is one of the most important steps that the city can take individually,” Wojtacha added. “Our goal is to prepare Kraków for the next stage – the ‘design and build’ phase.” The experiences of other recent major infrastructure projects in Poland, such as a major new airport and transport hub and Warsaw’s second metro line, show that environmental and tender procedures need not slow investments down, said Marek Grochowicz of the city’s strategy and European funds department. However, it is clear that the earlier timeline for Kraków’s metro outlined is slipping. Last September, the city said that it hoped construction would begin in 2030 and that the system would be finished by 2035. However, the current acting mayor, Stanisław Kracik, announced last month that construction is unlikely to start until between 2040 and 2045. Even the current tender for “pre-design” work envisages a timeline of up to 50 months for that work alone. Warsaw has announced 56m zloty for “pre-design” work on a fourth metro line. The mayor says improving public transport is an "absolute priority". But his rival in next month's elections says the mayor is digging up forgotten plans as part of the campaign https://t.co/lg3zkNeW2E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2024 Rafał Solecki, head of Kraków’s department of strategy and European funds, also made clear last week that “construction of the metro exceeds the financial capabilities of the local authorities”, and that therefore financial support from the national government and the EU will be necessary. “The metro should be treated as a national strategic investment, similar to large railway, road, aviation and metropolitan projects implemented in other parts of the country with state participation,” he added. The city also announced that it has received a proposal for a consortium of seven local universities and research institutions to provide scientific and expert support for the metro project throughout its preparation and implementation. “Building a metro in a historic city is an extremely complex undertaking, requiring special attention to the protection of cultural heritage,” said Andrzej Szarata, rector of Cracow University of Technology. “Therefore, the support of the scientific community…is of paramount importance.” Kraków has been named Europe's best city break destination by members of @WhichUK. World.title: Attempted illegal border crossings from Belarus to Poland down over 98% this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland says that the number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants over the border from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. “The effectiveness of [border guard] officers and the Polish armed forces discourages migrants from taking risks,” says Poland’s interior ministry. Bezpieczeństwo na granicy z Białorusią w pierwszej połowie 2026 r. w liczbach: 📉 Ponad 65-krotny spadek prób nielegalnego przekroczenia (ok. 235 vs ponad 15,5 tys. w pierwszym półroczu 2025 r.) 🛡️ 0 udanych prób nielegalnego przekroczenia granicy 💯 Skuteczność ochrony: 100%… pic.twitter.com/1lTXV56JdW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) July 18, 2026 Since 2021, large numbers of migrants and asylum seekers – mainly from Africa and Asia – have tried to irregularly cross the border from Belarus to Poland with the help and encouragement of the Belarusian authorities. In 2021 alone, just under 40,000 attempted illegal crossings were recorded. While Poland subsequently strengthened border infrastructure and sent thousands of additional officers to bolster security, attempted crossings remained high: there were just under 30,000 in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have now fallen dramatically in the first half of this year, when Poland’s border guard recorded only 235 crossings, compared to 15,500 in the equivalent period for 2025. Meanwhile, the interior minister says that the number of successful crossings by migrants – i.e. those who managed to get across the border and were not apprehended – has fallen to zero so far this year, down from around 1,700 in 2025, 5,000 in 2024 and 12,000 in 2023. However, when presenting such figures on successful crossings, the ministry does not indicate how it calculates them, given that successful crossings are often inherently undetected. Most of those who manage to cross do not remain in Poland, instead heading westwards, in particular to Germany. “The statistics clearly show that the 3 billion zloty (€692 million) investment in the security of the Polish-Belarusian border has delivered the intended results – we are effectively protecting our country from illegal migration organised by the Belarusian regime with the support of the Kremlin,” declared the ministry. Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland. Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 Among the measures taken to protect the border are a 5.5-metre-high steel fence as well as an electronic monitoring system that detects attempts to cross and dispatches officers to the scene. In 2024, following the death of a soldier who had been stabbed by a migrant attempting to cross the border, Poland also loosened the rules on the use of firearms by officers posted there. Since last year, it has banned asylum claims by people who cross from Belarus. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, also praised Poland’s “impressive” efforts “to stop illegal migration” and said that it was vital for the EU to offer financial and logistical support. EU chief @vonderleyen has thanked Poland for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” during a visit with PM @donaldtusk to the border with Belarus. She emphasised the “urgency” of protecting the EU’s frontier from the “predator” Vladimir Putin https://t.co/O9bhmLha44 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2025 However, while Poland has managed to significantly reduce the number of attempted and successful border crossings, there is evidence that Belarus has switched its focus to Latvia, another EU member state with which it shares a border. Last week, Latvian interior minister Jānis Dombrava told Euronews that his country has now “become the main target” for Belarus’s migrant trafficking, instead of Poland and Lithuania. On Thursday, Latvia recorded 111 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, compared to two in Lithuania on the same day and zero in Poland the previous day. World.title: Poland welcomes Zelensky’s five-point plan for resolving dispute over WWII massacres
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has cautiously welcomed an announcement by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of a five-point plan intended to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led massacres of Poles during World War Two. In a statement on Friday evening, Zelensky announced that, following a meeting on Kyiv’s policy towards Poland, “the priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighbourly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect”. He reiterated Ukraine’s gratitude for Poland’s “significant support” since Russia’s full-scale invasion and announced that his administration had “agreed on several key steps” in response to the current tensions. I held a meeting on our policy toward Poland. The priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighborly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect. Poland provided significant support to Ukraine after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, and we are… pic.twitter.com/5dNFQYqi1n — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) July 17, 2026 “First, there will be decisions on the diplomatic track,” said Zelensky, though without indicating what this would mean in practice. “Second, all archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the tragic events in Volyn during the 20th century will be opened.” The latter is a reference to the historical issues that are at the heart of the dispute. The historical region of Volhynia, which is now mostly in Ukraine, was part of Poland in the interwar period. There, and in some neighbouring areas, the UPA, a nationalist partisan formation, led massacres of around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, during World War Two, when the region was under Nazi-German occupation. Poland recognises those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine vehemently rejects that label, and also points to anti-Ukrainian measures in the region by the interwar Polish state as well as massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during the war. As his third pledge, Zelensky announced that there would be “decisions to grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. From 2017 to 2025, Ukraine prohibited searches for and exhumations of Polish massacre victims on its territory, where it is believed that tens of thousands remain buried in unmarked mass graves. In a diplomatic breakthrough, such work was allowed to resume last year. However, Ukraine has so far only approved a small number of requests for searches and exhumations, prompting some complaints from Poland. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 As a fourth point, Zelensky said that his team had “discussed possible formats for expanding dialogue between the societies of Ukraine and Poland”, though again without providing details as to what this would involve. Finally, he said that he had agreed with the head of the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINP), Oleksandr Alfyorov, to expand the institute’s capabilities and funding, so that it can “properly represent Ukraine’s interests”. Alfyorov caused anger in Poland earlier this year when he said that the Volhynia massacres are viewed in Ukraine as “just a local historical episode” and suggested they did not constitute a genocide. That prompted a rebuke from Poland’s own Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). Poland's state historical institute has criticised remarks by the head of its Ukrainian counterpart about massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. He said they are regarded in Ukraine as a "local episode" and suggested they do not constitute a genocide https://t.co/MAi6RhpRDL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 11, 2026 In response to Zelensky’s announcement, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he “accepted the words and decisions with satisfaction and hope”. He reiterated that Poland is “ready for a serious and friendly dialogue on the matters that unite us and those that divide”. However, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, a deputy prime minister, emphasised that it was important now for “the announcements regarding the opening of archives, exhumations and dialogue to turn into concrete actions”. “Today, Poland and Ukraine have a common enemy: Russia,” added Kosiniak-Kamysz. “That is where the threat lies. Sowing discord between our nations serves the interests of the Kremlin.” Z satysfakcją i nadzieją przyjmuję słowa i decyzje @ZelenskyyUa, dotyczące relacji między naszymi państwami, które muszą być oparte na wzajemnym szacunku i prawdzie. Jesteśmy gotowi do poważnego i przyjaznego dialogu w sprawach, które nas łączą i tych, które nas dziś dzielą. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 Meanwhile, a senior aide to Polish President Karol Nawrocki – who deepened the crisis by last month stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour – also cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement. “Facing the historical truth is the only way to build further relationships,” Bartosz Grodecki, the head of Nawrocki’s National Security Bureau (BBN), told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “The Ukrainian president’s decision to open the entire archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the events in Volhynia, as well as additional permits for search and exhumation work, is a step in this direction,” he added. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Spicy, Not Spicy: How This Chef Is Bringing Authentic Chinese Street Food to Prague
World.content:
At Manifesto Market, the aroma of Sichuan peppercorns and chili oil stands out among the usual mix of street food and drinks.

It comes from Lá Bù Lá Street, the more casual sibling of the restaurant Lá Bù Lá, both founded by Wen, a Chongqing native who wants to introduce Prague diners to the real flavors of her hometown.

Wen arrived in Prague in 2019 after being accepted into a Master’s program at the Prague University of Economics and Business. But studying was only part of the reason she moved. At 22, she wanted a new beginning and the chance to discover a different version of herself.

“There was something about Prague that attracted me immediately,” she says. “The architecture, the pace of life, the atmosphere of the city —

it all felt very charming. I wanted to see what kind of person I could become here.”

That decision eventually led her into the restaurant business, with four concepts launched over the years — two that closed and two that continue today.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Lá Bù Lá Street (@labula_street)

Beyond the Stereotypes

For Wen, opening a Chinese restaurant in Prague was never only about selling food. It was also about showing people that Chinese cuisine is far more diverse than many stereotypes suggest.

“China is a huge country, and every region has its own culture and food traditions,” she says. Through her restaurants, she hopes guests become more curious about where dishes come from, how ingredients are used, and how different regions eat.

She also wants Chinese food to be seen as something connected to special occasions, not only a quick meal.

“Chinese food can create beautiful memories too,” she says. One example is Chongqing chili, which is often associated only with heat. Wen says there is much more to it.

“Many people think Chongqing chili is only about being spicy. But it is also about aroma,” she explains. The same applies to Sichuan peppercorns, where the famous numbing sensation is only part of the experience.

Learning the Hard Way

Wen’s path has not been simple. Her first two projects, Chi Xiao Mian and Mi I’m, did not succeed as she had hoped, but she sees them as important lessons.

“They taught me how to work with people, how to manage a team, and how important communication is,” she says.

The experience also taught her to stay focused on her original vision. Running a restaurant requires listening to others, but also knowing when to trust your own ideas.

“Building something meaningful always requires finding a balance between dreams and reality,” she says.

A Restaurant, and Then a Street

Today, Wen runs two concepts: Lá Bù Lá and Lá Bù Lá Street. The name, meaning “spicy, not spicy,” reflects the idea that Chongqing cuisine is about much more than just heat.

The original restaurant offers a deeper introduction to traditional Chongqing dishes, while Lá Bù Lá Street at Manifesto Market has a more relaxed atmosphere.

“It is more spontaneous and more social,” Wen says. The concept is inspired by street food culture in Chongqing, where people gather, share dishes, and spend time together.

At Manifesto, surrounded by music, travelers, and international crowds, the idea has naturally evolved. Some dishes work better for sharing, while others simply encourage people to stay longer.

“For us, food tastes better when shared,” Wen says. “Passed around a table. Offered to a friend. Or quietly stolen from someone else’s plate.”

Growing Step by Step

Like many restaurant owners, Wen faces daily challenges, from managing a team to introducing unfamiliar flavors to new customers. Building a group of people who share her values has been one of the most difficult parts.

When asked about opening more locations in Prague, she says the ambition is there — but there is no rush.

“Of course, I would love for more people to discover the food of my hometown,” she says. “But I am not in a hurry.”

For now, Wen is focused on improving the restaurants she already has and building a stronger team.

“When my team and I are truly ready, we can always begin the next journey,” she says. “For now, we are happy to keep growing step by step.”

World.title: Prague and Stockholm Launch Cross-Border Public Art Project
World.content:
Visitors in Prague and Stockholm will soon be able to communicate across borders through a pair of interactive public art installations designed to exchange anonymous messages between the two cities.

The linked installations, created by the Czech initiative Praho! project and its Swedish partner Stockholm! project, will open in Stockholm on August 20 and in Prague on August 31.

The installations are designed as private spaces intended for one visitor at a time.

After entering, participants answer a series of questions before listening to an authentic audio recording left by someone in the other city. They are then invited to record their own message, creating an ongoing exchange between residents and visitors in Prague and Stockholm.

According to the project team, the concept explores what happens when anonymous thoughts become personal through the human voice.

“The installation creates a space where you first listen to someone else—and only then can you speak,” the organizers said. “We want to explore how connecting two different cities through shared experiences can foster understanding.”

The initiative is part of Art & Design Without Borders, an international collaboration supported by the Erasmus+ programme. The project brings together organizations from the Czech Republic and Sweden to promote participatory art, community engagement and new approaches to public space.

Although they work closely together, Praho! project and Stockholm! project operate as independent non-profit organizations. Their partnership reflects a shared history rather than a branch structure.

Praho! project was founded in 2021 and focuses on participatory art in public and digital spaces. Through text-based interventions and an online platform, it has collected more than 30,000 anonymous responses addressing personal experiences and broader social issues. Those contributions have since been transformed into publications, exhibitions and artistic installations.

The concept, however, began even earlier. Founder Annamarie Čermáková first developed the idea in 2019 while studying at Stockholm University of the Arts. Returning to Sweden inspired the creation of Stockholm! project in 2025.

The project extends beyond the installations themselves. Organizers will also host workshops, educational programmes, international internships and prepare a methodology guide documenting best practices in participatory public art across different European settings.

World.title: BAY55: 114 Luxury Apartments Planned for Prague’s Riverfront in Smíchov
World.content:
One of the last undeveloped riverfront plots in central Prague is set to become home to a new luxury residential project.

Developer Daramis has unveiled plans for BAY55, a development featuring 114 high-end apartments on Hořejší nábřeží in Smíchov, just steps from the railway bridge and within walking distance of the city center.

According to Daramis, BAY55 is designed to compete with premium residential developments in leading European and North American cities. The company says the project will emphasize architecture, technology, privacy and resident services alongside its prime location.

The residence will include a wellness and fitness center covering roughly 600 square meters, a private residents’ lounge and hospitality facilities.

A restaurant or café is also planned on the ground floor, serving both residents and visitors. The developer says the level of amenities is intended to match those found in luxury hotels.

Designers have also focused on balancing density with comfort. Every apartment is planned to include either a spacious balcony or terrace, complemented by integrated shading systems intended to provide greater privacy despite the urban setting.

Before construction of the residential complex can begin, significant work will be carried out along the riverfront.

The existing Smíchov embankment will be extended, creating additional public space and improving pedestrian access along the Vltava. The infrastructure upgrades are expected to become part of the wider transformation of one of Prague’s fastest-growing neighborhoods.

Daramis acquired the land from BPD Development in 2024. Although the developer has not disclosed the value of the investment, it says BAY55 represents the largest and most expensive project in the company’s history.

Costs are driven not only by the location and construction standards, but also by flood protection measures, advanced building technologies and architectural features planned for the shared spaces.

The project is currently progressing through the permitting process. If approvals proceed as expected, construction of the new embankment will begin first, followed by the residential development itself.

Completion is currently scheduled for around 2030.

World.title: From Müller to Krispy Kreme, Global Chains Are Coming to Czechia
World.content:
International drugstores, fashion retailers, discount chains and restaurant concepts are preparing to open their first locations in Czechia, adding new competition for established players.

Here are some of the biggest brands expected to enter the Czech market.

Müller

German retailer Müller is preparing to launch in the Czech Republic. The company has already established a Czech branch and website, although it has not yet announced the opening date of its first store.

Unlike traditional drugstores, Müller combines cosmetics and personal care products with toys, stationery, household goods, pet supplies and organic food.

The chain operates nearly 1,000 stores across nine European countries and will compete with established Czech market leaders such as dm, Rossmann and Teta.

Krispy Kreme

American doughnut chain Krispy Kreme is reportedly searching for a location in central Prague and could open its first Czech store soon.

Founded in North Carolina in 1937, the company became famous worldwide for its Original Glazed doughnuts and stores where customers can watch the production process.

Ochnik

Polish fashion brand Ochnik plans an ambitious expansion in the Czech Republic, with 15 to 20 stores expected by the end of 2026.

The company specializes in leather jackets, footwear, luggage and accessories. It previously considered acquiring Czech brand Kara but decided to build its own network instead.

OVS

Italian fashion retailer OVS is also preparing its Czech debut.

The company focuses on affordable clothing for the whole family and is particularly strong in children’s fashion. It is positioned between discount retailers and mainstream brands such as H&M, C&A and Reserved.

Normal

Danish discount chain Normal is preparing to enter the Czech market after establishing a local company.

The retailer sells cosmetics, household products, snacks and everyday goods at permanently low prices. Its stores are designed to encourage impulse shopping, with customers walking through a changing selection of products.

MR. D.I.Y.

Malaysian discount retailer MR. D.I.Y. has some of the biggest expansion plans among new arrivals.

The company plans to open around 20 stores in Prague and eventually grow to more than 100 locations across the Czech Republic. Its first Czech store is expected to open at Forum Nová Karolina in Ostrava.

MR. D.I.Y. sells household equipment, DIY products, electronics and stationery.

Burgermeister

Berlin burger chain Burgermeister will enter the Czech Republic as part of its European expansion.

The brand started in 2006 inside a converted toilet building near Berlin’s Schlesisches Tor station before growing into a chain with more than 30 restaurants.

It focuses on its own production, including burgers made with Irish beef and ingredients prepared in Berlin.

Dave’s Hot Chicken

American fast-food chain Dave’s Hot Chicken is preparing to compete with KFC and Popeyes in the Czech market.

The brand specializes in Nashville-style spicy fried chicken, offering chicken tenders and sandwiches with different levels of heat.

Founded in Los Angeles in 2017, the chain has expanded to more than 400 locations worldwide.

Arthur Gelato

Slovak premium ice cream brand Arthur Gelato has already opened its first Prague location on Francouzská Street.

The company focuses on handmade ice cream, fresh ingredients and unusual flavors. It plans further expansion through franchising.

Sticks’n’Sushi

Danish restaurant group Sticks’n’Sushi will open its first Prague location this autumn.

The concept combines Japanese sushi with grilled skewers and will operate a three-story restaurant on Jungmann Square with around 160 seats.

World.title: Five Things to Know Before Flying From Prague Airport This Summer
World.content:
Passengers departing from Prague Airport this summer are being advised to plan ahead as the airport prepares for its busiest travel season in years.

To help travelers avoid unnecessary delays, the airport has released a list of practical recommendations covering transport, security screening, travel documents and baggage rules.

Leave Extra Time to Reach the Airport

The biggest challenge this summer is expected to be road access to the terminals. Construction at the Aviatická–Lipská intersection may cause traffic congestion on routes leading to the airport.

Airport officials recommend using public transport whenever possible, as buses are not affected by the roadworks. Travelers arriving by car should allow extra time to reach the terminals, particularly during peak holiday periods.

Self-Service Check-In Can Save Time

Passengers can speed up the departure process by using the airport’s self-service facilities. Prague Airport now offers 31 check-in kiosks and 32 self-service baggage drop counters, available for flights operated by 18 participating airlines.

Before heading to the airport, travelers should also verify the entry requirements for their destination. Those flying to the United Kingdom, for example, now need an Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) before departure.

Bring Physical Travel Documents

Although many travelers rely on digital wallets and electronic documents, Prague Airport reminds passengers that electronic IDs and passports cannot be used during passport control.

Travelers should carry a valid physical passport or national identity card, depending on the requirements of their destination.

Security Rules Depend on the Terminal

Passengers departing from Terminal 2 will notice a faster security process thanks to newly installed CT scanners.

The new technology allows travelers to leave electronics and liquids inside their cabin baggage during screening. In addition to the standard one-liter transparent bag containing containers of up to 100 milliliters each, passengers may also carry one extra liquid container with a capacity of up to two liters.

These updated rules currently apply only in Terminal 2. Security procedures in Terminal 1 remain unchanged.

Pack Power Banks Correctly

The airport is also reminding travelers about one of the most common packing mistakes.

Power banks, laptops and tablets must always be transported in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage. In addition, lithium batteries must not exceed 100 Wh unless specifically approved by the airline. Ignoring these rules can lead to delays during security checks or, in some cases, passengers being refused boarding.

World.title: Czechia Debates Social Media Ban for Children as France Moves Ahead
World.content:
France is moving toward stricter rules on children’s use of social networks, while a similar debate is gaining attention in the Czech Republic.

Lawmakers, educators and experts are increasingly discussing whether children should face age restrictions on social media and tighter limits on smartphone use in schools.

The issue has grown across Europe amid concerns about excessive screen time, cyberbullying, online safety and children’s exposure to unsuitable content.

France has become one of the first European countries to push forward with legislation that would prevent children under the age of 15 from creating accounts on social media platforms. The French Senate has approved the proposal, which still requires approval from the lower house of parliament before it can become law.

If adopted, the measure would take effect on September 1 and require online platforms to introduce age verification systems. Companies would also have to remove accounts belonging to underage users within four months.

The French proposal also includes restrictions on mobile phone use in secondary schools, reflecting a wider European discussion about the role of smartphones in children’s lives.

Czech Republic considers stricter rules for smartphones in schools

The Czech Republic has so far focused mainly on regulating mobile phone use during school hours rather than banning social media accounts for children.

This week, the Czech government backed a proposal that would introduce a nationwide restriction on the use of mobile phones and other electronic communication devices in schools. The regulation is expected to come into force in September 2027.

Concerns over gaming, online content and cyberbullying

Supporters of stricter rules argue that unrestricted access to smartphones can expose children to risks ranging from harmful online content to addictive behaviour.

Experts have raised concerns about easy access to pornography, excessive gaming and the development of unhealthy digital habits among young users.

Many Czech schools have already introduced their own rules. Some require students to hand in their phones when they arrive, while others collect devices at the beginning of lessons.

Several European countries, including Spain and Denmark, are preparing similar measures aimed at protecting children online.

World.title: Charles Bridge Undergoes Careful Cleaning as Restorers Protect Historic Stonework
World.content:
The Prague Technical Administration of Communications (TSK) has started regular maintenance work on Charles Bridge, with restorers and specialists currently removing algae, moss and unwanted vegetation.

The work is aimed at protecting the bridge’s sandstone elements from long-term damage caused by moisture and biological growth.

According to TSK, the maintenance will continue over the coming weeks and will not affect pedestrian access or tourism on one of Prague’s most visited landmarks.

Specialists are carrying out the work using climbing equipment and a support boat, allowing them to reach areas that are difficult to access from the bridge itself. The method enables detailed cleaning while avoiding any need to close the bridge to visitors.

Experts say removing vegetation is an essential part of preserving Charles Bridge. Plants and microorganisms growing on the stone surface can retain moisture, which gradually weakens the masonry and accelerates natural deterioration.

Restorers use traditional cleaning techniques

The maintenance is being carried out manually using traditional restoration methods. Workers remove algae and other growth with controlled water pressure, silicone brushes and specialised tools.

After cleaning the stone surfaces, restorers inspect and repair the joints between individual blocks. Damaged sections are cleaned to a depth of around two to three centimetres before being refilled with traditional lime mortar designed to match historical construction techniques.

Charles Bridge is among the most valuable architectural landmarks in the Czech Republic. Construction began on July 9, 1357, under the reign of Emperor Charles IV, after the previous Judith Bridge was destroyed by floods.

World.title: Canadian International High School in Prague: Your Pathway to Top Universities Worldwide
World.content:
Earning an internationally recognized high school diploma and preparing for admission to top universities no longer requires moving abroad.

Canadian International High School in Prague (CIHS) offers students in Grades 10-12 a fully English-language education based on the Canadian curriculum.

Located in the heart of Prague, CIHS combines the strengths of Canada’s education system with the quality of life and accessibility of the Czech Republic. Students receive a globally recognized diploma while studying in a familiar European environment, avoiding the higher costs and challenges of relocating overseas.

An International Diploma Recognized Worldwide

Graduates earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD), Canada’s official high school credential, recognized in more than 20 countries. The diploma provides access to over 30,000 universities and colleges worldwide, including leading institutions across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Europe.

Unlike the Czech education system, which typically spans 13 years, the Canadian program is completed in 12. As a result, students graduate a year earlier, begin university sooner, and gain an additional advantage as they build their academic and professional future.

Learning the Canadian Way

CIHS delivers its academic program in partnership with Toronto Imperial School, ensuring that students follow authentic Canadian educational standards. Courses are taught using modern curricula, teaching methods, and learning resources aligned with those used in Ontario schools.

English is the language of instruction across all subjects. An international faculty, including teachers from Canada, creates an immersive English-speaking environment that helps students strengthen their academic language skills and confidently transition into universities abroad.

To maintain high academic standards, all teachers undergo a rigorous selection process followed by professional training led by Canadian educators and the school’s academic partners.

Outstanding Value

Tuition is, on average, two to three times lower than at many international schools in Prague while offering an extensive range of included benefits.

Tuition covers:

the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD)

an iPad for both academic and personal use

for both academic and personal use a complete school uniform

an annual gym membership

continuous academic guidance and support

and support educational trips to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany

to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany participation in the Exchange program in the United States.

International Experience Beyond the Classroom

Education at CIHS extends well beyond the classroom. Each semester, students have the opportunity to join educational trips to Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Switzerland, and other destinations. These experiences include university campus visits, meetings with admissions representatives, and valuable insight into international higher education systems.

Students may also participate in the Exchange USA program, spending one or two semesters at one of 40 partner high schools across the United States. The program offers full immersion in American school life while strengthening English proficiency and developing valuable intercultural experience.

For students planning to continue their education in the U.S., CIHS also offers the opportunity to transfer to an American high school during Grade 12 on an F-1 student visa, complete their final year there, and graduate with a U.S. high school diploma.

A Modern Campus in Central Prague

The school is located in Holešovice, one of Prague’s fastest-growing and most vibrant districts. Its central location makes the campus easily accessible from virtually any part of the city by public transportation, while convenient parking is available for families.

The campus occupies a modern business complex close to parks and the Vltava riverfront, providing an ideal balance between study and recreation. Students also benefit from an on-site cafeteria and access to medical professionals, including general practitioners, dermatologists, immunologists, and allergists. Sports facilities, swimming pools, cafés, and shops are all within walking distance.

Personalized University Preparation

Beginning after Grade 10, students choose one of two academic pathways: Business & Social Science or Engineering, allowing them to focus on subjects aligned with their future university studies.

Throughout the program, experienced teachers and academic advisors provide personalized guidance, helping students develop essential academic skills, explore career options, and build competitive university applications.

Graduate Outcomes

By the time they graduate, CIHS students have gained far more than a high school diploma. They leave with:

the internationally recognized Ontario Secondary School Diploma

strong academic English proficiency

experience studying in an international environment

university admissions guidance

a global network of peers

participation in international educational programs

access to leading universities across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, and beyond.

Canadian International High School in Prague welcomes prospective students and their families to visit the campus, meet the faculty, and learn more about its Canadian curriculum. It’s an opportunity to experience a truly international education and earn a globally recognized diploma – while staying in the heart of Europe.

World.title: Former PM Orbán at the White House? Report points to discreet Washington visit
World.content:
The prospect of Orbán Viktor at the White House has returned to the Hungarian political agenda after an American newspaper reported that the former prime minister visited both the White House and the US State Department during a recent trip to the United States. However, it remains unclear whether Orbán personally met President Donald Trump.

According to the American news outlet Washington Examiner, Orbán made an unannounced stop in Washington while in the United States for matches at the football World Cup. The American report said a source familiar with the visit had confirmed that Orbán entered both institutions.

What is known about Orbán Viktor at the White House

No official account of the reported visit has been published by the White House or the State Department. The identities of the people Orbán met and the subjects discussed have also not been disclosed.

Orbán, who remains president of Hungary’s Fidesz party, said after returning home that he had held important meetings during his American trip, including unofficial discussions. He declined to identify the participants, adding further uncertainty to reports of Orbán Viktor at the White House.

The claims follow contradictory statements from senior Fidesz figures. Zsolt Németh, deputy chairman of the Hungarian Parliament’s foreign affairs committee, had said Orbán was expected to meet Trump. Bertalan Havasi, Fidesz’s communications director, subsequently denied that such a meeting was planned, insisting that Orbán’s trip was a private visit centred on the World Cup. As we wrote earlier, Viktor Orbán under fire after declaring Hungarian democracy dead — then flying to the World Cup

The available reports therefore confirm neither a face-to-face Trump–Orbán meeting nor any formal negotiations. They indicate only that Orbán reportedly visited key US government buildings during his stay.

Orbán’s changed political position

The trip was Orbán’s first known visit to Washington since losing Hungary’s parliamentary election on 12 April 2026. Péter Magyar’s centre-right Tisza party won 141 of the National Assembly’s 199 seats, ending Orbán’s uninterrupted 16-year period as prime minister. Orbán was later re-elected as Fidesz president and is now the leader of Hungary’s largest opposition party.

For international readers, this change makes the reported White House visit particularly significant. Orbán no longer represents the Hungarian government, meaning any meetings would have involved the leader of an opposition party rather than the country’s serving prime minister.

A long history between Trump and Orbán

Trump and Orbán have maintained close political relations for several years. Trump received Orbán for an official bilateral meeting at the White House in May 2019, when the two leaders discussed NATO, trade, energy and security cooperation. Trump praised Orbán’s record and his approach to border protection during the public portion of the meeting.

Their relationship continued after Trump left office. Orbán visited Trump at his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida in March 2024 and publicly supported his campaign to return to the presidency. The two met again in July 2024, following Orbán’s self-described Ukraine “peace mission”, and discussed possible ways of ending the war. A further Mar-a-Lago meeting took place in December 2024.

After Trump returned to the White House, he hosted Orbán for a bilateral lunch on 7 November 2025. Official White House photographs showed the two leaders meeting in the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room alongside senior members of the US administration.

Vice President JD Vance also appeared with Orbán in Budapest on 7 April 2026, just five days before the Hungarian election. The White House presented the visit as part of a broader US–Hungarian partnership covering energy, technology and security.

Many analysts believe that one of Orbán’s biggest mistakes was to assume that Hungarians were interested in the US Vice-President and Orbán’s battle against the EU. Voters sent a strong message in the election, and Viktor Orbán, who had been in power for 16 years, suffered a major defeat.

As we wrote a few days ago, Hungary lobbies Washington to avoid possible 100% US tariffs over Russian energy imports

Why the reported visit matters

Should the Washington Examiner report be officially confirmed, the visit would suggest that Orbán retains access to senior political circles in Washington despite his election defeat. His personal relationship with Trump could remain an important element of his international political influence and his domestic strategy as leader of the Hungarian opposition.

Until the White House, the State Department or Fidesz provides further details, however, the central question remains unanswered: Orbán may have entered the White House, but there is still no verified evidence that he met Donald Trump during this particular trip.

World.title: Hungary prescription drug VAT scrapped as government widens tax overhaul
World.content:
Hungary will abolish VAT on prescription medicines from 1 September, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on Thursday. The Hungary prescription drug VAT decision is the latest element of a large tax overhaul launched since the new government and parliament took office in May 2026.

Prescription medicines are currently subject to Hungary’s reduced 5% VAT rate, compared with the country’s 27% standard rate. The government’s decision would bring the tax on prescription-only products down to zero, regardless of whether a medicine is subsidised by the Hungarian health insurance system.

Hungary prescription drug VAT to be abolished from September

The government expects the measure to reduce the amount patients pay for medicines, although the exact saving will depend on pricing rules, health insurance subsidies and whether the full tax reduction is reflected in retail prices.

The change could be particularly important for people living with chronic conditions, elderly patients taking several medicines and those using newer, more expensive treatments.

According to Forbes Hungary, the measure could reduce annual budget revenue by around HUF 7 billion, equivalent to approximately EUR 19.2 million at the Hungarian central bank’s exchange rate on 22 July.

The announcement gives the measure a firm implementation date. Detailed legislation will still determine precisely how the zero rate is applied and how pharmacies and pharmaceutical companies must account for the change.

Five smaller taxes and charges targeted for abolition

The prescription medicine decision follows a separate tax package announced by Magyar’s government on 17 July.

Under the proposal, five relatively minor taxes and charges would be abolished: the special municipal tax, the dog ownership contribution, the immigration surtax, the carbon-quota tax and the transaction charge linked to the carbon-quota tax.

As 24.hu reported, the special municipal tax can currently be imposed by local councils, although only 25 of Hungary’s more than 3,000 municipalities reportedly use it. The dog ownership contribution is levied in 16 municipalities, while the government says the immigration surtax has never generated revenue.

The package was announced as a government decision and prepared for submission to parliament. Until the legislation completes the parliamentary process and is promulgated, the exact dates on which the taxes disappear should be treated as provisional.

Pollution charges to rise despite carbon-tax abolition

Removing the carbon-quota tax does not mean that Hungary’s largest polluters will face lower environmental costs overall.

According to 24.hu, the government also plans to double the air-pollution charge paid by companies. It intends to review the environmental impact of large industrial operators, including their water consumption and the pollution of surface water, groundwater and soil.

Companies that fail to reduce their water use or harmful emissions could eventually face further increases in environmental taxes and charges. The details of these additional measures have not yet been published.

The carbon-quota tax itself had already come under legal pressure. In April, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Hungary’s tax on carbon dioxide emission allowances was incompatible with EU law.

Corporate tax benefits and trust structures face tighter rules

The July package would also narrow selected corporate tax benefits used by large companies and certain asset-management foundations.

The government intends to end a provision under which companies could deduct three times the value of donations made to public-interest asset-management foundations from their corporate tax base.

It also plans to review tax practices connected with Hungarian private trusts, known as bizalmi vagyonkezelés. The government argues that these structures have sometimes been used to shelter large fortunes from taxation, although private trusts can also have legitimate roles in inheritance planning and the generational transfer of family businesses.

HVG said the government expects the tightening of corporate tax benefits and trust-related rules to generate tens of billions of forints in additional annual revenue. This remains a government estimate rather than an independently verified projection.

Wealth tax remains one of the largest planned changes

The most significant structural tax proposal is an annual wealth tax, but it has not yet been adopted.

The government’s current plan is based on a 1% annual tax on the portion of net wealth exceeding HUF 1 billion, approximately EUR 2.75 million. Property, investments, company shares and valuable movable assets could potentially form part of the tax base.

According to Portfolio, Magyar said the relevant legislation could be adopted by the end of October 2026, with the first revenue arriving in 2027. The government estimates potential annual receipts of HUF 300–600 billion, or approximately EUR 824 million–1.65 billion.

Important questions remain unresolved, particularly the valuation of privately owned companies, the treatment of debts and jointly owned family assets, and possible exemptions.

Other promised tax cuts have not yet been implemented

The government has also pledged to reduce VAT on fruit, vegetables and firewood and to introduce personal income tax relief for people earning below Hungary’s median wage.

One proposal would reduce the effective personal income tax burden on minimum-wage earners from the current 15% to 9%, using a tax rebate or credit. Smaller reductions would apply to earnings between the minimum and median wage.

These measures have not yet received the same firm implementation date as the Hungary prescription drug VAT change.

As Reuters reported, the government has also indicated that the special sectoral taxes imposed on banks, retailers, energy companies, telecommunications businesses and other industries will remain in place for the time being because they provide substantial budget revenue.

The emerging picture is therefore mixed: prescription medicines have received a clear starting date, several minor taxes are included in a proposed parliamentary package, while the wealth tax and broader personal income tax reforms remain under preparation.

World.title: Budapest hospital murder investigation: nurses questioned over suspected patient killing
World.content:
At least five nurses have reportedly been questioned as witnesses in a Budapest hospital murder investigation involving a 32-year-old female doctor who previously worked at the North Buda St John’s Centre Hospital. The doctor was detained in May and is suspected of killing an elderly patient receiving treatment at the hospital.

Nurses questioned in Budapest hospital murder investigation

Investigators from the Budapest Police Headquarters’ homicide division questioned nurses who were working when the patient died, according to information obtained by Hungarian news site Telex.

The questioning forms part of an investigation launched on reasonable suspicion of homicide. Police previously confirmed to the Hungarian state news agency MTI that a 32-year-old woman had been questioned as a suspect and taken into custody. A court subsequently ordered her pre-trial detention.

The woman has not been convicted of any offence. The allegations against her remain under investigation, and the principle of presumption of innocence applies throughout the criminal proceedings.

Few official details have been released because the investigation is being conducted under strict confidentiality.

Elderly cancer patient reportedly died in emergency department

According to Telex, the incident took place in May in an observation area connected to the emergency department of the North Buda St John’s Centre Hospital.

The patient was reportedly an elderly person with cancer who had been admitted to the department. The circumstances of the death have not been publicly detailed, and neither the police nor the hospital has disclosed what act the doctor is suspected of committing.

The case was reportedly brought to the attention of the hospital’s management by the head of the department. The institution later said it had immediately contacted the investigating authorities after becoming aware of a suspected crime against human life. It also initiated the necessary employment-related and professional medical measures.

The hospital confirmed that the doctor is no longer employed by the institution.

Investigators examining the doctor’s previous workplaces

Telex reported that investigators are also reviewing whether potentially suspicious deaths occurred at medical institutions where the doctor had previously worked.

The doctor graduated from medical university in 2020 and reportedly worked in anaesthesiology and intensive care before joining St John’s Hospital. She had also been employed at other hospitals in Budapest.

The reported review of earlier cases does not mean that investigators have established a link between the doctor and any other death. It is understood to be part of a wider examination of her professional history following the opening of the current case.

No further suspects have been officially identified.

As we wrote yesterday, four Hungarian paramedics beat intoxicated patient unconscious three times

What happens next in the investigation?

The statements given by nurses could help investigators reconstruct the patient’s final hours, determine who was present and establish which treatments or medicines were administered.

Medical records, staff schedules, pharmaceutical logs and expert medical opinions may also play a central role in the investigation. Authorities have not announced when the inquiry may be completed or whether prosecutors will ultimately bring charges.

Hungarian media reported that the doctor’s detention was extended until mid-September because the court identified risks including possible flight, interference with evidence or witnesses, and repeated offending.

Pre-trial detention is a procedural measure and does not constitute a finding of guilt.

The Budapest hospital murder investigation has attracted considerable public attention because it concerns an alleged killing in a medical setting, where patients are dependent on healthcare workers and often unable to protect themselves.

For now, the precise cause of the patient’s death and the evidence supporting the suspicion against the doctor remain undisclosed. Further information is expected only when investigators, prosecutors or the court release additional details.
