Police later arrived and rescued the BJP leader.

Reports of police brutality

The light-hearted moment was accompanied with multiple instances of police brutality. Police resorted to a baton charge, fired tear gas shells and deployed water cannons as a way to block the protesters.

CPI(ML) Liberation MLA Sandeep Sourav, a former AISA national general secretary, was leading the procession. "We are on the streets to bring the Modi government back to its senses.

Our demand is that in the wake of the brutal suppression of the Jantar Mantar protests, not only Pradhan but also Union Home Minister Amit Shah tender his resignation," he told PTI.

The issue also rocked the state legislative council, with RJD MLC Sunil Kumar Singh voicing anguish over the "brutal police action." Other opposition members joined in, prompting a walkout by the entire opposition after a heated exchange.

World.title: 'Sent four formal proposals': MoS Jitendra Singh invites protesters for talks at JP Nadda's place
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Union minister Jitendra Singh on Thursday invited the protesters against NEET paper leak for talks at JP Nadda's place on the central government's behalf. This comes after the talk on Monday with the Cockroach Janta Party's spokespersons failed to bear any results.

"I wish to share that in the last 24 hours as many as four offers were made to the student representatives for a dialogue. It is my humble appeal to the students on agitation that the government is ready for talks whenever you want, at whichever hour of the day and for as much length of time that you wish to," he said.

"We are ready to discuss the issue on which the agitation has happened, and all the other related issues as well.

The talks can be held with an open mind at the residence of Union health minister JP Nadda and of course I will be accompanying him. The talks could be held at Nadda's residence or at the office, or whichever of the two you wish to," he added.

Nadda reiterated Singh's remarks saying: "Yes, we are ready. Come to our residence or to our official office."

Singh further urged the protester to participate in the talks adding that the "government will go to any extent to safeguard the welfare of the students."





"Please come forward so that we find a way out of this situation in the larger interest of the students' community, youth community and the nation at large. As you would also appreciate, this morning itself, Prime Minister Narendra Modi candidly spelt out that the interest of the students is the foremost for this government. The government will go to any extent to safeguard the welfare of the students. Not only that, but the PM also took a very important decision to set up fast-track courts to deal with the cases related to those responsible for the recent paper leaks so that the final verdicts come early and decisively.

Once again, I very humbly, on behalf of the government, invite you to come forward," he said.

Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that he had ordered for setting up of fast-track courts "to ensure swift and stringent punishment for those involved in paper leaks."

"Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth! We have decided to set up fast-track courts to ensure swift and stringent punishment for those involved in paper leaks.

Have directed the concerned authorities and officials to take all necessary steps in this regard. This continues our series of steps for safeguarding the interests of students. Those who try to harm the future of our youth will not be spared," he said in a post on X.

Thursday's protest at Jantar Mantar came after overnight clashes between protesters and police, who fired tear gas and used batons to disperse crowds. It marked the second such confrontation in the national capital this week.

Despite barricades and heightened security, protesters gathered again at Jantar Mantar. Authorities also shut Delhi Metro services at 16 stations in central Delhi to curb access to the protest site.

On Monday, thousands of demonstrators attempted to march towards Parliament in defiance of restrictions before police intervened with tear gas and baton charges to stop them.

Demonstrators are seeking the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan, sweeping reforms to the examination system, and compensation for the families of students who allegedly died by suicide following exam leak incidents.

World.title: India's dying rivers: How our cities are choking their lifelines
World.content:
Yamuna river (PTI file photo)

Sahibi River in Delhi

Delhi: Yamuna that lost its floodplain



Agra: Garbage lines the polluted banks of the Yamuna near the Taj Mahal

Mumbai: When a flood exposed a dying Mithi river



Hyderabad: Musi river flowing mostly on sewage



Chennai: Cooum river reduced to urban sewer



Bengaluru: Vrishabhavathi river carrying city's waste downstream



Assam: A different kind of shrinking Brahmaputra river



Ganga: A river struggling under weight of India's cities



More than water, a test of India's cities



NEW DELHI: "Nature provides enough to satisfy every manâs needs, but not every manâs greed.â The words widely attributed to Mahatma Gandhi perhaps resonate nowhere more starkly today than along Indiaâs rivers.From Delhi to Mumbai, Chennai to Hyderabad and Bengaluru, India's urban rivers tell similar stories. They have been straightened, narrowed, encroached upon and increasingly turned into conduits for the waste generated by constantly expanding cities. Rivers that once shaped settlements now survive by carrying sewage.Yet every river has paid a different price.The Yamuna has lost much of its width to floodplain encroachments and water diversion. A recent study found that the river, which flows through the northern and southern stretches of the national capital and is also known as the Kalindi, has shrunk by nearly 68% over the past 220 years.If the Yamuna is struggling, the Sahibi River in national capital has already crossed the brink and is now ecologically degraded, according to Central Water Commission report of Jal Shakti ministry.Once an important seasonal river flowing through western Delhi, the Sahibi has gradually disappeared beneath urban expansion.Today, most residents know it simply as the Najafgarh drain or nala, a heavily polluted water channel carrying black sewage through the city.Meanwhile, Mumbai's Mithi river has been reduced to a storm-water drain overwhelmed by unchecked urban development. Hyderabad's Musi and Chennai's Cooum now carry far more sewage than freshwater, while Bengaluru's Vrishabhavathi has effectively become the city's wastewater channel.Even the mighty Brahmaputra in Northeast, relatively cleaner than most urban rivers, is steadily losing land to relentless erosion as climate change and urban pressures continue to mount.Together, they reveal a common truth: India's cities have grown by steadily reducing the space available for rivers.No river illustrates this transformation more dramatically than the Yamuna.A recent study by researchers from Delhi University and the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER), Bhopal, found that the Yamuna's average width through Delhi has shrunk by nearly 68%, from about 658 metres in 1799 to roughly 210 metres today. Water discharge has fallen by almost 90%, largely because of barrages, canals and diversion projects.The researchers also argue that shrinking floodplains have made Delhi more vulnerable to flooding. Embankments have confined the river to an increasingly narrow channel, helping explain why the capital witnessed record floods in 2023 despite lower river discharge than during the 1978 floods.The Yamuna has long occupied centre stage in Delhi's political discourse. Every election brings renewed promises to clean the river, with rival parties blaming each other for its deteriorating condition.Yet, despite repeated assurances, the river remains heavily polluted and is often described as being on the brink of becoming biologically dead.Its condition is impossible to ignore. As it winds through Delhi, the Yamuna carries dark, polluted water choked with untreated waste.Downstream, it reaches Agra, where it flows beside one of the world's greatest monuments -- the Taj Mahal. The contrast between the pristine marble monument and the foul-smelling river has become an uncomfortable reminder of India's environmental challenges.During US President Donald Trump's visit to the Taj Mahal in 2020, authorities even released additional water into the Yamuna to improve its appearance.For Mumbai, it took a disaster.The catastrophic floods of July 26, 2005, which claimed over 500 live, exposed what decades of urban expansion had done to the 17.8-km Mithi River.According to the Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA), suburban development over the past 25 years has "drastically degraded" the river's water quality. Once an important natural storm-water channel, the Mithi now carries untreated sewage, industrial effluents, municipal waste and sludge.Wetlands and floodplains have disappeared under roads, industrial estates and the Bandra-Kurla Complex. Encroachments have narrowed the river, reducing its ability to carry monsoon runoff.Although the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation said that widening and retaining-wall works have doubled storage capacity and tripled carrying capacity since 2005, officials admit pollution remains the biggest challenge.The Maharashtra Pollution Control Board identifies untreated sewage, industrial discharge and solid waste as the principal reasons behind the river's continued degradation.The BMC and MMRDA have undertaken widening, deepening, desilting, construction of retaining walls and pollution-control works along the river.The largest municipal body in country, BMC has said that retaining wall construction is nearly complete, while MMRDA is implementing sewage interception and an odour-control pilot project aimed at improving dissolved oxygen and reducing pollution.The renewed desilting and anti-encroachment initiatives after the alleged desilting scam were also reported.The Musi tells perhaps the clearest story of a river losing its natural identity.The Telangana government's Musi Riverfront Development Corporation said the river now runs "nearly dry" through Hyderabad because reservoirs upstream, catchment degradation and urban encroachments have drastically reduced natural flows.What remains is largely sewage.The Union environment ministry classifies stretches of the Musi among India's "Priority-I polluted river stretches", while the ministry of Jal Shakti said four sewage treatment plants with a combined capacity of 593 MLD have been created under the National River Conservation Plan.Even so, untreated wastewater continues entering the river through multiple nalas or drains as Hyderabad continues to expand its stretches and grow into a full-fledged metropolitan area.The state now proposes a 55-km riverfront restoration project centred on complete sewage interception, ecological restoration and flood management, an acknowledgement that beautification alone cannot revive a river whose biggest problem is pollution.The story of the Cooum is equally sobering.Flowing about 65 km, the river once supported transport and recreation before becoming overwhelmed by Chennai's urban growth.Government data cited in Parliament records Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) levels of 105 mg/litre in the Cooum -- among the highest for India's urban rivers. Healthy river water typically records BOD below 3 mg/litre.Under the National River Conservation Plan, projects worth Rs 404.25 crore created 264 MLD of sewage treatment capacity through four treatment plants, according to environment ministry. However, the project includes both Cooum and Adyar rivers.Yet Cooum's untreated sewage continues entering the river through multiple drains.A Comptroller and Auditor General audit mentioned that Tamil Nadu itself described the Cooum as "an urban sewer due to drainage of municipal and industrial waste."The Chennai River Restoration Trust has cleared encroachments, relocated thousands of families and restored stretches near Island Grounds.But officials continue to acknowledge that stopping sewage inflows remains the key challenge.If Hyderabad's Musi resembles an open drain, Bengaluru's Vrishabhavathi has effectively become one.The Central Pollution Control Board describes the river as acting as "a drain for domestic and industrial wastewater."Flowing into the Byramangala reservoir before joining the Arkavathi, the river carries much of Bengaluru's treated and untreated sewage downstream.CPCB has repeatedly directed Karnataka authorities to strengthen sewage treatment, improve industrial effluent management and protect floodplains.Heavy rainfall frequently transports garbage and plastic downstream. Residents near Bidadi have complained that truckloads of Bengaluru's waste accumulate around bridges after every major spell of rain.The river illustrates how pollution generated inside one city increasingly affects communities far beyond municipal boundaries.The Brahmaputra also nurtures some of the Northeast's fastest-growing urban centres. From Dibrugarh to the bustling metropolis of Guwahati, cities have risen and continue to expand along the banks of the mighty river.Unlike India's urban rivers, the Brahmaputra's greatest challenge is not just sewage.It is erosion.Every year, villages, farmland and public infrastructure disappear as one of the world's largest braided rivers shifts course.Recognising the scale of the problem, the Centre and the Asian Development Bank signed a $200-million agreement in 2024 to strengthen flood and erosion management across 650 km of the river in Assam.The Assam government documents described erosion as one of the state's biggest developmental challenges. Protection works continue around vulnerable areas such as Majuli, while future planning increasingly relies on satellite imagery, GIS mapping and hydrological modelling.Although pollution levels remain far lower than those in India's metropolitan rivers, officials warned that urbanisation and untreated sewage around cities such as Guwahati are emerging concerns.The Brahmaputra demonstrates that shrinking rivers are not always about pollution. Sometimes, rivers lose land while people lose homes.The Brahmaputra's relentless erosion and annual floods continue to threaten millions in the Northeast. Fed by heavy monsoon rains, the river frequently swells beyond its banks, leaving large parts of the region inundated.If the Ganga is India's most revered river, it is also among its most stressed. Flowing through some of the country's fastest-growing cities, including Haridwar, Kanpur, Prayagraj, Varanasi, Patna and Kolkata.The Ganga faces a different challenge. Unlike the Yamuna, its biggest burden stems from industrial pollution, compounded by religious offerings, ritual waste, funeral remains and the enormous crowds that gather during events such as the Mahakumbh.For centuries worshipped as "Maa Ganga" and celebrated as a symbol of purity, the river today ranks among the world's most polluted waterways.The river has increasingly become a victim of urban expansion, pollution and shrinking natural floodplains.As cities have grown, the Ganga's floodplains have steadily disappeared beneath roads, residential colonies, commercial developments and embankments. These encroachments have narrowed the river's natural corridor, reducing its ability to spread during the monsoon, recharge groundwater and sustain wetlands.Pollution remains the river's biggest challenge. Despite significant investments under the Namami Gange programme under PM Modi-led government, untreated sewage from expanding urban centres continues to enter the river through hundreds of drains.Industrial effluents, particularly from leather tanneries, sugar mills, distilleries and textile units, add to the pollution burden, although regulatory enforcement has improved in recent years. During the lean season, reduced environmental flows due to barrages and water diversion further limit the river's ability to dilute pollutants.Large-scale restoration efforts have expanded sewage treatment capacity, intercepted drains and improved riverfront infrastructure in several cities. Yet government assessments continue to emphasise that engineering projects alone cannot revive the Ganga.Taken together, these rivers tell a remarkably similar story despite their different geographies.Some have been narrowed by embankments. Others have lost wetlands, floodplains and natural channels to highways, commercial districts and housing colonies. Many now receive more sewage than freshwater.Governments have invested thousands of crores in programmes such as Namami Gange, the Yamuna Action Plan, the National River Conservation Plan and city-specific restoration projects. New sewage treatment plants, riverfronts and desilting drives are important interventions.But almost every official report arrives at the same conclusion: rivers cannot be revived by engineering alone.Unless untreated sewage is intercepted, floodplains are protected, encroachments are prevented, and ecological flows are maintained, India's rivers will continue to shrink-even if they appear cleaner on the surface.The question is no longer whether India's cities need rivers. They always will. The real question is whether India's cities can continue to grow without taking away the very space that allows rivers to remain alive.

World.title: FSSAI must finalise, notify Front-of-Pack nutrition Labelling norms in a time-bound manner: Parliamentary Panel
World.content:
A Parliamentary Panel on Thursday (July 23, 2026), asked food regulator Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to finalise 'Front-of-Pack Nutrition Labelling' (FOPNL) regulations in a time-bound manner to ensure that consumers get to know nutritional information in a simple manner.

A Standing Committee on Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution has presented a report on 'Regulation of Packaged Commodities with Specific Reference to Sugar Content in Baby Products and other Food Products' in Parliament.

The panel was dismayed to note that the draft FOPNL regulations were notified on September 13, 2022, and that more than 14,000 stakeholder comments have been received, which are presently under examination and wider consultation.

"The Committee observe that over two years have lapsed since the draft notification, and the continued delay in finalising the regulations has resulted in the absence of simplified and interpretative front-of-pack information, particularly in relation to sugar content," the report said.

With rising consumption of packaged and ultra-processed food, the panel stressed the timely availability of clear and easily understandable nutritional information to consumers for enabling informed dietary choices.

The panel pointed out that the present labelling framework relies primarily on numerical disclosures such as grams and percentage of recommended dietary allowance. Such labels might not be readily understood by all consumers at the point of purchase.

"The absence of simple interpretative tools such as warning labels or colour-coded indicatory limits the effectiveness of such disclosures in guiding consumer behaviour," it stated.

Hence, the committee recommended that the FSSAI should finalise and notify the FOPNL regulations within a defined and time-bound framework.

It further suggested that the FOPNL should provide accessible, at-a-glance information to help consumers quickly and easily identify the nutritional status of a product.

The panel advised that the notified regulations should incorporate simple, clearly visible and interpretative labelling mechanisms, including colour-coded indicators for sugar levels in all products, using a three-colour format (red, yellow, and green) to denote high, medium, and low sugar levels.

The labelling should incorporate appropriate warning labels for products high in sugar.

World.title: India sends 4.5 tonnes of medical aid to Kenya to boost Ebola preparedness
World.content:
India has delivered the first tranche of medical assistance to Kenya to strengthen the country’s preparedness and response to the Ebola virus and other infectious diseases, according to an official statement.

The first consignment, weighing 4.5 tonnes, was handed over by Indian High Commissioner Adarsh Swaika to Kenya's Cabinet Secretary for Health Aden Duale at the Jomo Kenyatta International Airport in Nairobi on Wednesday (July 22, 2026), the Indian High Commission said in the statement.

The initiative follows India's supply of more than 45 tonnes of medical assistance to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention in May and June to bolster the continent's preparedness against Ebola.

India has been among the first responders during Kenya's public health emergencies. During the COVID-19 pandemic, it supplied 1.12 million doses of made-in-India vaccines to Kenya under the Vaccine Maitri initiative, besides providing medicines and other medical assistance.

The recent shipment comprises 279 packages of essential medical supplies, including personal protective equipment (PPE) kits, sample transportation kits, infrared thermometers, face shields, heavy-duty protective boots and other infection-prevention materials, the High Commission said in the statement.

A second tranche of assistance will be delivered shortly, it said.

The assistance is aimed at strengthening Kenya's long-term public health preparedness and response capacity by supporting disease surveillance, safe collection and transportation of samples, infection prevention and control, and the protection of frontline healthcare workers, it said.

The two countries have also expanded cooperation in the health sector through grant assistance for medical equipment, including a Bhabhatron radiotherapy machine for Kenyatta National Hospital and diagnostic equipment for the Kenya Navy Hospital in Mombasa.

According to the High Commission, over 10,000 Kenyans travel to India every year for medical treatment, while Indian pharmaceutical products account for more than half of Kenya's pharmaceutical market.

World.title: Pandemonium in both Houses of the legislature over Patna protests
World.content:
Both Houses of the Bihar legislature on Thursday (July 23, 2026) witnessed turmoil as members of the ruling NDA and the Opposition traded charges over the violent students' protest in the State Capital a day earlier.

Proceedings in the Assembly, which began at 11 a.m., were adjourned by Speaker Prem Kumar till lunch within minutes when several members of the ruling side rose in their seats, blaming the opposition for the day-long pitched battle between the police and the protesters. Many of the NDA legislators had trooped into the Well and some of them, including Sanjeev Chaurasia and Vinay Bihari of the BJP and JD(U)'s Manjeet Singh, were seen heading menacingly towards the opposition MLAs.

The NDA legislators were heard alleging that "goons, not students" were taking part in the "so-called protests" on Wednesday (July 22, 2026) when at least 22 police personnel sustained injuries in a day-long pitched battle, which had ended in a final showdown close to the Chief Minister's residence.

Emerging from the House after it was adjourned, opposition MLAs led by Alok Mehta of the RJD told reporters, "The BJP and its allies have not learnt their lessons despite seeing so much public anger. They alleged that the protesters were goons, though their own conduct today befitted ruffians.

We had to run for our lives." However, BJP leader and Minister Ram Kripal Yadav maintained, "The Congress-led opposition is trying to plunge the country into anarchy. The diabolical plan was on display in Patna yesterday when anti-social elements, posing as students, clashed with police, roughed up journalists and even manhandled a couple of our fellow MLAs. The government will identify the miscreants and take them to task."

Notably, at least two BJP MLAs, Vinay Bihari and Rohit Pandey, were also attacked by the protesters who spotted them heading for the assembly to attend the monsoon session, which comes to a close on Friday (July 24, 2026). Vehicles of the legislators were also damaged by the rampaging mob, and videos of the two MLAs running to safety have gone viral.

In apprehension of further nuisance, gates of the Vidhan Sabha premises were sealed, and legislators, journalists and staff members remained locked inside well after the day's proceedings had come to an end.

Mr. Yadav also claimed to have learnt that "a female constable was stabbed with a dagger by one of the criminals who prowled the streets pretending to be student activists". "It was all part of a huge conspiracy that was aimed at bringing a bad name to our Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary and, eventually, destabilise the government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi", alleged Mr. Yadav.

When Patna Senior Superintendent of Police Kartikeya K. Sharma was asked about the reported stabbing of a female constable, he replied, "We are looking into it. Action will be taken upon investigation". However, CPI(ML) Liberation MLA Sandeep Saurav, who had led the protest, debunked the charge and said, "It is high time that the BJP and its allies realised that the country's youth is outraged over the brutal repression of Jantar Mantar protests in Delhi where policemen had the temerity to poke sticks into the bodies of girls who were demanding action over NEET exam paper leaks".

"It is laughable that the NDA, which rules the Centre as well as the State, and has made all the institutions dance to its tunes, is pointing fingers at the opposition. They run the risk of facing greater public fury unless they stop quarrelling with us and get down to solving the problems that have brought our youth out on the streets," he said. Meanwhile, uproarious scenes were also seen inside the legislative council after an adjournment motion moved by RJD's Abdul Bari Siddiqui was rejected by Chairman Awadhesh Narayan Singh.

Soon, a number of the opposition MLCs rushed into the Well, prompting the chairman to adjourn the proceedings till 2.30 pm. Later, senior JD(U) leader and Minister Ashok Choudhary told reporters, "The government will take action against those involved in unlawful activities yesterday. Of course, they have been instigated by the opposition parties. We have learnt that BJP workers were attacked by their counterparts in the Congress with sticks fitted with nails".

Mr. Choudhary was referring to the clash that had erupted at Sadaqat Ashram, the State Congress headquarters, where several BJP workers, led by State President Sanjay Saraogi, were demonstrating to register their protest against the gherao of PM Modi's residence by Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi, among others.

However, Mr. Siddiqui, whose party is a Congress ally, said, "The ruling dispensation is shutting its eyes to the fact that the atmosphere today is very much like in 1974, when the youth had rallied behind Jayaprakash Narayan and the mass uprising set the tone for the overthrow of the government a few years later."

World.title: Kerala government accords top priority to empowerment of women and backward communities, says Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan
World.content:
Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan has that the United Democratic Front government has accorded top priority to make women and backward communities self-reliant.

Women were the most impacted at times of a social or financial crisis as they had to bear the brunt of economic crisis in their families, illness and other difficulties in their lives, he said after inaugurating ‘Samagra – 2026’, the State-level inauguration of various welfare projects initiated by the Kerala State Backward Classes Development Corporation at Palluruthy in Kochi on Thursday (July 23, 2026).

He said that the government would ensure steps to provide skill training, guidance and facilities to market the products made by women to make them self-reliant. The government had lined up over 540 projects as part of its 100-day action plan. A separate portal had been set up to provide information to the public on the progress of each project. Review meetings were held every 20 days to ensure that the projects were implemented as per the schedule, he said.

‘Invest money’

The Chief Minister urged the women to invest the money they saved by availing themselves of the ‘Priyadarshini’ free travel scheme on Ordinary buses of the Kerala State Road Transport Corporation in the ‘pink chitty’ scheme of the Kerala Sate Financial Enterprises.

K.A. Thulasi, Minister for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Backward Classes Welfare, said in her presidential address that the Kerala State Backward Classes Development Corporation had drawn up plans in tune with the government’s resolve to provide a helping hand to the backward communities. She said that the ‘Priyadarshini’ free travel scheme and the low-interest loan initiatives had gained attention among the public.

V. E. Abdul Gafoor, Minister for Fisheries; Kochi Mayor V.K. Minimol; and MLAs Mohammed Shiyas, Deepak Joy, and Tony Chammany took part in the function.

World.title: Jantar Mantar protest LIVE: CJP rejects Centre's talk offer, calls for nationwide protest on July 24 against police brutality
World.content:
Union Minister Jitendra Singh on Thursday (July 23, 2026) said that the Centre is ready for talks with the Cockroach Janta Party amid the latter’s protest in Delhi’s Jantar Mantar over paper leaks and the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. However, CJP has declined the invitation and said that the talks need to happen at Jantar Mantar or at another neutral venue.

Earlier today, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, in a social media post, said that his government will set up fast-track courts for action against those involved in paper leaks. “Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth! We have decided to set up fast-track courts to ensure swift and stringent punishment for those involved in paper leaks. Have directed the concerned authorities and officials to take all necessary steps in this regard. This continues our series of steps for safeguarding the interests of students. Those who try to harm the future of our youth will not be spared,” Mr. Modi said.

Also read: The cockroach dilemma facing India’s political parties

The CJP reacted to the announcement and said that while fast-track courts will address what happens after the paper leak, why there are paper leaks is a larger issue that the government must address.

Mr. Wangchuk on Wednesday (July 22, 2026) said he would end his indefinite hunger strike if the Centre gives an unequivocal assurance that no punitive or retaliatory action would be taken against students and youth who participated in the protest against alleged examination irregularities.

Also Read: 16 metro stations, including Rajiv Chowk, Patel Chowk, Delhi Gate and Central Secretariat, closed, says DMRC

Delhi Police has registered 10 FIRs against unidentified persons in connection with the ongoing protest by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at Jantar Mantar, an officer said on Wednesday (July 22). Of these, four FIRs have been filed at the Sansad Marg police station, three at Connaught Place, and one each at Mandir Marg, Kartavya Path and Barakhamba Road.

World.title: Centre invites protesters for talks at J.P. Nadda’s office; CJP rejects offer
World.content:
As the ongoing protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhi’s Jantar Mantar refuse to die down, Union Minister Jitendra Singh on Thursday (July 23, 2026) said the Central Government has reiterated its commitment to dialogue, stating that it has extended multiple formal invitations to student representatives for discussions.

Follow Jantar Mantar protest LIVE updates on July 23

Mr. Singh, speaking to ANI, said it’s not a ‘prestige issue for the government’ and emphasised he along with Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda are ready for discussions with the CJP, either at Mr. Nadda’s residence or office, beyond any time-limit.

“This is a part of the series of continuous steps taken by the government for the welfare of the students. Humbly, I appeal to you all to come and have discussions,” he said. Mr. Singh stated that four invitations for talks have been extended to the CJP since Wednesday (July 22).

The CJP has categorically rejected the Minister of State PMO’s offer. Addressing the students gathered at Jantar Mantar, spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka said the CJP has declined the offer to have talks at Mr. Nadda’s residence or office.

“The Ministers told us not to call them to Jantar Mantar since people are very angry and they won’t be able to come there. We offered to hold talks at a neutral venue,” Mr. Ranka said as the crowd cheered. The CJP will only hold talks with the government at either Jantar Mantar or a neutral venue nearby, he said.

“We have also told the government the talks will only proceed if the Centre can offer us something concrete, otherwise, don’t waste our time,” Mr. Ranka added.

The government outreach comes as as the national capital witnesses large-scale protests at Jantar Mantar, led by ‘Cockroach Janta Party’ and various student organisations. The protesters are demanding Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation following a series of irregularities in exams, including the leak of NEET-UG paper.

Earlier this week, Mr. Nadda had met with a CJP delegation to hear their demands, which include the resignation of the Education Minister and compensation for affected students.

PM Modi speaks on students’ protest

Prime Minister Narendra Modi, earlier in the day, said that the government has decided to set up fast-track courts for paper leak cases. Mr. Modi stated in a post on X, “We have decided to set up fast-track courts to ensure swift and stringent punishment for those involved in paper leaks,” in his first direct comments tied to major protests by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on NEET-UG paper leak.

World.title: West Asia war LIVE: Houthis strike tankers in Red Sea; first since Saudi-linked shipping blockade via Bab el-Mandeb
World.content:
The Houthis said in a statement issued via their SABA news agency that they had struck two tankers named Encelia and Layla in the Red Sea, leading to fires on both vessels.

Also read: How the second phase of the Iran-U.S. war started and why it is raging | Explained

That would be their first reported attack on a vessel since they announced a blockade of Saudi-linked shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait earlier this week in retaliation for the kingdom’s blockade on Yemen and a recent attack on the international airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sanaa.

The continued American airstrikes are occurring as a dispute over the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for global energy, remains largely closed. The closure of the strait, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas passed during peacetime, has jolted the world economy with effects far beyond West Asia.

World.title: Things to do in Kochi
World.content:
Looking for things to do in Kochi this weekend? Here are some options for you.

Art with a heart

A Place Called Tommorow, an upcoming exhibition, is a gathering of 22 contemporary artists from Kerala. This group showcase is more than a visual excellence; it is a fundraising initiative organised under the patronage of the Rotary Club of Cochin Pioneers. The show, which opens at Durbar Hall Art Gallery, is being held in association with Federal Bank.

The curatorial note states that each canvas and sculpture in this collection represents a gesture of solidarity. The participating artists address the need to secure housing for the underprivileged. In this context, the gallery ceases to be a passive space and becomes a site of active transformation.

“In the cultural landscape of Kerala, a home is more than a structure; it is a thara (foundation) for dignity and a padi (threshold) for the future. The works presented here — diverse in media and visual language — are united by a singular objective: to transform artistic value into the bricks and mortar of social change. By making these original works available for acquisition, the artists and the Rotary Club invite the public to participate in a direct act of community building. The participating artists include Aji Adoor, Anto George, Martin OC, Prakasan KS, Radha Gomaty, Sabita Kadannappally, and Sara Hussain. The show, curated by Deepa Gopal and Jiss Victor, is on from 11am to 7pm, July25-28.

Watch a play

As part of BEAME’s monthly programme, in assocation with Ernakulam Karayogam, Nanthyattukunnam Nataka Arangu presents the Malayalam play Chappa, written and directed by MS Shivakumar. The play recounts the labour allocations system of the 1940s-50s at the Cochin Port. Copper tokens — chappa — would be thrown into crowds of workers forcing them to fight each other to earn a day’s wage. The play blends Chavittunadakam with the action. To be staged at TDM Hall, Ernakulam, on July 28, 6.30pm.

Interactive show

Watch Six Seven, an interactive theatre improv show by The Improverts. Expect scenes made on the spot, characters born in seconds and moments you may never see again. The spontaneous act is sure to be full of surpises and energy. On July 25 at 6.30pm at Mamangam Dance Company, Kadavanthra. For information, check out @beacn.social on Instagram.

World.title: Can’t deny father child’s overnight custody citing mom’s transfer: Karnataka High Court
World.content:
Noting that the child was comfortable with both parents, the Karnataka High Court has upheld a family court’s order granting a father monthly overnight custody of his minor daughter, and held that the mother’s transfer was no ground to deny such custody.

Justice P Sree Sudha observed that the mother had no objection to the seven-year-old child continuing audio and video calls with her father as per the family court’s directions.



“It appears to the court that the child is comfortable with both parents. The distance between Bengaluru and Pune is 838 kilometres. Even a flight journey takes one and a half hours…It seems that both the parents are educated and well placed in society. In view of her transfer to Pune, her contention that overnight custody cannot be granted is not acceptable,” the July 22 order noted.

World.title: Writer’s Corner: How a Bengaluru techie fell in love with Gothic horror
World.content:
Bengaluru is a city teeming with writers, in Kannada and English alike. Walk through the city’s bookstores, festivals, or cafes, and it’s hard not to meet an author. Shival Gupta is an exception, though—one of the few writing in gothic horror in English.

“I was always a big fan of gothic horror,” says Gupta. “I used to read a lot of it growing up, including Shirley Jackson and Edgar Allan Poe…psychological horror that uses the storytelling medium to convey grief, ambition, or a dark psychology within humanity.”



A software engineer working with a major payment portal, Gupta is the author of The Violins That Play at Kiff House, a gothic novel published in 2023. But this foray into gothic fiction is not his first brush with publishing. As a schoolboy, Gupta wrote ‘Truth Trust & Promise: Discovery of the Sword Case’, which was released at an event by then President A P J Abdul Kalam after the young author reached out to him over email.

World.title: ‘Anyone who took law into their own hands not students’: Rupali Ganguly on CJP protest
World.content:
As the student protests demanding education reforms continue to gather momentum and dominate the national conversation, more voices from the film and television industry have been weighing in on the issue. Over the past few days, celebrities including Salman Khan, Alia Bhatt, Hrithik Roshan and Naseeruddin Shah have expressed solidarity with the students while urging the government to engage in dialogue. Now, television actor Rupali Ganguly has expressed her opinion, saying while their demands for accountability over paper leak is valid, anyone who takes law in their own hands cannot be called a student.

‘Do not let anyone hijack your movement’

Taking to X, Ganguly wrote, “Those who take the law into their own hands, vandalize public property, and attack the police cannot be called students. Such actions only weaken a legitimate cause.” She further said, “The demand for justice over paper leaks is valid. Students deserve a fair examination system, accountability, and strong safeguards to ensure that such incidents never happen again. In recent paper leak cases, governments and investigating agencies have launched probes, arrested suspects, and initiated legal action against those allegedly involved. At the same time, efforts have been announced to strengthen the examination process and prevent future leaks.”

World.title: Army, NDRF deployed as torrential rain floods South Gujarat
World.content:
Relentless rain pounded south Gujarat for a second straight day Thursday, triggering widespread flooding that brought parts of Valsad, Navsari, and Surat districts to a standstill and forced the evacuation of thousands of residents.

It also prompted the deployment of the Indian Army, the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), and the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) for rescue operations.

Even as Prime Minister Narendra Modi reviewed the situation with Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel, Ahmedabad’s first major spell of monsoon rain flooded roads, shut schools for two days, and paralysed transport across the city.

According to Nitin V Sangwan, District Collector, Valsad, more than 500 people had been shifted from low-lying areas to district shelter homes. A government statement said 70 Army jawans had been deployed, along with a team of 25 firemen in the district, for rescue operations.

Army, NDRF deployed as torrential rain floods South Gujarathttps://t.co/4cD2H3MvE5 pic.twitter.com/gtGDpsqHJx — The Indian Express (@IndianExpress) July 23, 2026

“All three rivers, Daman Ganga, Par and Auranga, are flowing above the danger and top-up level in the district, causing a flood-like situation in different talukas, including Valsad town. Three teams of SDRF and three teams of NDRF are on their toes to carry out rescue and relief operations. So far, no casualties have been reported, but we have sought a chopper from Mumbai, which will land shortly, and it will be used during emergencies,” Sangwan said.

By 12 pm, Valsad town had received 199 mm of rainfall, Dharampur 340 mm, Pardi 341 mm, Kaprada 370 mm, Umbergaon 684 mm, Vapi 319 mm, and Nanapondha 312 mm.

Over thousands of cars parked on the roadside and in the basements of residential and commercial complexes were submerged in the rainwater. The water entered the houses in low-lying areas.

All industrial and commercial establishments, schools, and colleges remained shut in the district. Over 500 district and taluka panchayat roads were closed to traffic and barricaded to prevent accidents.



Three NDRF and five SDRF teams were currently deployed in Valsad district, even as the state government sent in five more boats for rescue.

Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi, State Finance Minister Kanu Desai, and the in-charge minister of Valsad district, Naresh Patel, also reached the district and visited different areas affected by the downpour.

The ministers also met with the district administration and ensured that affected people were shifted to shelter homes and that they received proper care.

Rain havoc in Ahmedabad

Ahmedabad came to a halt as the heavy rain flooded roads, leading to traffic jams, suspended bus services, flooded underpasses, and water in low-lying residential areas and forced authorities to shut schools on Thursday and Friday, placing “safety on top priority”.



According to the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation control room, areas in the southwest and northwest received the highest rainfall between 6 and 10 am. These included Sarkhej and Bopal with 115 mm of rainfall each, Bodakdev with 112 mm, Jodhpur with 111.5 mm, Thaltej with 108 mm, Science City with 100 mm, Memnagar with 95.5 mm, Gota with 76.5 mm, Ognaj with 74.5 mm, and Chandlodiya with 72.5 mm.

Several roads in Sarkhej, Bopal, Bodakdev, Jodhpur, Thaltej, Shilaj, Science City, Gota, Ognaj, and Akbharnagar areas were flooded, leading to the closure of 15 Bus Rapid Transit System (BRTS) stations.

The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation also shut down seven underpasses around 10 am to avoid accidents. The Shahibaug underpass was opened around 1 pm.

District Education Officer, Ahmedabad, declared all schools shut on Thursday and Friday, placing “safety on top priority”, a statement said.



Authorities also issued warnings of flooding in the Sabarmati after the flood control department opened 15 of the 30 gates at the Vasna barrage, releasing 29,994 cusecs of water downstream, which could put villages around it at risk.

A waterlogged Surat

Two weeks after the heavy rain-triggered floods in the creek claimed nearly 40 lives in Surat, the city was waterlogged again following continuous rainfall since Wednesday night, disrupting traffic and forcing road closures.

In a grim reminder of the previous floods, thousands of cars and bikes were submerged in flooded basement parking lots.

The Surat Municipal Corporation (SMC) shifted 2,392 people from affected areas to shelter homes by Thursday morning.



Evacuations were carried out from low-lying areas across six city zones. As many as 890 people were shifted from the Pandesara, Bhestan, and Sachin areas alone, including textile units and the GIDC industrial estate. Over 16 boats were deployed to move residents from rainwater-affected areas.

Sources in the civic body said one NDRF team and three SDRF teams were on alert in flood-affected areas across the city. The civic body distributed over 1,100 food packets, 1,550 drinking water bottles and 1,250 milk pouches among affected residents. During surveillance, more than 30 people found unwell were provided with on-the-spot medical assistance.

Waterlogging was reported at 60 locations across the city, with eight spots cleared so far. The SMC has closed over 24 roads and suspended city bus and BRTS services on affected routes.

Civic body sources said 77 JCB machines, 249 trucks, and tractors were deployed in rain-affected areas. More than 37 dewatering pumps were also put into operation at residential basements, shopping complexes, and other locations to drain accumulated water.

Thousands evacuated in Navsari



Manish Gurwani, Collector, Navsari, said two men were washed away amid the heavy flow of water after they removed the barricade ahead of a road connecting Ganpur to Linjar village in Vansda taluka in the district. Gurwani said authorities are trying to locate them.

The district administration has shifted more than 2,000 people from low-lying areas along the river to safer places.

Over 230 panchayat roads and 12 state highway roads at various locations have been blocked to the public amid heavy rain in Navsari. Over thousands of cars and vehicles were submerged in the water in the Navsari district.

The district administration has closed all schools, colleges, and other educational institutions amid the red alert declared by the Meteorological Department.



The rainfall on Thursday morning was recorded at 17 inches in Vansda and 14 inches in Khergam, while other talukas received around 7 inches each.

The water level in the Purna River was at 25 feet, above the danger level of 23 feet; the Ambika at 39 feet, above the danger level of 28 feet; and the Kaveri at 29 feet, above the danger level of 19 feet. Juj and Keliya dams were also overflowing.

Sources said that two SDRF teams are on the spot in low-lying areas, shifting the people.

World.title: ‘Woh soft launch…’: Anshula Kapoor on introducing her fiancé to family early; expert explains
World.content:
Anshula Kapoor, who recently got married, once opened up about her relationship with fiancé Rohan Thakkar, explaining why she chose to introduce him to her family early on rather than keep the relationship private. Speaking in an old interview with Hauterrfly, she said, “Why should you hide? There’s nothing to hide. So the minute that I was sure that I was giving this relationship a proper go-ahead, Jhanvi was the first person Rohan met.”



Explaining why she chose Janhvi Kapoor to meet Rohan first, Anshula clarified that it was not about seeking approval. When asked whether Janhvi is a good peer lens to check. She joked, “No. She’s a very nice person; she’s very sweet, gharelu. But it was more than that; she has my best interests at heart… Yeah, it was more of the fact that she was just trying to — I just wanted, firstly, to introduce, woh soft launch hota hai na family mein, and she felt like a safe place to do this in. So this worked out great, as they say, the rest is history (sic).” Her remarks highlight how having a trusted family member can sometimes make important relationship milestones feel less intimidating.
