World.title: At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.content:
This year’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai was larger, more crowded, and more politically prominent than in previous editions.

President Xi Jinping attended the event for the first time, while more than 1,100 companies showcased computing systems, AI agents, robots, and other products aimed at workplaces, factories, and consumers. In-person visits topped 400,000, and tickets were reportedly resold for more than 1,000 yuan.

Xi called for wider access to open-source AI, and China launched a 29-country AI cooperation body, placing issues of governance, access, and international coordination alongside the usual displays of commercial technology.

Beyond the speeches and packed exhibition halls, the most revealing conversations were practical: lowering computing costs, putting AI agents to work, managing new safety risks, and building businesses that can last.

Here are four takeaways from this year’s WAIC.

Computing power gets practical

Computing power was one of the most discussed topics at this year’s WAIC, second only to AI applications by number of related forums. But the focus moved beyond building more data centers or training ever-larger models.

Two questions dominated: what the next generation of computing power might look like, and how to make today’s resources cheaper and more efficient.

At one flagship forum on the future of computing, scientists discussed emerging approaches including quantum computing and space-based computing. Among the speakers was Pan Jianwei, a leading quantum physicist and recent recipient of a top United Nations science award, who outlined recent advances in the field.

Pan also urged caution. Although the field has reached a series of important milestones, he said, building a general-purpose quantum computer capable of quickly solving problems with clear practical value will still require years of sustained research. The academic community, he added, has a responsibility to help the public assess the technology realistically and guard against an industry bubble.

Companies also seemed more focused on improving the efficiency of existing computing resources and reducing the cost of each AI query.

Some were working to improve the performance of models trained mainly on Nvidia chips when deployed on Chinese chips. Others focused on allocating and managing computing resources more efficiently.

Rather than chasing only the most powerful and expensive models, many Chinese AI companies appeared more concerned with making AI cheaper to run.

AI Governance and Safety

AI governance and safety were prominent throughout this year’s WAIC, from high-level forums to the opening ceremony and President Xi Jinping’s speech.

Brian Tse, an AI safety expert and founder and CEO of Concordia AI, said he has seen more discussion in China around cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure, especially the risks posed by frontier AI models.

“The threat landscape is evolving rapidly,” Tse said. “Many experts at the forums expressed concern that threats and potential misuse are developing faster than society’s current defenses.”

The concerns also appeared to be shifting beyond large language models and the harmful content they can generate. More attention was paid this year to the risks posed by autonomous AI agents, which can plan tasks, make decisions, and interact with other tools.

On July 15, just before WAIC, China’s new rules on AI anthropomorphic interaction took effect, targeting services that simulate human personalities and sustained emotional interaction. The rules prohibit providers from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors and bar services from inducing emotional dependence or addiction.

In May, regulators also released guidance on the standardized application and development of AI agents, including plans to explore digital identity management for them.

“China is positioning itself as an architect of multilateral AI governance,” Tse said.

AI lands at work

One phrase heard often at this year’s WAIC was AI’s real-world “landing” — the push to move the technology out of demos and into everyday work. Companies ranging from Tencent and Alibaba to smaller startups showed AI products aimed at offices, factories, and consumer services. AI agents were among the most visible examples.

At booths run by major tech firms, exhibitors demonstrated how agents could be built into corporate workflows, from searching internal documents to generating reports and coordinating routine tasks.

The impact could be broad because many of these companies’ software systems are already embedded in Chinese workplaces. Adding AI agents to existing platforms may prove easier than persuading companies to adopt entirely new tools.

Still, genuinely effective applications appeared limited. Office productivity remained the most obvious use case, while other areas were less developed.

Robotics and embodied AI occupied an entire floor at this year’s WAIC. Visitors could still see robots performing awkward dances or taking six minutes to make a cup of tea. But some companies were beginning to move beyond staged demonstrations, showing robots designed for inspection, manufacturing, logistics, and other industrial uses.

The founder rush

Some of the most revealing conversations at this year’s WAIC took place after the official sessions ended.

Across after-hours gatherings, private meetups, and open-mic sessions, young founders and industry professionals swapped ideas on AI agents, robotics, and productivity tools. Some gatherings ran late into the night, with almost any topic open for discussion.

Many entrepreneurs seemed eager to absorb every new idea, experiment, business opportunity, and professional connection they could find.

But that urgency also carried risks. Some founders said their AI ventures were burning through years of savings. Many still lacked a convincing answer to a basic question: how their projects would generate lasting value and revenue.

That tension ran through WAIC: crowded halls, founders eager to share projects and failures, and a palpable fear of moving too slowly and missing the AI wave. The mood mixed optimism with anxiety, much of it fueled by the speed of the technology and the sheer volume of information surrounding it.

The conversations also suggested a maturing industry. More speakers and founders were asking not only what AI could do, but where it could be useful, how it could be governed, and which businesses could survive once the initial excitement fades.

(Header image: A humanoid robot from a Chinese robotics firm waves Chinese national flags during the 2026 WAIC in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP Photo via VCG)

World.title: The Soybean That Built Northeast China
World.content:
In 2020, I traveled to Kaishantun, a town in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture near the China-North Korea border. It fit every stereotype of the deindustrialized Northeast. Young people had left. The government had built two rows of barracks-style apartment blocks for the elderly residents who remained. Kaishantun railway station had long been abandoned. On the station sign, the space for the next stop was blank. North Korea lay only a few hundred meters away.

On the walk back, I wandered into a derelict movie theater and discovered several reels of old film. Later restored, they revealed something astonishing: clips of a symphony orchestra and a traditional folk orchestra.

What kind of small town could support two orchestras of its own?

As I dug deeper into the history of my home region, Northeast China, I found that part of the answer lay in a crop that today frequently appears in international headlines: soybeans. A century before China became a major importer of American soybeans, it was the world’s leading producer.

In August 1872, three Japanese army officers, disguised as merchants and acting on the orders of General Saigō Takamori, traveled through “Manchuria,” the term they used for Northeast China. Saigō was studying relations between Japan, Korea, and China as he prepared a future campaign against Korea. A year later, the officers submitted their “Report on an Inspection of Manchuria,” one of Japan’s earliest intelligence briefings on China. The report includes a detailed discussion of soybeans:

“From winter through spring, soybeans are continuously transported by inland waterways. Regardless of the cold, day and night, dozens of horse-drawn carts move in a single direction. Large merchants purchase the beans and pile them into circular mountains more than two rooms across and over 6 meters high … The quantity stored is beyond counting.”

In 1885, another Japanese military officer, Kikuchi Setsuzō, passed through Northeast China on his return from the Russian Empire. Along the way, he studied how Qing forces fed their military horses, which he regarded as superior to those of Japan and Russia. Qing troops processed the residue left after soybean oil extraction into pressed soybean cakes for animal feed. Each cake weighed about 12.5 kilograms and could feed three horses for a day. Kikuchi even claimed such soybean resources would be “indispensable” for training military horses.

In the 19th century, Kikuchi was among the few who grasped soybeans’ strategic significance. The crop had reached Europe and North America in the 18th century but remained largely a botanical curiosity. A handful of enthusiasts, such as the Austro-Hungarian agronomist Friedrich Haberlandt, sought to introduce soybeans into Western diets. Yet while they imported the crop, they did not import the culinary traditions that had made it a staple across Asia.

In East Asia, by contrast, people had accumulated more than a thousand years of experience cooking and consuming soybeans. They also recognized the crop’s value as animal feed. After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Japanese rice farmers gradually abandoned traditional fish-based fertilizers in favor of soybean cake. Between 1882 and 1902, Japan’s soybean imports increased four-hundredfold.

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 finally alerted the world to soybeans’ importance. European military observers noted that both sides relied heavily on the crop. Japanese forces consumed soybeans directly and used them in military logistics. Russian forces fed them to cavalry horses. Soybean oil served as a raw material for soap and as a lubricant for artillery equipment and wagon axles.

The soybean trade expanded rapidly. A 1911 report from the Customs Service in Shanghai observed that “It is only in the last three years that soya beans have become important in intercontinental commerce,” calling their rapid emergence from obscurity “one of the most remarkable commercial events of recent times.” In the same year, the U.S. ambassador in Beijing told the State Department that Northeast China had until recently been largely unknown for its commercial potential, despite supplying soybeans to global markets. He observed that its economic trajectory was now drawing attention in major cities including New York, London, Hamburg, and Seattle, and attributed this shift to soybeans, whose rapidly growing demand he characterized as “phenomenal in trade annals.”

Estimates suggest that Northeast China accounted for between 16% and 42% of global soybean production between 1908 and 1930, shipping soybeans, soybean oil, and soybean cakes to the rest of China, Japan, and Europe. Until the eve of World War II, China produced more than 80% of the world’s soybeans. The crop became widely known as the “Manchurian bean.”

Soybeans were also among the most important exports of a then largely impoverished China. After World War I, their importance grew rapidly, and by the 1920s they had overtaken tea and silk to become China’s leading export, accounting for more than 20% of export earnings.

As trade expanded, so did Japan’s territorial ambitions. In the run-up to Japan's formal annexation of Korea in 1910, Yanbian became a frontier along the China-Korea border where Chinese and Japanese spheres of influence met directly. Japanese strategists viewed the wider Yanbian area as a gateway to the interior of Northeast China and sought to build a railway linking the Korean port of Chongjin with China’s inland Northeast. General Hasegawa Yoshimichi, commander of Japanese forces in Korea, regarded Yanbian as a vital supply corridor for sustaining colonial rule on the peninsula. He advocated occupying the region to secure access to strategic commodities such as soybeans.

Over the following three decades, Japan steadily expanded its influence in Northeast China. In 1931, Japanese forces seized the region and took control of its economic resources. This expansion, justified in the name of protecting economic “lifelines,” would later extend across Asia during the Pacific War to the oil fields of Burma, Sumatra, and Borneo; the rubber plantations of Malaya; and the chromium and iron deposits of the Philippines.

In Yanbian, war and colonial rule only reinforced the region’s economic importance. Beyond soybeans, Japanese authorities coveted the region’s timber. In Kaishantun they established the Eastern Manchuria Rayon Pulp Company, whose output eventually surpassed that of most producers in Japan. After the Chinese Communist Party won the civil war and founded the People’s Republic of China in 1949, the new state’s flagship pulp and paper enterprise was established in the same town.

Factories brought more than jobs. They brought hospitals, movie theaters, and even symphony orchestras.

Yet by then Northeast China was no longer the sole center of the global soybean trade. By the early 20th century, American farmers were already familiar with soybeans, using them to replenish soil and support other crops. After the Russo-Japanese War, however, the crop’s industrial potential attracted growing attention.

One unlikely champion was Henry Ford. He used soybean protein and soybean-oil derivatives in automotive components and in 1941 unveiled a prototype car with body panels made largely from soybean-based plastic. To demonstrate its strength, he famously struck it with an axe.

Ford’s soybean car was hardly a commercial success, but it generated publicity for the crop. When Japan severed America’s access to Asian supply routes during the Pacific War, soybeans were transformed from an industrial curiosity into a strategic resource. Combined harvesters and advances in plant breeding helped American farmers scale up production.

By the 1950s, the center of gravity in soybean production had shifted decisively to the Americas.

One final piece was still missing from the modern soybean map: Brazil. In the early 1970s, a major El Niño event, a climate pattern that warms the Pacific Ocean, devastated the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, a key source of animal feed, driving demand for soybean meal. Prices surged, and in 1973 the Nixon administration imposed restrictions on soybean exports.

History then took an ironic turn. Japan, heavily dependent on imported American soybeans, increased its investment in South American agriculture, while Brazil’s agricultural research agency, Embrapa, developed soybean varieties suited to tropical conditions. The result was a dramatic expansion of Brazilian production.

In 2024, more than 70% of China’s soybean imports came from Brazil. When trade tensions between China and the United States intensified in 2025, Brazil became China’s principal alternative for former U.S. suppliers.

Northeast China remains the country’s most important soybean-growing region, producing the beans that become tofu and soy milk on Chinese tables. But it no longer supplies the world with soybean oil and soybean meal. Once-thriving industrial towns have been swept up in the tide of deindustrialization, leaving behind abandoned railway stations and empty movie theaters.

From an unassuming plant in Northeast China to one of the world’s most traded agricultural commodities, the soybean’s history is ultimately a story of globalization. A soybean harvested in Paraguay may be processed in Argentina, sold to China by a trading house in Geneva, and eventually find its way into milk, cakes, or meat products. It shapes what we eat, how we farm, and how nations interact with one another. It also shapes the fate of countless small towns, including places like Kaishantun.

(Header image: A soybean field in Xingkai Lake Farm, Heilongjiang province, 2023. VCG)

World.title: China Bans AI Romantic Partners, Virtual Relatives for Minors
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018790/China Bans AI Romantic Partners, Virtual Relatives for Minors
World.content:
China’s first regulations on AI companion services have taken effect, setting new limits on chatbots designed to simulate emotional bonds with users and barring platforms from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors.

The rules, jointly issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China and four other government departments in April, came into force July 15. They cover AI products designed to mimic human personalities, emotions, and communication styles.

The measures come after years of growing use of AI companion apps in China, where users have created virtual lovers modeled on TV characters, recreated deceased relatives through customized voices and personalities, and treated chatbots as long-term emotional confidants.

Regulators and state media have warned that such apps carry security and compliance risks, including emotional dependence, sexually suggestive content, and weak protections for minors.

As such, the new regulations prohibit AI apps from generating content for minors that may incite unsafe behavior, trigger extreme emotions, or foster habits that could harm their physical or mental health. They also should not excessively cater to users in ways that induce emotional dependence or addiction and damage their real-life relationships; manipulate users’ emotions to push them toward unreasonable decisions that harm their legitimate rights and interests; and act as virtual relatives or virtual partners to minors.

If a user is believed to be overly reliant on or addicted to a service, the platform must send them a reminder about overuse every two hours.

Zhang Linghan, dean of the Institute of Artificial Intelligence Law at China University of Political Science and Law, told domestic media outlet China News Weekly that the emotional investment offered by anthropomorphic interactive services can easily lead to psychological dependence in users, resulting in a decline in real-world social skills, particularly a weakening of the ability to resolve emotional conflicts and build deep relationships.

The new regulations apply to any services deemed as designed to foster emotional connection and interaction. Other AI chatbot functions, such as intelligent customer service, knowledge-sharing tools, and workplace assistants, are not affected.

The same day the regulations went into effect, tech giants ByteDance and Alibaba discontinued their AI companion features on Doubao and Qianwen, respectively. Qianwen shut its companion service down immediately, while Doubao is offering users a three-month grace period to migrate their data to its sister app, Maoxiang, before it is permanently deleted on Oct. 15.

Tech companies had already begun increasing regulations of their chatbots and companion services, primarily due to findings of suggestive content in their chats. On June 30, Tencent removed its AI companion service from its chatbot Yuanbao.

In April 2023, leading Chinese AI model developer MiniMax removed its AI companion product, Glow, from multiple app stores due to pornographic content. Its product manager told domestic media that “80% of users would engage in suggestive or sexually explicit conversations with the AI companions they created within Glow.”

In June 2025, AI chat app Zhumengdao was summoned to appear before the Shanghai Municipal Cyberspace Administration for generating vulgar and suggestive content that harmed minors.

After the new regulations took effect, several other AI chatbots reported an influx of users migrating from Doubao and Qianwen, and began requiring ID verification before use.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Malte Mueller/Getty Creative/VCG)

World.title: Between Two Needles: The Chinese Garment Factory Built Around Dialysis
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018794/Between Two Needles: The Chinese Garment Factory Built Around Dialysis
World.content:
GUANGDONG, South China — Above a dialysis clinic in Guangzhou, southern China’s Guangdong province, 67 kidney patients sew, iron and finish garments for customers in China and overseas. Many once worked as chefs, truck drivers or machine technicians before illness pushed them out of their jobs. Three times a week, they leave the factory floor for four hours of dialysis, then return to work.

The workshop was opened in 2023 by Xie Qiang, a retired oncologist who wanted patients to earn an income without hiding their condition. It offers routine, independence and a community of people living with the same illness. But it is also a business struggling to survive. Dialysis interrupts production, inexperienced workers make costly mistakes, and delayed orders threaten already narrow margins.

In June, Sixth Tone followed the workers, managers and Xie as they tried to keep the factory running. Their daily routines show how difficult it is to meet deadlines and maintain quality while making room for dialysis, fatigue and medical complications.

Additional reporting: Jiang Xinyi; story editors: Qi Ya and Apurva; script editors: Apurva and Wu Huiyuan.

World.title: Philippines: No permission-seeking in 2024 Ayungin ‘understanding’ with China
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) The DFA pushes back after China’s envoy claims the Philippines agreed not to construct on the BRP Sierra Madre in a 2024 temporary deal

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Thursday, July 23, that a temporary deal with China in 2024 does not mean Filipinos seek permission for resupply missions, allow the boarding or inspections of Philippine ships, “concede the Philippines’ sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction” in Ayungin Shoal in the West Philippine Sea.

“As stated from the outset, the Provisional Understanding is a set of principles and approaches observed by both sides in order to avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation in the conduct of the Philippines’ routine rotation and resupply (RORE) missions for daily necessities to the BRP Sierra Madre in Ayungin Shoal,” said the DFA in a statement.

The provisional understanding, sometimes called a provisional agreement, was made between the two countries in 2024 a month after China Coast Guard (CCG) personnel harassed Filipino soldiers who were already moored by the BRP Sierra Madre, a warship that serves as a makeshift outpost in Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal in the West Philippine Sea. That 2024 incident resulted in one soldier losing his thumb and Philippine Navy equipment destroyed as the CCG intervened in a RORE mission to the Sierra Madre.

It’s a deal that’s made headlines recently after a July 20, 2026 confrontation between the CCG and Philippine soldiers, the first in two years. CCG personnel entered Ayungin Shoal and sailed around the BRP Sierra Madre, taking photos and videos, according to the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP). Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan, speaking to media on Tuesday, July 21, said the CCG were reportedly inspecting the warship to check on reported construction activities as proof of the Philippines bringing in supplies — a supposed violation of the agreement, according to the ambassador.

Play Video

Much has been said about the provisional agreement — many of it rooted in speculation, no thanks to its secrecy.

The exact details of the understanding have never been made public. Ironically, its secrecy is one of the few things made public about the agreement.

“The Philippines’ legal position, grounded in [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea] and vindicated by the Arbitral Tribunal, remains unchanged and non-negotiable,” said the DFA.

By stating that the agreement “does not concede the Philippines’ sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction,” the DFA is indirectly addressing Jing’s claims.

Ayungin Shoal, as affirmed by the 2016 Arbitral Award, is a low-tide elevation that is part of the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone where it should enjoy exclusive rights to exploit and protect resources. That means the Philippines should not be restrictied from activities in those waters, to include building or strengthening structures such as the BRP Sierra Madre.

“The Philippines continues to conduct rotation and resupply missions, including normal shipboard activities in BRP Sierra Madre, as a matter of routine government function within Philippine jurisdiction and in the exercise of its sovereign rights under international law particularly UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award, and will continue to do so for as long as necessary in line with the national interest,” said the DFA.

The agreement was made under former foreign affairs secretary Enrique Manalo, although the current Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro was then the undersecretary that led efforts to speak to China.

“There is no mention of that undertaking in the provisional understanding,” Lazaro said in a press briefing following the ASEAN foreign ministers meeting on Thursday, referring to Jing’s claim that construction and construction materials were not permitted. – Rappler.com

World.title: SEA Games champion Dines Dumaan seeks financial help after road crash
World.content:
STANDOUT. Pencak silat athlete Dines Dumaan of the Philippines during the 2017 Southeast Asian Games.

MANILA, Philippines – Pencak silat standout Dines Dumaan, who delivered medals for the country on the international stage, needs financial help for a head surgery following a motorcycle accident.

According to the Philsilat Sports Association, the 31-year-old pride of Panitan, Capiz, underwent operation on Thursday, July 23.

“Dines needs financial assistance. He was brought to Capiz Doctors’ Hospital yesterday morning,” the Philsilat Sports Association told Rappler on Thursday.

No official report has been released but a video circulating online shows Dumaan riding a motorcycle before he crashed into a roadside structure at around 4:25 am on Wednesday, July 22, his helmet falling off after the impact.

“At this time, only Dines knows exactly what happened, as the family was informed only after he had already been brought to the hospital yesterday morning,” the Philsilat Sports Association said.

In one of the biggest feats of his career, Dumaan captured the Philippines’ lone gold medal in pencak silat in the 2017 Southeast Asian Games in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

That ended the country’s 12-year drought for a pencak silat gold in the SEA Games, or since Marniel Dimla ruled in the 2005 edition hosted by the Philippines.

A year later, Dumaan bagged bronze in the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta, Indonesia.

His other accolades include a gold in the 2017 Asian Pencak Silat Championship in Chungju, South Korea, and a bronze in the Philippines’ hosting of the 2019 SEA Games.

Fellow pencak silat athlete Ian Christopher Calo appealed for help for his “brother,” saying Dumaan needs approximately P100,000 as downpayment for his surgery.

Dines Dumaan. Papart Ian Facebook page

“Dines is a Filipino athlete who wholeheartedly brought honor to our country through the medals he won. Now, he is the one who needs our support in the most important battle of his life,” Calo wrote on his Facebook page in Filipino.

“Any amount or help you can give will be a great help to him and his family.”

Rappler reached out to Dumaan’s family members but has yet to get a response. – Rappler.com

World.title: Google hit with $1-billion EU fine, in ‘constructive’ talks to avoid more penalties
World.content:
GOOGLE. A Google logo is seen at a company research facility in Mountain View, California, US, May 13, 2025

Google is likely to avoid fresh fines as regulators laud good progress in its ongoing efforts to comply with the European Union rules

BRUSSELS, Belgium – Alphabet’s Google was fined a total of €890 million ($1 billion) on Thursday, July 23, for flouting European Union rules aimed at reining in the power of Big Tech, the European Commission said.

However, the US tech giant is likely to avoid fresh fines as EU regulators lauded good progress in its ongoing efforts to comply with the landmark legislation.

The fines underscored Europe’s determination to prevent Big Tech companies from thwarting rivals, defying US criticism and retaliatory tariff threats.

One fine of €460 million was handed out to Google by the European Commission under the Digital Markets Act for favoring its own services in shopping, hotels, transport, and sports results in search results.

A second fine of €430 million targeted Google’s restrictions on its app store Google Play preventing app developers from steering users free of charge to cheaper offers on rival app stores or websites.

Reuters was the first to report on both fines, which are the first for the US tech giant under the DMA but the fifth and sixth overall for anti-competitive practices, making for total penalties of €10.38 billion over nearly two decades.

“Our duty and obligation is to comply with the laws, that our laws are fully respected,” EU antitrust chief Teresa Ribera told reporters when asked about US pushback.

“The DMA is to make sure we have a fair and level playing field. With these decisions we want to make sure there is competition,” EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told reporters.

Google, which has 60 days to comply with the Commission’s orders to treat rivals in a fair and non-discriminatory manner and to allow app developers to steer users away from its app store, criticised the EU findings and said it might take the Commission to court.

“To comply, we are having to strip away real-time Search features Europeans love – like instant pricing and direct availability for hotels, flights, and restaurants – and dismantle safety protections on Google Play,” Google President of Global Affairs Kent Walker said in a statement.

“This isn’t fair competition; it’s product degradation driven by a small group of self-serving complainants, with European businesses and consumers taking the hit. Regulation should improve products, not make them worse,” he said.

More fines unlikely given ‘constructive dialogue’

The Commission, which acts as the EU competition enforcer, pointed to a “constructive dialogue” with Google and significant progress made to comply with the DMA, indicating that daily penalties for non-compliance are likely off the table.

“Google has proposed and started testing changes to how it presents its own services on Google Search for free services such as shopping, hotels and flights,” the Commission said, calling it substantial progress.

“The Commission also notes that Google has proposed and started testing changes to how it presents shopping ads and content related services, such as sports,” it said, adding it would assess the changes and continue talks with Google.

The EU watchdog also said Google may apply the principles of Thursday’s decision to its AI-generated summaries known as AI Overviews and AI Mode and that talks would continue to this end.

Google’s changes to its steering terms on Google Play received a tentative thumbs up from the Commission.

“These constitute good progress towards compliance and will also be assessed in light of the cease and desist order of today’s decision,” it said.

Europe’s crackdown on Big Tech has angered US President Donald Trump’s administration, which has threatened to retaliate with tariffs for what he said are moves targeting US companies while US lawmakers have also piled on the pressure.

The fines are the third under the DMA after penalties handed out to Apple and Meta Platforms in April last year. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tropical Depression Kiyapo speeds up as it heads for extreme Northern Luzon
World.content:
PAGASA emphasizes that Tropical Depression Kiyapo may trigger floods and landslides, as moderate to intense rain will be hitting Northern Luzon. The southwest monsoon is also affecting various parts of the country.

MANILA, Philippines – Tropical Depression Kiyapo accelerated on Thursday, July 23, as it continued heading for extreme Northern Luzon, where it could make landfall on Friday, July 24.

In a briefing at around 5 pm on Thursday, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Kiyapo was already 640 kilometers east of Tuguegarao City, Cagayan, as of 4 pm.

The tropical depression is moving northwest at a relatively fast 30 kilometers per hour (km/h).

It maintained its strength, with maximum sustained winds of 45 km/h and gustiness of up to 55 km/h.

Kiyapo is still expected to pass very close to the northeastern portion of mainland Cagayan on Friday morning or afternoon, then pass very close to or make landfall in Cagayan’s Babuyan Islands in the afternoon or evening.

PAGASA added that Kiyapo may strengthen into a tropical storm on Friday, and subsequently into a severe tropical storm on Saturday, July 25.

The weather bureau emphasized that Kiyapo may trigger floods and landslides, as moderate to intense rain from the tropical cyclone will be hitting Northern Luzon in the next 48 hours. Likely to be most affected are the following provinces:

Thursday afternoon, July 23, to Friday afternoon, July 24

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 millimeters): Cagayan, Apayao, Ilocos Norte

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Isabela, Batanes, Abra, Ilocos Sur

Friday afternoon, July 24, to Saturday afternoon, July 25

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Abra, Ilocos Sur

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Cagayan, Apayao, Batanes, Ilocos Norte, Kalinga, Benguet, La Union

At least a dozen provinces on the western side of the country are also dealing with significant rainfall from the southwest monsoon or habagat. Floods and landslides are possible, too.

Thursday afternoon, July 23, to Friday afternoon, July 24

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Antique, Guimaras, Negros Occidental, Negros Oriental, Zamboanga del Norte, Zamboanga del Sur, Zamboanga Sibugay, Lanao del Norte, Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Sultan Kudarat, Sarangani

Friday afternoon, July 24, to Saturday afternoon, July 25

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Palawan, Occidental Mindoro, Antique, Iloilo, Guimaras, Negros Occidental

Saturday afternoon, July 25, to Sunday afternoon, July 26

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Occidental Mindoro

Meanwhile, as of 5 pm on Thursday, the following areas are under Signal No. 1 due to the expected strong winds from Kiyapo:

Batanes

Cagayan including Babuyan Islands

Isabela

Apayao

Abra

Kalinga

Mountain Province

Ifugao

Ilocos Norte

Ilocos Sur

northern part of Aurora (Dilasag, Casiguran, Dinalungan)

northern part of Nueva Vizcaya (Bagabag, Diadi, Bayombong, Ambaguio, Villaverde, Quezon, Solano)

northern part of Quirino (Maddela, Cabarroguis, Saguday, Diffun, Aglipay)

northern part of Benguet (Buguias, Mankayan, Bakun, Kibungan)

The highest possible tropical cyclone wind signal due to Kiyapo could be Signal No. 2, but PAGASA is not ruling out Signal No. 3 if Kiyapo becomes a severe tropical storm while crossing the Batanes-Babuyan Islands area.

PAGASA added that the southwest monsoon and the periphery or outer bands of the tropical cyclone will bring strong to gale-force gusts to these areas:

Thursday, July 23

most of Mindanao, Siquijor, Bohol, Southern Leyte

Friday, July 24

most of the country

Saturday, July 25

most of Luzon, most of Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Davao Oriental, Dinagat Islands

As Kiyapo is moving faster and relatively nearer to extreme Northern Luzon, sea conditions are also worsening, particularly in Batanes, Babuyan Islands, and the tip of mainland Cagayan.

Up to very rough seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

Seaboards of Batanes and Babuyan Islands; northeastern seaboard of mainland Cagayan – waves up to 4.5 meters high

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

World.title: San Miguel ‘hiding’ behind PPP law? Students launch constitutional challenge
World.content:
'We thought about not just the remaining trees that they intend to cut down but also the people of Manila who will be affected by this,' the petitioners say

MANILA, Philippines – Students are challenging before the Supreme Court the constitutionality of the provisions in the Public-Private Partnership Code that insulates PPP projects from temporary environmental protection orders (TEPO) and similar legal reliefs.

The petitioners are Joaquin Lorenzo Bautista, Elisha Marielle Zantua, Benjamin Luis Francia, Paul Benedict Carollina, Hanna Eliza Marie Guerra — the same five students who filed a petition before the Manila Regional Trial Court Branch 41 in May to try to stop San Miguel Corporation’s tree-cutting activities for its Southern Access Link Expressway project through the issuance of a TEPO.

The court junked their petition, prompting them to go to the Supreme Court.

“When the Manila RTC denied our TEPO, we were ready to withdraw our application,” Joaquin Bautista, one of the petitioners in both cases, told Rappler. “We were ready to give up, but we thought about not just the remaining trees that they intend to cut down but also the people of Manila who will be affected by this.”

During the hearing at the Manila regional trial court in June, San Miguel cited provisions in the PPP law to argue their exemption from such temporary reliefs. The students are now saying these are unconstitutional as it violates their right to a balanced and healthful ecology.

The provision in Section 23 of the PPP Code says only the Supreme Court can issue such temporary reliefs to PPP projects.

The students said limitations set in the PPP Code not only violate their constitutional right to a balanced and healthful ecology “but also render trivial and effete the doctrine of intergenerational responsibility.”

“When a statute establishes a complete judicial shield over an infrastructure project, preventing any timely judicial review of its ecological toll, it leaves future generations entirely unprotected against reckless ecological modifications,” read their petition filed before the High Court.

They added, “By hiding behind the absolute immunities of the PPP Code, respondent SMC [San Miguel Corporation] may successfully weaponize statutory technicalities to shield itself from environmental accountability.”

PROTECT. Members of environment protection group Kalikasan People’s Network for the Environment, along with other civil society organizations, march in Manila to protest the widespread cutting of trees for the 40.62-kilometer Southern Access Link Expressway (SALEX) project, on May 26, 2026.

Moreover, the provision in the code that suspends lower court judges if they do issue a TEPO against PPP projects “engenders an unconstitutional chilling effect,” they said. The petitioners argued that this intimidates lower court judges and undermines judicial independence.

“It may be about time that the deleterious provisions of this PPP Code, designed obviously to protect the interests of private corporate behemoths that enter into PPPs with the government,” they said.

The PPP Code or Republic Act 11966 is the legal framework that governs the implementation of PPP projects in the country. Under this law, the prohibition for lower courts does not apply “when the matter is of extreme urgency involving a constitutional issue, such that unless a temporary restraining order is issued, grave injustice and irreparable injury will arise.”

The respondents in the petition are Manila RTC Branch 41 Presiding Judge Rosalyn Mislos-Loja, SMC Southern Access Link Expressway Corporation, and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources.

– Rappler.com

World.title: MariBank now officially reclassified as digital bank by BSP
World.content:
MariBank is the Philippine banking arm of Singapore-based MariBank, which belongs to Sea Limited, the technology group behind e-commerce platform Shopee

MANILA, Philippines – MariBank has officially become a licensed digital bank after the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) approved its reclassification from a rural bank, formalizing a business model that had already been operating almost entirely through digital channels.

For existing customers, however, little changes. Customers do not need to take any action following the reclassification. (READ: [Finterest] Is a digital bank safe, and how can you best use it?)

MariBank said clients can continue using the app and services as before, with deposits of up to P1 million remaining insured by the Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation (PDIC). The bank also remains under BSP supervision.

The change is largely regulatory. Before securing its digital banking license, MariBank operated under a rural bank license while offering app-based banking products nationwide. As a rural bank, it had to operate a physical banking presence in Laguna. With the new digital license, Maribank may operate without branches that offer banking services, though it must still maintain a head office in the country. MariBank can also now officially market itself as a digital bank.

“MariBank has been an early supporter of the Bangko Sentral’s digital payments agenda, having been among the first financial institutions to offer free fund transfers. Now, as a fully operational digital bank, I am confident that MariBank will deliver an even stronger value proposition, driving innovation and competition while benefiting both consumers and the broader banking industry,” BSP Deputy Governor Mamerto Tangonan said in a statement.

MariBank is the Philippine banking arm of Singapore-based MariBank, which belongs to Sea Limited, the technology group behind e-commerce platform Shopee. The company rebranded from SeaBank Philippines to MariBank in 2025.

One feature that helped MariBank stand out in its early years was its unlimited free fund transfers, which came well before many larger banks droped their transfer fees. That advantage has since narrowed in recent weeks after the BSP pushed banks to drop their transfer fees.

But perhaps counterintuitively, Lim said the shift has actually eased one of the costs of being an early mover.

“When we were one of the few banks offering unlimited free transfers, we attracted customers making hundreds of transactions, and subsidizing that became expensive,” he said in a LinkedIn post.

Now that more banks have adopted free transfers and switch costs have fallen, heavy transaction volumes are spread across more institutions. Lim said MariBank no longer had to absorb outsized transfer costs simply to remain competitive.

The country’s digital banks now include Maya Bank, GoTyme Bank, Tonik Digital Bank, UNO Digital Bank, UnionDigital Bank, Overseas Filipino Bank, and MariBank. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: No gov’t order to seize homes without solar panel permits
World.content:
An analysis using Google's SynthID technology showed the audio contained an AI-generated watermark, while two other AI detection tools found the clip likely to be AI-generated

Claim: Palace Press Officer Claire Castro announced that the government will be taking over houses that use solar panels without the proper permits.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: Several videos containing the claim have been circulating on Facebook, with the most popular one gaining 3.2 million views, 19,200 reactions, and 3,400 shares as of writing.

The video shows Castro, seemingly in a press briefing with the Malacañang Press Corps, saying: “Pag nakita ang bahay mo na may solar at walang permit, ang bahay mo ay kukunin ng gobyerno. Ito ang magiging patakaran para sa lahat ng mamamayan simula ngayon.”

(If your house is found to have solar panels without permits, then your house will be taken by the government. This will be the rule for all citizens starting now.)

Comments on the videos show that users believe the video to be authentic, with most expressing anger toward the supposed policy. “Bakit ninyo kukunin? Binili ko ‘yan. Ubos na ba ‘yung nasa kaban?” one of the top comments says.

(Why will you take our houses? I bought it. Have our public funds run out?)

The facts: An analysis of the viral video clip using Google’s SynthID technology showed the audio contained an AI-generated watermark. This means that the audio was generated or altered using Google’s AI tools.

Two other AI detection tools found the clip likely to be AI-generated. HiveDetect found it 81.8% likely to be an AI-generated video, while UndetectableAI found the audio to only be 1% real compared to the likelihood of it being AI-generated.

None of the transcripts of Malacañang’s press briefings in July 2026 contain the statement in the fake video clip.

The government has made no such announcement on any other channel, either. No credible media outlets have reported on the supposed policy.

SynthID: SynthID is Google’s watermarking tool that embeds digital watermarks directly into AI-generated images, audio, text or video across Google’s generative AI consumer products. These watermarks are invisible, but can be detected using Gemini.

Permits for solar panels: Solar panel regulation has drawn criticism in recent months. This came after Meralco called for stricter guidelines on solar panel installation earlier in May, with the Department of Trade and Industry later saying it was preparing rules to regulate manufacturers of solar panel systems.

These moves have been met with strong backlash online that has continued into the month of July. Rising power rates this month have renewed public criticism toward attempts to regulate solar panel installations.

Debunked: Castro has become a regular target of several false claims in recent months. Rappler has debunked some of these claims:

– Shay Du/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. You may also report dubious claims to the #FactsFirstPH tipline by messaging Rappler on Facebook or Newsbreak via Twitter direct message. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Legarda demands urgent action on classroom shortage
World.content:
Sen. Loren Legarda —Photo from her office

MANILA, Philippines — With Congress preparing to deliberate on the proposed 2027 national budget, addressing the nationwide classroom shortage should be one of the government’s most urgent priorities, Sen. Loren Legarda said in a statement issued on Thursday.

“When a child goes to school, the only thing he should be thinking about is his studies and not where he will sit or if the classroom is safe or if there’s still space for him,” Legarda said in Filipino.

“It’s hard to learn in a classroom that’s crowded, hot, and unsafe. Teachers also find it hard to teach when there’s a lack of space and facilities. Every classroom not built, or left unusable, is a direct blow to access and quality of education,” she added.

Article continues after this 

Legarda stressed that the 2027 national budget must respond to the scale of the classroom backlog by ensuring sufficient funding for school infrastructure, including the construction of new classrooms and the repair, rehabilitation, and replacement of aging and unsafe school buildings.

READ: Bicam-approved voucher bill to ease classroom crowding

Disrupted education

Citing figures from the Second Congressional Commission on Education (Edcom II), she said the country would need more than 165,000 classrooms, considering that over 51,000 existing classrooms may need to be condemned by 2028 due to age and deterioration.

The classroom deficit is projected to rise to more than 200,000 by 2028 if current gaps are not addressed.

According to Legarda, the education of millions of Filipino children is disrupted every day due to overcrowded classrooms, shifting schedules, makeshift learning spaces, and aging school buildings.

Article continues after this 

These conditions put students’ safety at risk, limit teachers’ ability to teach effectively, and deny children the learning environment they need.

Besides the classroom shortage, the country continues to grapple with a learning crisis.

Article continues after this 

Edcom II has also identified inadequate school infrastructure, overcrowding, and unequal learning conditions among the structural barriers that continue to undermine learning outcomes.

Support for schools in far-flung areas

The classroom shortage, Legarda said, is a challenge affecting students nationwide, from densely populated urban schools struggling with severe overcrowding to remote communities where access to safe and adequate learning facilities remains limited.

She added that while the problem is nationwide, children in geographically isolated and disadvantaged communities continue to bear the heaviest burden of decades-long infrastructure gaps.

In this regard, Legarda underscored the importance of the proposed Geographically Isolated and Disadvantaged Areas (GIDA) Schools Act, of which she is the principal author, as a key measure to address the unique challenges faced by the country’s most underserved schools.

The measure, whose enrolled copy was transmitted to the Office of the President on June 25, 2026, awaits presidential action.

The bill seeks to institutionalize stronger government support for schools in geographically isolated, disadvantaged, and conflict-affected communities by addressing long-standing gaps in infrastructure, learning resources, teacher support, and access to quality education.

“The classroom shortage is a problem not only in far-flung areas. It is a national challenge that schools face in cities and towns,” she said.

“But schools in GIDA are usually the ones with the biggest needs and the hardest to reach. So while we’re addressing the nationwide classroom shortage, we also need to ensure that children in the farthest communities will not be left behind,” she added.

READ: Loren Legarda demands real funding for education law at CHED anniversary

Accelerating classroom construction

Legarda acknowledged that local government units, the private sector, and civil society can help accelerate classroom construction. But these partnerships with them should complement — not replace — the government’s responsibility to invest in public education.

On June 9, Legarda filed Senate Resolution No. 434, seeking an inquiry into classroom congestion, infrastructure gaps, land titling bottlenecks, procurement delays, and inter-agency coordination issues affecting the timely construction of school facilities.

Legarda is also a co-author and co-sponsor of the proposed Classroom-Building Acceleration Program Act, which seeks to speed up classroom construction by allowing qualified local government units and civil society organizations to undertake school building projects using national appropriations, subject to Department of Education standards.

“Not only do we need to set aside a big budget. We also need to make sure that every peso set aside for education will become classrooms that are finished on time, safe to use, and will benefit children. This is our responsibility to every parent hoping to give their children a good future through education,” Legarda said.

She stressed that laws, budgets, and government programs must be measured by the difference they make in the lives of Filipino children.

“The measure of success is not how many laws are passed or how big a budget is approved. The true measure is if more Filipino children can study in a safe, orderly, and decent classroom,” she said.

World.title: Angara issues rules for program to aid learners, coaches in contests
World.content:
Qualified student athletes, along with their coaches, will get financial support under the Gas-Tuklas Program —Photo from the Department of Education

MANILA, Philippines — Education Secretary Sonny Angara has issued the guidelines for the pilot implementation of a program that will give targeted financial aid to students and teacher-coaches participating in national and international competitions endorsed or acknowledged by the Department of Education (DepEd) for the school year 2026–2027.

The program is called the Government Assistance and Subsidies-Training and Upgrading Knowledge for Learners, Teachers, and Achievers in Schools (Gas-Tuklas).

It’s backed by an allocation of P100.8 million under the 2026 General Appropriations Act, according to a DepEd statement issued on Thursday.

Article continues after this 

READ: Marcos vows support for student-athletes

“President [Ferdinand] Bongbong Marcos [Jr.] believes that we should not allow any talent to be left behind just because of a lack of support,”

“Through Gas-Tuklas, we aim to lessen the burden for our learners and teacher-coaches so that they can focus on improving themselves and giving honor to the country,” he added.

The program covers the following:

students in public and private elementary and secondary schools

students under DepEd-recognized Alternative Learning System modalities

officially designated teacher-coaches who provide direct coaching and training

Those from low-income households will be given priority.

Article continues after this 

The program supports participation in individual and team competitions, including academic, sports, creative and cultural, and other related and interdisciplinary competitions.

Subject to approval, availability of funds, and applicable government rules, the assistance may cover registration fees, training and preparation expenses, travel expenses, and boarding and lodging.

Article continues after this 

The actual amount of assistance to be approved will depend on the allowable expenses, competition requirements, availability of funds, and applicable government rules.

Applications, which are open throughout the school year 2026–2027, will undergo review and endorsement at the school, Schools Division Office, and Regional Office levels before final validation and approval or disapproval by the DepEd Central Office through the Government Assistance and Subsidies Service (GASS).

Applicants must submit the required documents to their respective school heads at least 45 working days before joining the competition.

The list of competitions endorsed or acknowledged by DepEd will be posted and periodically updated on the official DepEd website.

READ: Marcos pushes world-class sports education for future Filipino champions

Competitions not included in the published list may be submitted to GASS for evaluation.

Through the pilot implementation, DepEd will gather implementation data, policy insights, and operational evidence to guide policy refinement and future decisions on the possible expansion of Gas-Tuklas as a national support mechanism for learners and teacher-coaches across all regions.

World.title: ‘Ipaglaban Mo’ long-time TV host Atty. Jose Sison dies
World.content:
Atty. Jose Sison, long-time host of television show “Ipaglaban Mo,” dies on July 23, 2026. (Photo by Jopet Sison / Facebook)

MANILA, Philippines — Lawyer and long-time host of television show “Ipaglaban Mo” Attorney Jose Sison died on Thursday at the age of 88, his son confirmed.

“This morning, July 23, 2026, our Papa Ping peacefully joined our Creator,” his son Jopet, who is also a lawyer, wrote in a Facebook post.

READ: ‘Ipaglaban Mo’ ni Atty. Jose Sison balik-ABS-CBN

Article continues after this 

“We are comforted that he lived a full life as a lawyer, a husband to Josie, a father to his six children, and a grandfather to his sixteen grandchildren,” Jopet noted.

The son also said that his father’s wake will be held at Ascension Chapel in The Immaculate Conception Cathedral of Cubao in Quezon City starting Friday afternoon.

The interment will be at Heavens Gate 1 Memorial Park in Antipolo City on Tuesday, July 28.

“Ipaglaban Mo” is a drama anthology which featured real life legal cases brought before the Supreme Court.

Hosted by the elder Sison, it first aired on IBC-13 in 1988 until it was transferred to ABS-CBN in 1992 until its last episode in 1999.

Article continues after this 

READ: Jopet Sison replaces Noli de Castro as Senate bet under Aksyon Demokratiko

The award-winning show returned to television under the ABS-CBN in June 2014 with both Jose and Jopet as hosts.

Article continues after this 

Meanwhile, recent social media posts claimed that Jose is the father of Vice President Sara Duterte’s lead defense counsel Sheila Sison.

However, Atty. Jose Sison, in his column, mentioned having an “only daughter” named Joyce.

In his column published by Philstar in 2012, Jose remembered the death anniversary of his daughter Joyce who died.

He wrote: “Tomorrow, our family will be commemorating one such event which happened nine years ago. This is the death anniversary of our beloved and only daughter Joyce.”

In another Philstar column published in 2024, Jose mentioned his six children namely Joyce, Jopet, Joel, Jay, Jolly and Jaybee. /apl

World.title: ‘Ex-NPA’ logistics officer nabbed in Bukidnon military intel compound
World.content:
CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — An alleged former logistics officer of the Maoist New People’s Army (NPA) wanted for murder was arrested inside a military intelligence compound in Malaybalay City, Bukidnon on Wednesday afternoon, July 22.

In a press statement, the Police Regional Office-10 (PRO-10) identified the suspect as Gemma Pensahan Tilucan, 32, who is wanted for murder and frustrated murder.

Article continues after this 

Tilucan, who is known by aliases Gina, Tata, Alex, Reps, and Jea, was apprehended inside the 43rd Military Intelligence Company compound in Barangay 10, Malaybalay City at 2:40 p.m., it said.

READ: Army uncovers 2 NPA arms caches in Surigao, Bukidnon

Lt. Col. Joe Patrick Martinez, 4th Infantry Division spokesman, told the Inquirer on Thursday that Tilucan was “a former NPA combatant” assigned to the logistics division of the Headquarters LOADER under the North Central Mindanao Regional Committee (NCMRC).

“We salute and congratulate all the brave units involved in this successful operation, especially our PNP (Philippine National Police) counterparts whose steadfast resolve ensures that justice will be served to the victims of these grave crimes,” Martinez said in a phone interview.

He added that through the seamless synergy between the 4th Infantry Division’s intelligence personnel and Bukidnon police units, the joint forces have delivered “overdue closure to the victims’ families.”

Article continues after this 

Martinez, however, did not elaborate why Tilucan was arrested inside a military compound.

“The Philippine Army remains proud to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the PNP in maintaining peace, safety, and justice across the region,” Martinez said.

Article continues after this 

Tilucan was arrested by virtue of warrants dated August 29, 2023. She faces frustrated murder (Criminal Case No. 41181-23) with a recommended bail of P200,000, and a separate non-bailable murder case (Criminal Case No. 41182-23).

She remains under the custody of the 43rd Military Intelligence Company in Malaybalay City. A motion for custody has been filed at the local prosecutor’s office for documentation and proper disposition.

Col. Oliver Navales, Bukidnon Police Provincial Director Police, reported the arrest to PRO-10 director Brig. Gen. Christopher Abrahano, who commended the responding personnel for a job well done.

World.title: Caap unveils air traffic simulators to train more aviation personnel
World.content:
Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (Caap).

MANILA, Philippines – The Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (Caap) on Thursday announced the inauguration of new air traffic control simulators that will be used in training aviation personnel as part of efforts to address the shortage of staff in regional airports.

In a statement, Caap said its new Aerodrome, Enroute, and Approach Simulators will help strengthen its Comprehensive Air Traffic Service Training Program by providing “highly realistic, scenario-based simulation training.”

“The Caap, especially the Air Traffic Service, have long wished for new and top-of-the-line simulators, and now, we see that their dream has come true. This is a world-class, state-of-the-art, top-of-the-line [simulator]—it is a market leader, so we can say we are no longer being left behind,” said CAAP Director General Raul del Rosario.

Article continues after this 

READ: Caap urges air travelers to follow dangerous goods regulations

Caap noted that its training program is “designed to replicate the different phases of an aircraft’s flight” and utilizes systems and tools that are used in actual air traffic control environments, allowing trainees to experience “realistic operational scenarios in a controlled setting.”

The new simulators, which cost P253 million, will help trainees develop skills such as “situational awareness, sound decision-making, effective coordination, precise communication, and management of complex traffic situations.”

“The simulators will likewise reduce reliance on live operational traffic as the primary training environment, providing a safer and more structured transition from classroom instruction to actual operations,” said Caap.

Del Rosario added that upgrading Caap’s training system will help improve aviation safety and address the shortage of air traffic controller personnel in regional airports, noting that many of them are choosing to leave the country for “lucrative jobs” overseas.

Article continues after this 

READ: CAAP told to lessen passenger service, airport navigation charges

In the same statement, Acting Transportation Secretary Giovanni Lopez explained that Caap provides free specialized air traffic training to students under its air traffic controller program.

Article continues after this 

Those who aspire to be air traffic management officers are also guaranteed to get employment in the country’s airports once they pass a qualifying exam, he added.

“Those who enter and want to train here, they do not pay any tuition fee to our government or Caap. They just need to finish their four-year course as well as a written exam and aptitude test,” said Lopez. /jpv

World.title: P5.5-M shabu, smuggled cigarettes seized in Lanao del Sur

COTABATO CITY — Some P5.5 million worth of suspected shabu (methamphetamine hydrochloride) and smuggled cigarettes were seized by the Police Regional Office–Bangsamoro Autonomous Region (PRO-BAR) in two separate law enforcement operations in Lanao del Sur on Wednesday, July 22.

Two suspects were arrested.

In a buy-bust operation conducted in Barangay Lalabuan, Balindong (Wato), authorities arrested a suspected drug pusher identified only by the alias “Khalid.”

READ: Search continues for 4 persons missing in Lanao del Sur landslide

“I commend our operating units for their swift coordination, professionalism, and unwavering dedication to law enforcement. This successful operation reflects our firm commitment to combating smuggling and other illegal activities,” Brig. Gen. Christopher Abecia, PRO-BAR director, said.
