Tech.title: People Are Getting Off to Porn About ICE Raids
Tech.content:
On July 8, X account @superioritymale posted an update about ICE’s ongoing crackdown on immigrants, describing the conditions being thrust upon detainees.

“Over 68,000 held in ICE detention centers around the United States, many of whom lack access to food, water, and any means to reach contact with their loved ones,” reads the post, which also includes a video. Only, the video wasn’t news footage from inside a detention center. It was a 14-second clip of a white man masturbating in a ski mask.

“Let me serve that cock massa,” replied @FreakedOut222.

Accounts like @superioritymale belong to a niche porn sphere on X where users project, and find sexual pleasure in, pro-MAGA messaging. Over the past two years under President Donald Trump’s second term, they appear to have become even more prevalent on the social media platform.

WIRED identified a dozen accounts, varying in reach and influence—some had tens of thousands of followers—but they all share a similar theme: the fantasy of white male domination. They promote the aesthetic of being a white god or alpha, post about “the natural order” and the “biological truth” white supremacy, while encouraging followers to claim their “birthright” as the ruling species.

The tone in many of the posts mirrors the extreme rhetoric often championed by the White House. In January, @malesupremacy13, whose bio reads “nazi-fascist” and “war is porn,” posted a list of “Things I jerk off to,” which included “Bombings of Gaza, LGBT rights being denied, gender inequality, [and] environment/plastic pollution.” In one video from last October, clips of white men engaging in various acts of straight and gay sex flicker like a highlight reel as Bruce Springsteen’s “Born in the USA” plays, and a giant text overlay in red, white, and blue reads: “JOIN ICE TODAY.” The X post, which implored followers to “HELP YOUR COUNTRY GET RID OF ILLEGAL CRIMINALS TODAY BRO,” included a link to ice.gov. (Springsteen has been one of Trump’s most vocal critics since entering office; while on tour in 2025 the singer said America was “in the hands of a corrupt, incompetent, and treasonous administration.”)

Tech.title: Google Turns a Selfie Video Into Your Account’s Spare Key
Tech.content:
Google has a new way for users to sign in to their accounts: a selfie video.

If you’ve ever lost your device and gotten locked out of your Google account, you know it can feel like a desperate, Kafkaesque process to recover access and get back in—especially for people who run their digital lives, from email messages to calendar appointments, on Google software. This new sign-in option is an additional way to unlock your Google account, like a spare key hidden in the bushes.

“We always recommend that you set up more than one option,” says Claire Forszt, a product manager at Google who focuses on identity and engagement. “Selfie is just the newest option in that list available for users. It's designed to help specifically in these vulnerable scenarios around not having access to the device where your passkey might be.” Additional sign-in options include using recovery contacts and backup codes.

I was able to set up my selfie video in less than five minutes, and the process was straightforward. Open your Google account and choose the Security & sign-in tab. Then scroll down to the How you sign in to Google section. If the selfie sign-in is currently available for your account, you’ll see it as a new option at the bottom. Google is in the process of rolling this out globally to most accounts.

Tech.title: Banning Social Media for Kids Is a Bad Idea
Tech.content:
It is clear that social media affects mental health and poses a danger to children and adolescents. One study showed it took just 40 minutes of browsing for a platform in Mexico to recommend content to a teenage girl that contains references to suicide.

What’s most concerning is that these aren’t isolated glitches but rather a result of how algorithms are designed to hook users and keep them on the platforms longer. With infinite scrolling and the instant gratification it provides, social media can become as addictive as cigarettes.

These factors, coupled with concerns about screen time and other worries, have led many countries to enact bans or restrictions on social media for kids. Last year, Australia became the first country to try to keep people under 16 off the apps. In June, the United Arab Emirates enacted a measure locking youth under 15 out of platforms like TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook, and X.

Just last week, the UK revealed a plan to institute a midnight social media curfew next spring for 16- and 17-year-olds—one they can opt out of. Prime Minister Keir Starmer said in June that he hoped to pass a more stringent ban on social media for under-16s “before Christmas.” Starmer formally resigned earlier this week, but the legislation is likely to proceed. On Tuesday, lawmakers in France passed a bill banning social media for anyone under 15. President Emmanuel Macron is expected to sign it into law.

However, something is happening that, at first glance, seems contradictory. Many of the organizations that have spent years researching these risks and defending children’s rights are not supporting such bans. On the contrary, they warn that disconnecting children from these spaces might address the symptoms but leave the root causes of the problem intact—and could even create new risks.

Australia’s measure was hailed internationally and held up as a model. Six months after its implementation, however, seven out of 10 parents reported that their children still have accounts on Instagram, TikTok, or Snapchat. This is not surprising. Not only because adolescence is typically a time of rebellion but also because it is natural to resist being excluded from spaces where a large part of their social life takes place and where the people they’ve grown up with are hanging out.

Kids These Days The youngs are facing problems that didn't even exist half a generation ago. They’re handling it better than you think.

Social media platforms are much more than just entertainment for young people, especially for those who grew up during the Covid-19 pandemic. Comparing them to cigarettes ignores the fact that they also serve important functions. They are spaces for socializing, learning, and accessing information that is often unavailable elsewhere, especially in places where educational gaps and disparities in access to public services persist. Generally speaking, how many times has Reddit saved us with an answer we couldn’t find in a textbook, at school, or at a public institution? And how many times has a YouTube tutorial or a thread on X taught us something that no one else explained to us?

Furthermore, social media can provide a sense of community and a space for self-expression to those who don’t always find it outside the internet. For teenagers who belong to historically marginalized groups—such as LGBTQ+ people, people of color, or people with disabilities—these spaces can also offer an opportunity to explore and build their identities with greater freedom, find role models, and feel less alone.

Precisely because social media is much more than just entertainment, it is worth asking whether some solutions might simply replace one harm with another. Age verification, for example, involves collecting highly sensitive data, making platforms more attractive to cybercriminals and putting the privacy and safety of minors at risk. This is not a hypothetical. When Discord implemented its age verification system in 2025, it suffered a data breach involving more than 70,000 identity documents.

Tech.title: Tesla Can’t Avoid Recall Fix for Cars With Overly Bright Headlights
Tech.content:
Drivers who’ve been blinded by the lights, it’s not just your imagination. There are cars on the road with headlights that are so bright they’re illegal.

Two years after Tesla informed the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration that low-beam headlights on some Tesla EVs exceed brightness limits, the company’s move to make those headlights street-legal has failed. The NHTSA denied Tesla’s petition to avoid a recall, meaning the company will need to issue a fix for nearly 20,000 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles from 2017 to 2023 for a problem the company called “inconsequential.”

A representative for Tesla didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tesla argued in its petition that because the bright lighting in question falls outside of the field of vision of oncoming drivers, “noncompliance is inconsequential as it relates to motor vehicle safety.”

In its response, NHTSA associate administrator for enforcement Eileen Sullivan wrote, “NHTSA disagrees with Tesla’s conclusion that there is no increased risk of glare for surrounding traffic or the driver of the subject vehicle in any driving conditions.”

The agency argued, citing public comment, that the headlights can still produce glare that could affect other drivers.

The group referenced a similar decision it made in 2022 involving GM Terrain vehicles.

For Tesla owners, the NHTSA ruling means the company must provide a free fix for the affected cars.

Additional steps are possible

The NHTSA isn’t commenting on pending legislation, including its denial of Tesla’s petition, but in an email to CNET, a spokesperson said that the organization is assessing studies about LED-headlamp glare and may take additional steps based on what it finds.

“Some issues may arise from the inappropriate use of high beams, illegal aftermarket lamps, improperly maintained lamps or misaligned lamps,” the spokesperson wrote.

Extra-bright headlights are illegal, and devices that don’t comply can be outlawed from sale on platforms like Amazon, while drivers using overbright headlights can face escalating fines, the suspension of their driver’s license or civil liability.

“Although headlight technology has changed over the years, NHTSA’s lighting standard has remained constant in limiting the amount of glaring light directed toward traffic both coming and going,” the spokesperson said.

SUVs, which sit taller on the road than sedans, have become the most popular vehicles in the US. That, combined with LEDs taking over as the prime technology for headlights, has led more people to notice that high-intensity low beams seem brighter and harder to avoid.

Some modern cars have benefited from adaptive lighting technologies that can adjust brightness, direction or lighting pattern as driving conditions change, but many cars on the road aren’t equipped with these systems.

Headlights in the congressional spotlight

Earlier this year, the US House of Representatives joined the discussion about bright headlights with the introduction of a bill from Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a Democrat from Washington state.

The LIGHT Safety Act would set maximum allowable brightness limits for low-beam headlamps on vehicles in the US. So far, the proposal has only been sent to committee, meaning it’s been assigned to a House panel for initial review, with no further action taken on it since March.

The bill seeks to revise existing federal standards by establishing a maximum allowable brightness for low beams.

Tech.title: I Test-Drove Substack’s New AI Detection Tool, and It Mostly Worked
Tech.content:
More and more, we want to know: Is it human, or is it AI? Is that image real? That song? That video? The publishing platform Substack is trying to add some clarity by partnering with the AI detector Pangram to help readers understand just how much AI is in all the content they consume on the publishing platform.

The tool is available to all Substack subscribers and works on posts, notes, comments and replies published on or after Tuesday that are longer than 100 words. Creators will also be able to scan their drafts with Pangram to see how much AI is detected and can also provide a statement to explain their writing process, Substack said.

Web and iOS users can try the Pangram features now, and Android users will get access later.

In a blog post announcing the new feature, Substack co-founder and CEO Chris Best said his platform aims to avoid “Claudefishing,” meaning when a reader consumes content without realizing it was generated by AI.

“When readers have to wonder if what they’re reading is real, it undermines trust in authorship and threatens the livelihood of writers — including those who use AI tools thoughtfully to produce work they believe in,” Best wrote.

From CNET: AI Slop Is Destroying the Internet. These Are the People Fighting to Save It

Pangram estimates that roughly 40% of text on some social media platforms is AI-generated, with a stunning two-thirds of that on the networking site LinkedIn. And AI growth agency Graphite recently published a white paper saying that AI is now writing as many online articles as humans. A Gartner survey found that 68% of people wonder if the content they see is real, and that half of consumers prefer brands that aren’t using AI in their marketing.

Testing it for myself

I’ve only recently joined Substack, but I wanted to check out the new Pangram AI detection tool. The tool works on posts, notes, comments and replies, so I decided to use posts as my makeshift testing lab. First, I logged in to my Substack account and published a new post. I copied and pasted text from an article I had written — by myself, no AI — into the Substack post and published it.

After a few minutes, I clicked on the live post. On the three-dot menu at the upper right of the page, I saw a “Scan for AI text” option. I clicked on it, and a small window popped up accurately declaring that my article was “Fully Human-Written.” A line appears below this that indicates the percentage of the text that is AI, AI-assisted, or human.

I next took the same post but added a long, fully AI-generated paragraph that I pasted from ChatGPT. When I performed the “Scan for AI text,” the tool reported that 10% of the article was written by AI, a roughly accurate estimate.

I next published a fully AI-generated post, and the scan correctly identified it as 100% AI-generated.

For another test, I added a couple of AI-generated sentences to a post that was otherwise purely human content, and the scan flagged it as 100% human-generated. Close, but not quite right. So, the Pangram tool worked pretty well for my crude experimentation.

How to use Pangram to detect AI content. Substack

Although I was fairly satisfied with how well Substack’s AI detection system worked on my own content, I was disappointed to learn that one of my favorite podcaster-bloggers apparently went full AI on his latest post. Other writers I checked out, however, used fully human-generated text.

What about false positives?

In his announcement, Best admitted that the AI detection tool is “not perfect,” but cited independent research that found Pangram’s software was 97.5% accurate in detecting fully generated AI text. The University of Maryland found that Pangram was 99.3% accurate in identifying “humanized AI-generated text,” which basically means a human has rewritten or paraphrased AI content.

Substack writers who do not use AI are understandably concerned about being incorrectly labeled as AI-assisted authors. As a result, the risk of false positives is a significant issue. Substack said creators can scan their content to see if it will be labeled as containing AI while it’s still in draft form. If Pangram incorrectly identifies AI text, the creator can report the error to Substack and have the false scan removed.

To promote greater transparency, publishers can now include a “How I make this” statement if they want readers to know how much, if any, AI they have used in their content. Best said Pangram can’t detect if AI was used to gather information or as a source for written pieces.

“We’re not against people using AI to assist their work, and we think people should be free to choose which tools they use to express themselves,” Best said. “But people should know what they’re getting.”

Tech.title: Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Is for Everyone Who Can’t Stop Scrolling
Tech.content:
Samsung has finally made a book-style foldable that’s geared less toward productivity and more toward entertainment. It seems the company has realized that some of us just want a better way to scroll and binge-watch.

The $1,900 Galaxy Z Fold 8 is Samsung’s new baseline book-style foldable, sitting between the $1,200 clamshell-style Z Flip 8 and the top-of-the-line $2,100 Z Fold 8 Ultra, which carries on the design of last year’s Z Fold 7. The phones debuted at the company’s Galaxy Unpacked event on Wednesday, and they’re available for preorder now before hitting shelves on Aug. 7.

With a 4:3 aspect ratio and a passport-sized design, the Z Fold 8 feels equally optimized for watching horizontal videos, multitasking in landscape mode and browsing vertically oriented apps in portrait mode. That versatility and compactness make the Z Fold 8 one of the most enjoyable phones I’ve used so far this year — though I still have some lingering questions I look forward to addressing in my full review.

The boldly reimagined Z Fold 8 arrives at a crucial time, as Apple reportedly gears up to launch its first foldable iPhone in the fall. Rumors suggest that device could also have a squarish 4:3 aspect ratio (similar to some iPad models), so this may well be Samsung’s attempt to stay ahead of the curve. And while Apple’s expected entry will mean fresh competition, Samsung has the advantage of several foldable generations — and years of consumer feedback — under its belt.

“This is Samsung going on the offensive,” Francisco Jeronimo, IDC’s vice president of client devices, said. “By bringing a wider, passport-style foldable to market ahead of Apple, Samsung gets to define the new format on its own terms rather than reacting to it later.”

He added, “With Apple’s announcement less than two months away, this is the first Unpacked where Samsung has to defend the category it created, and that’s why it cannot play it safe.”

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 takes up less space when closed than many other phones. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

What makes the Z Fold 8’s design different

I first got my hands on the Z Fold 8 during a visit to Samsung’s Korea headquarters last month, and I was eager to spend more time with it at this week’s Galaxy Unpacked event in London. The phone feels compact and palm-sized while folded. It’s a welcome break from the monotony of today’s smartphones, including Samsung’s other foldables, which haven’t changed much from last year’s models.

The Z Fold 8 fits snugly in my hand, giving the feel of a small pocket notebook you’d use to quickly jot down notes. It’s simply a fun phone to use because of its size and design. It’s not much thicker than the super-thin Z Fold 8 Ultra, measuring 4.5mm when open and 9.7mm when closed. It’s also the lightest Z Fold device, clocking in at 201 grams.

Samsung EVP Kihwan Kim told me the Z Fold 8 is “very well suited for people who really enjoy media and social networks.” He added that the company “collected a lot of feedback from different types of users” to better understand the needs of people who prioritize media consumption. I can see myself using the Z Fold 8 in landscape mode when watching a movie or browsing across multiple apps, and then rotating it vertically when I’m on Instagram or reading an ebook.

In portrait mode, the Z Fold 8 is great for scrolling through vertical social videos. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Customer feedback also led Samsung to make its new book-style foldables easier to open. That involved reducing tension on the hinge, which causes the phone to spring open. You won’t be able to unfold the Z Fold 8 partway, unlike the Z Fold 7, but it takes noticeably less force to pry it open.

One key spec hasn’t changed: The Z Fold 8 maintains an IP48 rating, meaning it can be submerged in up to 1.5 meters of water for 30 minutes and is protected against solid objects larger than 1mm, but not dust or sand. That aligns with most foldable phones, though last year’s Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold boasts an IP68 rating, which places its resistance to liquids and particles on par with premium non-folding phones.

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Display upgrades on the Galaxy Z Fold 8

The Z Fold 8 has a 5.5-inch cover screen and a 7.6-inch inside display. Both screens have an anti-reflective coating, which Samsung says can reduce glare up to 50%. Paired with a 3,000-nit peak brightness, it should be easier to use apps and watch shows, even in the bright outdoors. I noticed the reduced reflections even while filming the phones indoors ahead of Unpacked.

The Z Fold 8 uses a new display technology called Flex Titanium. It combines a titanium-alloy film with a titanium plate to create a thinner, more durable display structure that should better withstand drops and other impacts. I watched Samsung put those displays through their paces at its headquarters, offering some reassurance that the screen is designed to withstand everyday use and hundreds of thousands of folds.

Flex Titanium also reduces the display’s crease, a longtime sticking point with foldable phone critics. While I found the crease in last year’s Z Fold 7 to be negligible, the Z Fold 8’s is even harder to notice when using the phone. This could be yet another way Samsung is hoping to beat Apple to the punch, as rumors suggest the foldable iPhone could have a creaseless screen — which could also be made by Samsung Display.

The Z Fold 8’s 4:3 aspect ratio follows in the footsteps of other wider foldable phones like the Microsoft Surface Duo, the first Google Pixel Fold and the Huawei Pura X Max. Notably, the Galaxy Z TriFold also has a 4:3 aspect ratio, albeit with a more sprawling 10-inch main display. The Z Fold 8 reduces that into a more compact design that’s a better fit for people who don’t want to carry around a miniature laptop.

Still, it’ll be an adjustment for those of us who are used to bar-style phones. The Z Fold 7 was one of my favorite devices I reviewed last year because using the cover screen feels remarkably like holding a slab phone. I’m curious to see whether the Z Fold 8’s squareish cover screen will make me more inclined to unfold the phone and use the main display — something I didn’t do very often with the more conventional-feeling Z Fold 7.

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Battery life gets a boost on the Galaxy Z Fold 8

Samsung has equipped its foldable phones with a higher-capacity silicon-carbon battery. While the Z Fold 7 had a 4,400-mAh battery, which made it through the day but didn’t last much longer, the Z Fold 8 bumps that capacity up to 4,800 mAh. That should hopefully reduce the urge to anxiously check battery levels.

The Z Fold 8 also supports 45-watt wired charging, which Samsung says can get you from 0% to 63% battery in 30 minutes. That’s a notable upgrade from the 25-watt charging on the Z Fold 7, which was one of the phone’s weak points. The Z Fold 8 also supports 20-watt wireless charging, up from 15-watt charging last year. I look forward to testing these faster speeds, which are especially welcome given the high price tag.

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Cameras on the Galaxy Z Fold 8

One compromise you’ll make when opting for the Z Fold 8 over the Z Fold 8 Ultra is the more scaled-back camera system. The Z Fold 8 has just two rear cameras, a 50-megapixel wide-angle and a 50-megapixel ultrawide. There’s also a 10-megapixel selfie camera on the cover screen and another 10-megapixel camera on the inside screen.

That should be enough for most people, but the lack of a telephoto lens may leave some wanting more. I’m no professional photographer, but I do take a lot of photos, so I’m curious to see whether I’ll miss having a dedicated zoom lens. Hopefully, though, sensor cropping on 2x and 4x shots will feel like enough.

Photo Assist lets you enter a text prompt for how you want to change an image. I asked for sunnier skies. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

AI and processor on the Galaxy Z Fold 8

The Z Fold 8 has a handful of AI updates for the camera, including My FanCam. In videos you’ve shot with several people moving, like a ballet recital or a soccer match, you can choose one person for AI to track. You can also select the aspect ratio, so you can crop a horizontal video for posting on social platforms. It’s a fun feature, though video quality will be compromised as My FanCam zooms in on a subject.

As debuted in this year’s Galaxy S26 series, Photo Assist now lets you enter a text prompt for AI to alter an image to your liking. I tested this on a photo with cloudy skies, which I asked Galaxy AI to make sunny instead. I was impressed with how it even altered the shadows on the building below to better reflect this faux reality, though the brick detail became grainier. Unlike Generative Edit capabilities that let you erase someone in the background of a photo, this feature comes off as a bit more misleading, so I’m not sure I’ll ever really opt for it.

The Z Fold 8 is powered by a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip for Galaxy. That should make tapping into AI features, endlessly scrolling and multitasking a breeze.

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

A new foldable design at a critical time

Beyond its whimsical look, the Z Fold 8 underscores Samsung’s efforts to stay ahead in a category it’s dominated for years. But competition is heating up. Earlier this year, Motorola debuted its first book-style foldable, the Razr Fold.

Apple’s expected entry could give the foldable phones market an overall boost. In fact, global foldable phone shipments are expected to grow 21% year-over-year in 2026, according to Counterpoint Research. Samsung is projected to maintain the top spot with 32% share, compared to Apple’s anticipated 25% share. But the Korean phone-maker will have to keep innovating to maintain its lead, and the Z Fold 8 feels like a deliberate effort to stand out in an increasingly crowded space.

“Competition is good, actually,” Kim told me. “For the last seven generations, we’ve already experienced a lot of things [and received] a lot of feedback from users and the market, and we’ve evolved for those needs. … We’re pretty confident about what we’ve done.”

Now that I’ve spent some time getting a feel for the Z Fold 8, I’m eager to take it out into the real world to see how it fits into my media habits — and whether it pushes the foldable category forward.

Tech.title: Jimothy, the Viral Raccoon, Scurries Across Your Screen in Google Animation
Tech.content:
I live in Seattle, where we’ve always had our share of quirky local color.

If you’ve ever watched a home Seahawks game on Monday Night Football, you know about the Pike Place Market fish-throwing guys. There used to be a mystery vending machine in the Capitol Hill neighborhood that dispensed random drinks, and no one knew who stocked it. Outside of late-night bars and concerts, hot dog stands sell Seattle dogs, loaded with grilled onions and cream cheese (don’t knock it till you’ve tried it).

So, of course, Jimothy had to come from the Emerald City. Jimothy, the short-spined raccoon that went viral this month, is now a Google animation for the whole internet to enjoy. As of Wednesday, if you Google “Jimothy,” a cute little animated version of the raccoon races across your screen. A green paw icon also shows up, and you can click that to see Jimothy scurry again and again.

As of 3 p.m. PT, Jimothy has been summoned for his little Google run over 1.5 million times.

The raccoon hangs out in my neighborhood, Seattle’s Scandinavian-accented Ballard area. Local resident Kiana Hall told the Seattle Times she thought it was a cat: “I just have never seen any other animal like it.” She posted her video on Instagram and gave him the name because “he looked like a Jimothy.”

(Note: I can’t independently confirm Jimothy’s sex or gender.)



In addition to the Google animation, the National Bobblehead Hall of Fame and Museum, which I didn’t know existed, is making a Jimothy bobblehead. You can preorder it now for $30, with shipping in December, when Jimothy will almost surely be forgotten in favor of a newer viral phenomenon. Y’all remember Moo Deng?

The Seattle Mariners were joking around on X, pretending that Jimothy was at their batting practice, but then the team got real and put a raccoon-suited person in their regular ballpark salmon race. Jimothy won, and the crowd went wild.

There’s more: On July 26, my neighborhood is celebrating the goofy little Jimothy with a proclamation in his honor and an art competition.

And Oatmeal cartoonist Matthew Inman, a Seattle-area resident, drew a “police sketch of Jimothy in case the cops need it.” (Why would they? Who would narc on Jimothy, and for what?)

Jimothy appears to have a rare disorder called short spine syndrome, which accounts for his hunched-up, cartoon-like appearance. Essentially, he looks like he has no neck. A veterinary professor told the Seattle Times that he appears to be functioning well and is “very spry.”

Another neighbor, Ben Trammell, dug out some video he found of Baby Jimothy with what appears to be Mom and Dad Jimothy, and posted it on Instagram.

“We saw Jimothy … almost daily for months,” Trammell wrote. “He was so small and clumsy, but his mother and siblings were always so patient and caring, keeping him from falling and sometimes just carrying him.”

I know the part of my neighborhood Jimothy hangs out in, but I refuse to head over there and stalk the poor guy. It’s rare that we get a solidly good thing to focus on in this messed-up world, and I would hate to hear that people were messing with Jimothy.

Let the nation’s newest furry friend hang out unbothered, foraging for Dick’s cheeseburger wrappers in trash cans and savoring Seattle’s perfect summer temperatures.

If I need my Jimothy fix, I can just run his Google animation again. Stay safe, little buddy.

Tech.title: Samsung’s Foldables Got Pricier. The RAM Shortage Is Part of the Bill
Tech.content:
Samsung’s latest foldables bring upgrades over last year’s models — including a new wider-screen device — but they also carry the industry’s favorite trend: higher prices.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Z Flip 8 each cost $100 more than last year’s Z Fold 7 and Z Flip 7, while the brand-new, confusingly named Galaxy Z Fold 8, lands between them in price. Foldables have always sat at the top of the smartphone price ladder, and none of Samsung’s new ones are bucking that trend. Raising prices on some of the most expensive phones you can buy only pushes them further into niche territory.

Samsung said the higher prices reflect increased memory and component costs, which have affected phones, PCs and other products across the tech industry. The company also pointed to improvements over last year’s devices, including the new Titanium Flex displays, larger batteries and better 50-megapixel ultra-wide cameras on the Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra.

That pricing pressure isn’t unique to Samsung. Nearly every 2026 phone has either cost more than its predecessor or arrived with so few upgrades that the price stayed flat, and Samsung’s foldables are also facing similarly pricier competition from Motorola’s Razr lineup.

The bigger picture is the RAM shortage, fueled in large part by the AI boom, which has driven memory prices sharply higher and left manufacturers with a choice: raise prices or cut specs. The explosive demand for AI data centers and models has pushed chipmakers to prioritize high-bandwidth memory for AI workloads, leaving less capacity for standard DRAM and NAND used in phones and PCs. Tariffs and other costs may be adding to the squeeze, but AI-driven memory demand is the main culprit behind the broader run-up in phone prices.



Outer screens of the folded-up Galaxy Z Fold 8 (left) and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra (right). Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Prices of Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Galaxy Z Flip 8

The Galaxy Z Fold 8, Samsung’s newest foldable, is the company’s new entry-level book-style foldable. In addition to its wider, shorter format that unfolds to reveal an inner 4:3-screen, the device lacks a handful of features of its more premium sibling. The Z Fold 8 starts at $1,900 for 256GB of storage, goes up to $2,100 for 512GB, and reaches $2,500 for 1TB.

256GB 512GB 1TB Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 $1,900 $2,100 $2,500

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, in comparison, is a taller book-style foldable with slightly more premium features — namely, a 10-megapixel telephoto camera and a large 5,000-mAh battery. It starts at $2,100 for 256GB of storage, then goes up to $2,300 for 512GB and tops out at a staggering $2,700.

256GB 512GB 1TB Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra $2,100 $2,300 $2,700

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 is the newest clamshell foldable from Samsung and has minor improvements over its predecessor: it’s lighter, has a slightly thinner design, and, like Samsung’s other foldables released alongside it, runs on Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip. It starts at $1,200 for 256GB and rises to $1,400 for 512GB.

256GB 512GB Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 $1,200 $1,400

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 in pink, cream and graphite colors. A mint color is also available as an online exclusive. Joseph Maldonado/CNET

Colors for Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Galaxy Z Flip 8

The new wider-format Galaxy Z Fold 8 debuts with colors in lavender, graphite and cream, with a pistachio hue exclusive to Samsung’s online store.

The slightly more premium Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s colors are violet shadow and graphite cream, with a green shadow hue as an online-only exclusive to Samsung’s store.



The clamshell Galaxy Z Flip 8 colors are pink, graphite and cream, with mint as an exclusive to Samsung’s online store.

Tech.title: Original Xbox Games Are Coming to PC Starting With 4 Fan Favorites
Tech.content:
Four classic Xbox games are heading to PC as part of a new program from Microsoft. These older titles, which are currently available on Xbox Game Pass, will now be playable on desktops, laptops and handhelds such as the ROG Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X.

On Wednesday, the Xbox Backward Compatibility preview went live, allowing owners of four titles first released for the original Xbox – Blinx: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge and Fuzion Frenzy – to play them on their Windows PC and handhelds. Microsoft says it will roll out more features for these games in the future, including Xbox Achievements.

Microsoft

The four games may be more than 20 years old, but Microsoft did add some options to improve the gaming experience. Players can change the graphics settings, including up to 4x resolution upscaling, VSync support, display mode options, anisotropic filtering, enhanced anti-aliasing and more customizations to improve the look of these older titles.

Each game is available for $10 on the Xbox Store, and once owned on Xbox, it can be played on PC or handhelds via Xbox Play Anywhere or streamed with Xbox Cloud Gaming. The titles are also available on Xbox Game Pass.

To play these games on a desktop, laptop or handheld, it must meet certain hardware specs:

Minimum system requirements:

GPU: Nvidia GTX 950 or AMD Radeon RX 550 or Intel UHD 770 or Intel Arc A310

Nvidia GTX 950 or AMD Radeon RX 550 or Intel UHD 770 or Intel Arc A310 CPU : Min 4 Cores Intel Core i3-8100 or AMD Ryzen 3 1200 or AMD Ryzen Z2 A Processor

: Min 4 Cores Intel Core i3-8100 or AMD Ryzen 3 1200 or AMD Ryzen Z2 A Processor RAM: 8GB

8GB OS: Windows 11

Windows 11 Drivers and Versions: Latest Version as of January 2026

Recommended specifications:

GPU : Radeon RX 68005 or Nvidia GTX 1070 Ti or Intel Arc A770

: Radeon RX 68005 or Nvidia GTX 1070 Ti or Intel Arc A770 CPU : 6 cores and 12 threads Intel Core i5-10400 or AMD Ryzen 5 3600 or AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme

: 6 cores and 12 threads Intel Core i5-10400 or AMD Ryzen 5 3600 or AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme DirectX Version : DirectX12 API, Hardware Feature Level 11

: DirectX12 API, Hardware Feature Level 11 GPU VRAM: 8GB

8GB OS : Windows 11

: Windows 11 Drivers and Versions: Latest Version as of January 2026

Microsoft says the Xbox Backward Compatibility program is a form of game preservation, which has become a concern for gamers. With Sony announcing it will phase out physical discs and Nintendo’s Game-Key Cards that don’t contain the actual games, many worry that game ownership will become entirely dependent on publishers rather than having a physical medium to hold onto. There is a growing number of delisted games that are no longer available to those who purchased them, and with the future of gaming looking increasingly uncertain because of the current memory shortage, many fear their digital game collections could simply disappear from their accounts.
